The breakpoint (chow test ) is here <a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/aC6Tk.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/aC6Tk.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a> An analysis of the last 44 values led to this equation <a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/UHRiO.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/UHRiO.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a> (1,1,0) with three pulses , The statistics of the model are here <a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/JvqII.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/JvqII.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a> and here <a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/22WRV.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/22WRV.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a> . The acf of the residuals somewhat suggests randomness <a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/F0mGH.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/F0mGH.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a> with the residual plot here <a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/mQiBY.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/mQiBY.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a> . The actual/fit/forecast is here<a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/rP5sl.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/rP5sl.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a> with forecasts here <a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/kjSVM.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/kjSVM.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a> . The whole idea is that sometimes parameters and or error variance change over time. One shouldn't simply model all the data as if it were homogeneous as the composite/global parameters may not be uniformly representative due to an exogenous (i.e.unknown) factor. You could say that two sets of parameters .. one for the first 29 and one for the last 47 is a kind of nonlinearity as was (partly) suggested here. This is one of the possible \"elephants in the room\" that nobody talks about but I do.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2016-01-22T01:22:15.463000", "posts_rownum": "posts_134804", "provsql": "6db8860d-80a5-4c13-8c4c-720729c50153"}, "posts_150362": {"id": 218418, "owneruserid": 119633, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 218493, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Comparing RMSE to model", "tags": "<logistic><poisson-distribution><rms>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm assessing the accuracy of the prediction of my model using the RMSE on a new data set. Or should I compare the RMSE of the model on the 'train' data to the RMSE of the 'test' data?</p>\n\n<p>The model that I'm currently using is the best with all my available predictors based on BIC scores, but I'm trying to figure out how well the model actually does. I've also calculated the adj. R-square, which says that 20.7% of the variance is explained by my model, but I doubt whether this is a good accuracy measurement.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2016-06-11T09:32:23.490000", "posts_rownum": "posts_150362", "provsql": "ca784856-abae-4d3d-99e9-222b392761e1"}, "posts_155930": {"id": 227119, "owneruserid": 125522, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 227107, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>The rules for choosing the shape parameters (hyperparameters) are those rules that apply to any prior choice: choose them in such a way that the prior distribution reflects your prior knowledge.</p>\n\n<p>If your prior knowledge says that most of the prior probability should be concentrated around 75%-85% with mode at 80%, then you could choose the hyperparameters $Beta(800,200)$, which has mode at $\\approx 0.8$ and cumulates $99.9\\%$ of the mass in the interval $(0.75,0.85)$.</p>\n\n<p>The choice of the Jeffreys priors is completely different since it is based on a formal criterion to produce a noninformative prior.</p>\n\n<p><strong>Comment:</strong> The use of \"confidence interval\" in the R package <code>binom</code> is rather unfortunate in this case since they actually calculate posterior <em>credible intervals</em> based on the beta prior which happen to have good frequentist properties. See: <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_proportion_confidence_interval\" rel=\"nofollow\">https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_proportion_confidence_interval</a></p>\n", "creationdate": "2016-08-03T16:53:49.513000", "posts_rownum": "posts_155930", "provsql": "caa8657b-d63f-477c-9014-70096331895c"}, "posts_253928": {"id": 383512, "owneruserid": 209540, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 383359, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I figured out the issue, kjentil b halvorsen pointed me in the correct direction. As I mentioned in the comment this makes forecasting slightly difficult but I'll make the assumption that if next years holidays are the same as this years (I think what's happening is the owners have updates the control system, programming holidays in so aircon / lighting etc is now shutting down but it wasn't in the past)</p>\n", "creationdate": "2018-12-18T02:41:45.383000", "posts_rownum": "posts_253928", "provsql": "7bc9ef89-615f-42ad-b046-3c680d9d7eaa"}, "posts_160782": {"id": 235025, "owneruserid": 131090, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 129703, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Ludbrook clarifies the evolution of analysis of 2x2 tables including the problems and improvements; see  Int. (2008) 37 (6): 1430-1435. doi: 10.1093/ije/dyn162  found at <a href=\"http://ije.oxfordjournals.org/content/37/6/1430.short\" rel=\"nofollow\">http://ije.oxfordjournals.org/content/37/6/1430.short</a></p>\n\n<p>Citing is open to your intent, so be careful.  Choose an original publication to honor precedence - the first mention in print (1900), or how the testing is viewed today in a more professionally acceptable form. These are not the same and you should be clear in what you write which is being cited.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2016-09-14T20:08:40.113000", "posts_rownum": "posts_160782", "provsql": "1b64ed11-3dd9-42e9-acfa-44d19fc2a4eb"}, "posts_177650": {"id": 259772, "owneruserid": 17147, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 259934, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to analyze random variables with non normal distribution", "tags": "<regression><t-test><nonparametric><law-of-large-numbers><truncated-normal-distribution>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm wondering how random variables can be analyzed using parametric methods if the distribution is not normal.  </p>\n\n<p>For example if a variable Y is normal distributed but I'm interested only on values Y2 which are lower than a certain limit due to agreement.     </p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/K1srT.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/K1srT.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a></p>\n\n<p>Can I use the common statistical tools to compute estimation, standard deviation, standard errors and P-values if the sample is large? </p>\n\n<p>To clarify my question I created the following theoretical population:</p>\n\n<pre><code># 100,000 values with mean 300 and sd = 50\nset.seed(1234)\nn <- 100000\ny <- rnorm(n,300,50)\n\n# Only y < 300 are of interest\ny2 <- y[y<300]\nlength(y2)     # [1] 49,828\n\npar(mfrow=c(2,1))\nhist(y, breaks=seq(0,max(y)+10,10))\nhist(y2, breaks=seq(0,max(y)+10,10))\n\n# mean and sd of y\nmean(y)        # 300.1465\nmedian(y)      # 300.2244\nsd(y)          # 49.97292\n\n# mean and sd of the interested values (y2)\nmean(y2)       # 260.1354\nmedian(y2)     # 266.3348\nsd(y2)         # 30.04559\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Now, I make an experiment. I take a sample of $s=100$: </p>\n\n<pre><code># Experiment:\ny.exp <- sample(y,s)\n\n# Only y<300 are of interest (for example due to a game rule)\ny.int <- y.exp[y.exp<300]\nmean(y.int)     # 259.3562\nsd(y.int)       # 32.56482\nlength(y.int)   # 38\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>I'm interest in the following hypothesis:<br>\n$H_0: \\mu_0 = 250$<br>\n$H_{alt}: \\mu_0 \\ne 250$</p>\n\n<p>Assuming that the sample is large enough I do a t-test:</p>\n\n<pre><code># t-test:\nmu0 <- 250\nt.test(y.int,mu=mu0)  # t = 1.7711, df = 37, p-value = 0.08478\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Here are my questions:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>If a sample size is large enough can I use the common statistical tools\nlike t-test, linear regression, etc. (maybe supported by the law of large numbers)?</li>\n<li>Are there alternative methods which consider special distributions (like this truncated\nnormal distribution). <em>I know there are non-parametric methods or truncated regression.\nI'm interested in parametric methods. Truncated regression answer another question:\nwhat is it the mean value of the normal distribution if the data a truncated. I'm interested\nin the mean value of the truncated data.</em></li>\n<li>Does standard deviation makes sense if the underlying distribution is not normal?</li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2017-02-03T10:24:59.923000", "posts_rownum": "posts_177650", "provsql": "80c4f2fa-c94d-4bd6-83ed-73fddd57fccb"}, "posts_178734": {"id": 261475, "owneruserid": 148969, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Explaining Stochastic Gradient Descent In Simple Terms", "tags": "<neural-networks><deep-learning><gradient-descent>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>This year I am doing a science fair project that involves deep learning and neural networks. When I write my report and present my project, I want to do so in very simple terms so that my teachers or classmates, who know absolutely nothing about neural networks, can understand. How can I explain Stochastic Gradient Descent and parameter updates in a way anyone could understand?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-02-12T16:40:58.070000", "posts_rownum": "posts_178734", "provsql": "8b0efea2-52c3-4a74-82f4-c8250a3a6d28"}, "posts_182293": {"id": 266830, "owneruserid": 152664, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 266821, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I don't know what software you're using, but you might draw several samples (of the same size as your data) from an actual normal distribution, make a Q-Q plot for each sample, and compare this ensemble to the Q-Q plot of your data. I think you'll see that the edge effects are normal (no pun intended) because of the small number of values that come from the tails of the distribution.</p>\n\n<p>There are also formal tests for normality, such as Anderson-Darling.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-03-11T11:08:58.283000", "posts_rownum": "posts_182293", "provsql": "d6330d0f-07a2-4b3f-be51-b880586e4bdf"}, "posts_186044": {"id": 272512, "owneruserid": 155637, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 272550, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Multiple seasonal time-series : interpret tbats.components() function results in R", "tags": "<r><time-series><forecasting><multiple-seasonalities><tbats>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm using the <code>TBATS</code> model of the forecast package with Google Analytics data, to forecast web trafic containing multiseasonal effects (<code>msts</code>). </p>\n\n<p>I have two year of daily data that contains two columns like these :</p>\n\n<pre><code>date           sessions\n2015-01-01     2667\n2015-01-02     3542\n2015-01-03     2383\n2015-01-04     2772\n2015-01-05     7797\n2015-01-06     7599\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>I made one forecast for all my data and another forecast with data containing only a segment of users.</p>\n\n<p>In the first case (<strong>all data</strong>), I obtained this result :</p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/xibD3.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/xibD3.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a></p>\n\n<p>And in the second case (<strong>segment data</strong>), I obtained this :</p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/BjlQS.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/BjlQS.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a></p>\n\n<p><strong>My questions</strong> :</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>How to interpret the slope component? I get it in the first case but not in the second. Is there a reason for that?</li>\n<li>What could do that the Lo/Hi points are so much wider in the second case?</li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2017-04-07T16:58:45.423000", "posts_rownum": "posts_186044", "provsql": "bda615b7-e6e3-40dd-88e6-57dfc1ec55b1"}, "posts_186956": {"id": 273990, "owneruserid": 43625, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 273755, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm taking your word for Naive Bayes' popularity here as language processing isn't my specialty: </p>\n\n<p>One reason NB is useful is the bias–variance tradeoff. Spam/sentiment type data are often noisy and usually high-dimensional (more predictors than samples, $n \\ll p$). The naive assumption that predictors are independent of one another is a strong, high-bias, one.</p>\n\n<p>By assuming independence of predictors we're saying that covariance matrix of our model only has non-zero entries on the diagonal. Since estimating covariance structure in $n \\ll p$ situations is very hard indeed we are usually forced to put some constraints on the problem. The independence assumption is a particularly strong constraint that yields a highly interpretable model. The introduced bias may sufficiently reduce variance that you get better predictions.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-04-16T10:31:36.517000", "posts_rownum": "posts_186956", "provsql": "b5b51bfe-8477-45a2-9a3f-e5ea3b6f927a"}, "posts_196402": {"id": 288492, "owneruserid": 8336, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 288491, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>If you can convince yourself that \n$$\n\\max(X,Y) \\overset{d}{=} -\\min(X,Y),\n$$ \nthen taking the variance on both sides will give you your answer.</p>\n\n<p>Regarding the other part, you'll probably have to integrate by hand.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-07-03T00:56:37.317000", "posts_rownum": "posts_196402", "provsql": "b98bf1ab-5a82-4687-933b-3d7787efa4b7"}, "posts_197194": {"id": 290725, "owneruserid": 115441, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Understanding hypothesis testing-compare two series", "tags": "<hypothesis-testing><statistical-significance><p-value>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>This is rather simple, but am always confused so perhaps somebody can explain me once for all. \nI have two sets of observations coming from two sources that I want to compare, say $e_1$ and $e_2$ both having $N$ points. Three things could happen: </p>\n\n<p>i) $e_1$ is consistently larger than $e_2$, \nii) $e_1$ is consistently smaller than $e_2$, \niii) there is no significant difference between $e_1$ and $e_2$.</p>\n\n<p>I compute the difference in the two series, $e_1 - e_2$, create a test statistic. This could be for example the mean of  $e_1 - e_2$ divided by the standard deviation of  $e_1 - e_2$ (divided by square root of $N$), or it could be another test statistic. If I wanted to do the Diebold-Mariano test it would be another test statistic. But the point is I get some test statistic. I don't know how to interpret this statistic. </p>\n\n<p>I know I need to compare it against say the extreme value of a $T$ distribution or Normal distribution. But know my test statistic could be >1.96, <-1.96, or between -1.96 and 1.96. Help me understand how to interpret the three cases to answer the question- which is consistently larger, $e_1$ or $e_2$.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-07-10T09:28:31.030000", "posts_rownum": "posts_197194", "provsql": "d26cdd8a-d108-4d9a-8a84-94fdaa485eb0"}, "posts_199832": {"id": 295887, "owneruserid": 98672, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Time normalisation for time series using sliding window", "tags": "<time-series><normalization><finance><cross-correlation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>As part of my research into eigenvalue dynamics of financial time series I am reading a <a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.0497\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">paper</a> which introduces the idea of time series normalisation between stocks before computing the zero-lag cross-correlation.</p>\n\n<p>The formula provide is as follows:</p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/NwAPp.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/NwAPp.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a></p>\n\n<p>where Ri(t) is the stock returns for 1...N stocks and Ri(t).bar is the time average of Ri over a time window of size T and sigma i is the standard deviation of stock i=1...N.</p>\n\n<p>How I am reading this formula is, at time t=10 I take the value of stock i and subtract the average value over the last 10 time periods and divide by the standard deviation for the entire time period, have I got this right? Should I expect a value between 1 and -1 or could my normalised value be greater than these ranges? </p>\n\n<p>I have seen in <a href=\"https://arxiv.org/pdf/cond-mat/0108023.pdf\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">other literature</a> I've see slightly different notation, rather than R's they use G's to denote gain. I've also read about range normalisation between 0 and 1 <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/70801/how-to-normalize-data-to-0-1-range\">here</a> but i am not sure if this is the same approach. </p>\n\n<p>I would be really  gratefully if anyone could help me better understand this approach. And apologies for all the pics and poor syntax, I'm not familiar with inserting mathematical notation in these posts.</p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/xwouJ.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/xwouJ.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a></p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/ni90H.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/ni90H.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a></p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-08-02T19:09:17.550000", "posts_rownum": "posts_199832", "provsql": "3b8a9f62-4085-468a-8604-85d6b0253bba"}, "posts_204668": {"id": 303321, "owneruserid": 101426, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 303177, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>The gold standard way to do this sort of random allocation when you are allocating people or groups of people (units) to treatment arms proceeds like this.</p>\n\n<p>1 - form the units to be randomised into strata based on the relevant variables (in your case you mention just one). Make the sizes of the stratum a multiple of the number of arms to which you wish to allocate (in your case this is four) but not all the same size, so some 8, some 12, some 16 and so on..</p>\n\n<p>2 - now for each stratum draw a sample without replacement so you get exactly equal numbers of each arm (so 2 of each for stratum size 8, 3 for 12, 4 for 16). Search for permuted blocks if that needs more detail.</p>\n\n<p>The reason for having a variable block size is to stop people being able to guess which is going to come next as after seven have been allocated from a block of size eight they know which is left if they have been counting. In your application it may not be so necessary to conceal the allocation from the units so you can use the same size stratum throughout. You could even use size four which is what I think you suggest in your question.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-09-15T13:40:06.870000", "posts_rownum": "posts_204668", "provsql": "42c3fae8-7704-4dbd-a83a-dff9a7f87f12"}, "posts_220002": {"id": 327210, "owneruserid": 14188, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 248045, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>This started as a comment, but went long. I don't think a random effects model is appropriate here. There are only 3 ponds -- do you want to estimate a variance from 3 numbers? That's kinda what's going with a random effects model. I'm guessing the ponds were chosen by reason of their convenience to the researcher, and not as a random sample of \"Ponds of the Americas\". </p>\n\n<p>The advantage of a random effects model is that it allows you to construct a confidence interval on the response (activity level) that takes pond to pond variation into account. A fixed effects model -- in other words, treating pond like a block -- adjusts the response for the pond effect. If there were some addidtional treatment effect -- say two species of frog in each pond -- blocking reduces the mean square error (denominator of the F test) and allows the effect of the treatment to shine forth.</p>\n\n<p>In this example, there is no treatment effect and the number of ponds is too small for a random effects model (and probably too \"non-random\"), so I'm not sure what conclusions can be drawn from this study. One could get a nice estimate of the difference between the ponds, but that's about it. I don't see inferences being drawn to the wider population of frogs in other pond settings. One could frame it as a pilot study, I suppose. </p>\n\n<p>Bear in mind that any use of a random effects model here is going to give a very unreliable estimate for the pond variance and must be Used With Caution.</p>\n\n<p>But as to your original question -- isn't this more of a rate problem? The go-to distribution for events-per-unit-time is the Poisson. So you could do Poisson regression using the counts with the time interval as an offset. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2018-02-06T20:27:07.063000", "posts_rownum": "posts_220002", "provsql": "95dd1d8b-068f-4f5c-a4fa-0024140353ed"}, "posts_369446": {"id": 565551, "owneruserid": 348492, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 565537, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>In general, there is no good reason. Grouping the data as you describe means that some information is being thrown away, and that can't be a good thing.</p>\n<p>The reason you see people do this is probably out of practical convenience. Libraries for classification might be more common and easily accessible, and they also automatically provide answers that are in the correct range (while regression for example can output negative values etc.).</p>\n<p>One slightly better motivation I can think of is that the typical outputs of  classification algorithms can be interpreted as class probabilities, which can provide a measure of uncertainty on the result (for example, you can read a result as giving 40% probability for the range 10-20, 50% for the range 20-30 etc.). Of course regression models can in general provide uncertainty estimates as well, but it is a feature that is lacking in many standard tool and is not "automatic" as in the classification case.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2022-02-23T17:12:06.963000", "posts_rownum": "posts_369446", "provsql": "6aab8213-8580-4336-871e-0f727af4be45"}, "posts_243207": {"id": 365051, "owneruserid": 176202, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 364974, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I think this approach is wrong and an example of the <a href=\"https://meta.stackexchange.com/questions/66377/what-is-the-xy-problem\">XY-problem</a>. </p>\n\n<p>As suggested by the name (and confirmed by the link you included), these data are a time-series. Modelling these without accounting for the covariance structure violates the <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_regression#Assumptions\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">independence of observations</a> of ordinary linear regression. It is therefore no surprise that the diagnostic plot looks strange. However, trying to fix it will not fix the underlying problem.</p>\n\n<p>Instead, you could model these data with an <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autoregressive_integrated_moving_average\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">autoregressive model</a>, or a <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_model\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">mixed model</a> with an appropriate covariance structure.</p>\n\n<p>You may also want to have a look at the <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/tagged/time-series\">time-series tag</a>.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2018-09-02T09:49:32.877000", "posts_rownum": "posts_243207", "provsql": "48b2c03e-53e6-4d9f-96e7-d04aadbd84e6"}, "posts_248825": {"id": 373613, "owneruserid": 61518, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 373612, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>If I am understanding you correctly, you wish to see if the proportion of 1's in your data is significantly different from .5. You can calculate the sample proportion, say, <span class=\"math-container\">$\\hat{p}=\\frac{\\# \\ of \\ 1}{N}$</span>. You can then calculate a <span class=\"math-container\">$z$</span>-statistic: <span class=\"math-container\">$z=\\frac{\\hat{p}-p_0}{\\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{N}}$</span> where <span class=\"math-container\">$p_0=.5$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$N$</span> is your total sample size. Then you can calculate a <span class=\"math-container\">$p$</span> value given the <span class=\"math-container\">$z$</span> statistics and conclude statistical significance or lack thereof.</p>\n\n<p>This can be done for each type of stimuli. If the stimulus are independent of each other and the order is randomized, a Bonferroni correction can be applied: you should compare your <span class=\"math-container\">$p$</span> value to <span class=\"math-container\">$\\frac{\\alpha}{ \\# \\ of \\ stimulus}$</span>, e.g., you have 4 different types and your overall significance level is .05, then you should compare your <span class=\"math-container\">$p$</span> values to .0125.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2018-10-24T18:37:49.890000", "posts_rownum": "posts_248825", "provsql": "bbf2244a-2a5f-4595-93d7-2931a8843739"}, "posts_251384": {"id": 377726, "owneruserid": 1352, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 377723, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Note first of all that your plot does not come from a call to <code>auto.arima()</code>, but from one to <code>arima()</code>. There is a difference. </p>\n\n<p>By supplying <code>order=c(0,1,0)</code> to <code>arima()</code>, you tell it to fit a model of the following type:</p>\n\n<p><span class=\"math-container\">$$ y_t-y_{t-1} = \\epsilon_t, $$</span></p>\n\n<p>or</p>\n\n<p><span class=\"math-container\">$$ y_t=y_{t-1} + \\epsilon_t. $$</span></p>\n\n<p>That is, you believe that the <em>increments</em> over the last observation follow a normal distribution, <span class=\"math-container\">$\\epsilon_t\\sim N(0,\\sigma^2)$</span>.</p>\n\n<p>For your point forecast, <code>forecast()</code> will use the expected value for <span class=\"math-container\">$\\epsilon_t$</span>. Which is zero. So your next forecast is simply the last observation:</p>\n\n<p><span class=\"math-container\">$$ \\hat{y}_t=y_{t-1}. $$</span></p>\n\n<p>And this is iterated. You end up with a flat line.</p>\n\n<p>Try actually fitting using <code>auto.arima()</code>. However, your time series does not exhibit any obvious structure, like trend or seasonality. (Autoregressive or moving average behavior are harder to spot by eye.) In such a situation, a flat line may well be the best forecast: <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/q/124955/1352\">Is it unusual for the MEAN to outperform ARIMA?</a></p>\n\n<p>You may be interested in the excellent free online book <a href=\"https://otexts.org/fpp2/\" rel=\"noreferrer\"><em>Forecasting: Principles and Practice</em> (2nd ed.) by Athanasopoulos & Hyndman</a>.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2018-11-19T07:08:58.510000", "posts_rownum": "posts_251384", "provsql": "3b279279-a345-42ef-99b5-c78d3cf27b7c"}, "posts_259237": {"id": 390274, "owneruserid": 204068, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 390262, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<blockquote>\n  <p>where exactly would the operations for apply filters/averaging take\n  place? During the weights section or the [conv. layer / max-pooling]\n  section itself</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>Weights actually belong to filters, i.e. the convolutional layer. Pooling occur afterwards and doesn't relate to the weights. </p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>Assuming the inputs take in a 28 * 28 pixel, how would I take a 2 * 2\n  filter and change the original matrix, would I have to split the\n  inputs into 2 * 2 chunks and recombine them?</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>You <a href=\"https://www.wikiwand.com/en/Multidimensional_discrete_convolution\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">convolve</a> the input image and the filter. You can convolve different sized images (signals), no need to split the larger one into smaller chunks. This step sometimes can slightly differ from the usual convolution, in which zero-padding can be used, or reversal of filter (which isn't important in learning) is not performed etc.</p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>If I wanted to perform max-pooling on the same inputs would I also\n  have to also split the image into 2x2 chunks to downscale the image\n  and add all of those little chunks together to form a new matrix?</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>After the conv. layer, you divide the image into 2x2 non-overlapping chunks, choose the max amongst the 4 pixels, and form a new image. Yes, this is a form of downscaling, but not in the usual sense in signal processing, where you apply, for example, low-pass filters and subsample.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2019-02-01T08:13:51.790000", "posts_rownum": "posts_259237", "provsql": "45c77bc7-2842-402a-8e03-7f512793991b"}, "posts_279022": {"id": 419929, "owneruserid": 805, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 419881, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Let <span class=\"math-container\">$X,Y$</span> have some joint distribution, such that some <span class=\"math-container\">$Z=t(X,Y)$</span> has a known (fully specified) continuous distribution. Let <span class=\"math-container\">$F_Z$</span> be the cdf of <span class=\"math-container\">$Z$</span>. Let  <span class=\"math-container\">$G_0$</span> be the cdf of a standard Gumbel.</p>\n\n<p>Then <span class=\"math-container\">$f_{0}(X,Y) = G_0^{-1}(F_Z(t(X,Y)))$</span> has a standard Gumbel distribution. Any other Gumbel may be obtained by considering <span class=\"math-container\">$f_{\\alpha,\\tau}(X,Y) = \\alpha+\\tau G_0^{-1}(F_Z(t(X,Y)))$</span>.</p>\n\n<p>Thus we can construct any number of examples with ease.</p>\n\n<p>For example, let <span class=\"math-container\">$X$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$Y$</span> be independent standard normals, let <span class=\"math-container\">$\\Phi$</span> be the standard normal cdf. Then <span class=\"math-container\">$G_0^{-1}(\\Phi(\\frac{X+Y}{\\sqrt{2}}))$</span> will be standard Gumbel.</p>\n\n<p>Note that <span class=\"math-container\">$G_0^{-1}(u) = -\\log(-\\log(u))$</span> is very simple in form.</p>\n\n<p>Let us simulate, so you can see it in action:</p>\n\n<pre><code> n <- 1000000L\n x <- rnorm(n)\n y <- rnorm(n)\n v <- -log(-log(pnorm((x+y)/sqrt(2))))\n hist(v,n=100,freq=FALSE)\n curve(exp(-(x+exp(-x))),-3,10,col=4,add=TRUE)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/yw7Bj.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/yw7Bj.png\" alt=\"histogram of simulated values with overlaid standard Gumbel cdf\"></a></p>\n\n<p>Another example would be to take <span class=\"math-container\">$X,Y$</span> to be independent standard uniform, and let <span class=\"math-container\">$Z=\\max(X,Y)^2$</span>, then <span class=\"math-container\">$V=-\\log(-\\log(Z))$</span> will again be standard Gumbel.</p>\n\n<pre><code> n=1000000L\n hist(-log(-log(pmax(runif(n),runif(n))^2)),n=100,freq=FALSE)\n curve(exp(-(x+exp(-x))),-3,10,col=4,add=TRUE)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>(I won't include the plot this time, it looks the same as before).</p>\n\n<p>... and so forth. You could construct a hundred examples in an afternoon, were you so inclined.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2019-07-31T03:52:35.753000", "posts_rownum": "posts_279022", "provsql": "9cc1bdd9-d5c2-4c32-860a-1800bbdc7d24"}, "posts_288574": {"id": 434586, "owneruserid": 264742, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 434602, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Solving Variance of Time Series AR process", "tags": "<variance><markov-process><autoregressive>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I am trying to solve for the variance of <span class=\"math-container\">$x[n]$</span>, a time series process. \n<span class=\"math-container\">$$x[n] +a_1x[n-1]=w[n]$$</span>where <span class=\"math-container\">$w[n]$</span> is white noise with zero mean and variance <span class=\"math-container\">$\\sigma^2_v$</span>. Also <span class=\"math-container\">$|a_1|<1$</span>.</p>\n\n<p>I am aware that the equation can be solved using the Yule Walker Equations, but I was trying to solve it brute force using expectation.</p>\n\n<p>Here is what I did:</p>\n\n<p>Take the z-transform of the process,\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$X(z) + a_1X(z)z^{-1} = W(z)$$</span>\nSolving for the system function,\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$ H(z) = \\frac{X(z)}{W(z)} = \\frac{1}{1+a_1z^{-1}}$$</span>\nInverse z-transform,\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$h[n] = (-a_1)^nu[n]$$</span>\nUsing convolution,\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$x[n] = \\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-a_1)^kw[n-k]$$</span>\nSolving for the variance,\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$E[x[n]x^*[n]]=E[\\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-a_1)^kw[n-k]\\sum_{l=0}^{n-1}(-a_1)^lw[n-l]]$$</span>\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$E[x[n]x^*[n]] = \\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-a_1)^k\\sum_{l=0}^{n-1}(-a_1)^lE[w[n-k]w[n-l]]$$</span>\nSince w[n] is a white noise process,\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$E[w[n-k]w[n-l]] = 0, k\\neq l $$</span>\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$E[w[n-k][w[n-l]] = \\sigma^2_v, k=l$$</span>\nSo the expectation becomes,\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$E[x[n]x^*[n]] = \\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}(a_1^2)^m \\sigma^2_v$$</span>\nTherefore,\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$Var[x[n]]= \\sigma^2_v \\frac{1-(a_1^2)^n}{1-a_1^2} $$</span></p>\n\n<p>But this is not correct, this answer is nonstationary, and we should expect a stationary solution for the zero mean white noise.</p>\n\n<p>The correct answer is <span class=\"math-container\">$\\frac{\\sigma^2_v}{1-a^2_1}$</span></p>\n\n<p>It would be very helpful if someone could point out what I did wrong. I would like to solve this problem using this method. That way I can more appreciate using Yule-Walker equations. Thank you!</p>\n", "creationdate": "2019-11-05T00:22:59.970000", "posts_rownum": "posts_288574", "provsql": "d11bb6cf-3dd8-4a34-9f6d-495438518a25"}, "posts_298352": {"id": 448922, "owneruserid": 116440, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 432576, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>One example that comes to mind is the <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receiver_operating_characteristic#Area_under_the_curve\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">area</a> under the <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receiver_operating_characteristic\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">ROC curve</a> (AUC). For binary classification problems where the model outputs a continuous score (e.g. logistic regression or SVMs), AUC gives the probability that the model will score a randomly selected 'positive' instance higher than a randomly selected 'negative' instance.</p>\n\n<p>For evaluating prediction performance, AUC plays the same role as other metrics/loss functions (e.g. misclassification rate, log loss, etc). Namely, it maps predicted scores and true labels to a real number that summarizes performance. And, it can be used as the basis for decision rules; in particular, as an objective function for model selection. Higher AUC is more desirable, so AUC is actually a utility function rather than a loss function. But, this distinction is minor, as one can simply multiply AUC by negative one to obtain the loss incurred by choosing a particular model.</p>\n\n<p>Unlike misclassification rate, log loss, etc., AUC is non-additive (in the sense defined in the question). That is, if <span class=\"math-container\">$y_i$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$s_i$</span> are the true label and predicted score for the <span class=\"math-container\">$i$</span>th test case and <span class=\"math-container\">$g$</span> is an arbitrary function, AUC can't be expressed in the form <span class=\"math-container\">$\\sum_{i=1}^n g(y_i, s_i)$</span>. Rather, AUC is calculated by integrating the estimated ROC curve, which consists of the true positive rate vs. false positive rate as the classification threshold is varied. The integral is typically calculated using the trapezoid rule between points on the ROC curve. Although this involves a sum over trapezoids, AUC is non-additive because the area of each trapezoid depends non-additively on the predicted score and true labels of multiple test cases. For details, see section 7 and algorithm 2 in Fawcett (2006).</p>\n\n<p>Bradley (1997), Huang and Ling (2005), and others have argued for the use of AUC over accuracy (which is additive). Although AUC has found wide use (e.g. ~247k google scholar results for +auc +classification), there are arguments against it as well; e.g. see Lobo et al. (2008).</p>\n\n<p><strong>References</strong></p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><p>Fawcett, T. (2006). An introduction to ROC analysis. Pattern recognition letters, 27(8), 861-874.</p></li>\n<li><p>Bradley, A. P. (1997). The use of the area under the ROC curve in the evaluation of machine learning algorithms. Pattern recognition, 30(7), 1145-1159.</p></li>\n<li><p>Huang, J., & Ling, C. X. (2005). Using AUC and accuracy in evaluating learning algorithms. IEEE Transactions on knowledge and Data Engineering, 17(3), 299-310.</p></li>\n<li><p>Lobo, J. M., Jimenez‐Valverde, A., & Real, R. (2008). AUC: a misleading measure of the performance of predictive distribution models. Global ecology and Biogeography, 17(2), 145-151.</p></li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2020-02-11T07:16:00.990000", "posts_rownum": "posts_298352", "provsql": "a747b513-2966-4456-9d8d-9258e53f1cb9"}, "posts_299253": {"id": 450198, "owneruserid": null, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": "R_10", "title": "More robust measure than Mean", "tags": "<estimation><mean><robust>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I am currently dealing with data with many outliers and I shall not to eliminate them from the data for analytical purposes. So basically doing it P times and combining the output afterward.</p>\n<p>I am attempting to replicate the results of <a href=\"https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume8/pan07a/pan07a.pdf\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">this</a> paper. The aim is to do variable selection.\nData was simulated as follow</p>\n<p>There are a total of P = 1000 variables with the first\n150 effective while the other 850 as noise variables in forming two clusters. Hence, there were 150\ninformative attributes and 850 noise ones.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2021-07-24T19:33:14.793000", "posts_rownum": "posts_353555", "provsql": "6de81b95-7a18-4ad5-934f-05fd7be58291"}, "posts_359929": {"id": 548137, "owneruserid": 337757, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "factor score formula in lavaan", "tags": "<categorical-data><structural-equation-modeling><confirmatory-factor><lavaan>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I would like get the factor scores of R/lavaan, achieved by a CFA model (single factor, 4 continuous indicators), by hand. Which is the formula (equation) as function of the observed indicators. In addition, I would like also get them by ordinal Likert indicators (again single factor). How I can get the continuous values that R/lavaan assigns to the Likert categories after the fit?</p>\n<p>Many thanks in advance.</p>\n<p>Best,</p>\n", "creationdate": "2021-10-13T13:06:50.020000", "posts_rownum": "posts_359929", "provsql": "14aca088-aa35-4977-982a-6c2a13c038c8"}, "posts_359947": {"id": 548164, "owneruserid": 22311, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 548159, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>The <a href=\"/questions/tagged/boruta\" class=\"post-tag\" title=\"show questions tagged 'boruta'\" rel=\"tag\">boruta</a> algorithm is a feature selection method that is based on random forest. The reason you might care is that lasso is a linear model, so anything that matters for your outcome that isn't linear in the parameters under estimation is at risk of getting eliminated. An example: <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/7935/what-are-disadvantages-of-using-the-lasso-for-variable-selection-for-regression/225709#225709\">What are disadvantages of using the lasso for variable selection for regression?</a> In other words, the disadvantage to lasso for feature selection of a nonlinear model is that the lasso assumes a more restrictive set of assumptions than the random forest.</p>\n<p>Additionally, one might wonder why you care about feature selection at all. Random forest has a <em>kind</em> of feature selection built in, in the sense that it selects the best features to split on when building trees (but this isn't foolproof).</p>\n<p>In the particular case you outline, where you have a small number of observations overall, a random forest is probably not the right tool. Overfitting is a very real risk. Regularized regression might be the best you can do.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2021-10-13T15:28:28.733000", "posts_rownum": "posts_359947", "provsql": "61d8c1c9-2ec9-4983-bab5-9b9580306f05"}, "posts_372980": {"id": 568302, "owneruserid": 352204, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Ideas on machine learning algorithms to paint on a canvas", "tags": "<machine-learning>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I am completely new to machine learning.<br />\nI explain the problem with an example.</p>\n<p>I have a two dimensional white canvas.<br />\nThe shape of the canvas is an arbitrary closed curve.<br />\nI have a brush, it is represented as a circle having a radius small enough to reach all corners of the canvas.<br />\nI have also blue paint.</p>\n<p>I would like use a machine learning algorithm to create a trajectory of the brush in order to paint all the canvas in blue.<br />\nI attach a sketch of the problem.<br />\n<a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/B45e4.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/B45e4.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\" /></a></p>\n<p>Q1) Is there any machine learning algorithm available for such kind of problems?<br />\nQ2) If an algorithm does not exist, then may you indicate any reference I could study (book, paper, website) to learn how to write such an algorithm, please?</p>\n<p>Any other suggestion of where to focus my studies for this problem is appreciated.</p>\n<p>In my problem I have a "painter" acting as a reference motion. I would like my machine learning to mimic the painter.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2022-03-18T18:03:13.520000", "posts_rownum": "posts_372980", "provsql": "e20d45c9-63f1-49e9-bde4-a21a7e6ab66c"}, "posts_395094": {"id": 598853, "owneruserid": 260660, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 598849, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I will answer assuming <span class=\"math-container\">$X$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$Y$</span> are from normal distribution with mean <span class=\"math-container\">$0$</span> and variance <span class=\"math-container\">$1$</span>.</p>\n<p>Now, <span class=\"math-container\">$Cov(Y,X) = Cov(X,Y)$</span> does not imply covariance is zero. This is just a general fact that covariance is symmetric.</p>\n<p>Indeed <span class=\"math-container\">$Cov(X,Y) = E(XY) - E(X)E(Y)$</span>, and clearly this is equal to <span class=\"math-container\">$Cov(Y,X)$</span>.</p>\n<p>If <span class=\"math-container\">$X$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$Y$</span> were independent, it would be sufficient to get <span class=\"math-container\">$Cov(X,Y) = 0$</span>.</p>\n<p>Also, variance of <span class=\"math-container\">$Z$</span> is not <span class=\"math-container\">$1$</span>. Once again assuming independence for convenience, <span class=\"math-container\">$Var(Z) = Var(aX+bY) = a^2 Var(X) + b^2 Var(Y) = a^2+b^2$</span>.</p>\n<p>I think those two were the big things to go over.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2022-12-12T21:14:54.327000", "posts_rownum": "posts_395094", "provsql": "6e3a45a0-1711-4b9f-b95a-aa4b7bbe1d59"}, "posts_403550": {"id": 610219, "owneruserid": 7290, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 610210, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Running a single cross-validation loop yields an estimate of the out of sample predictive error associated with your modeling procedure, nothing more.  You have 10 different models because stepwise selection is unstable, as @Dave explains.  There is no reason to believe that <em>any</em> of your 10 models is 'right', but the mean of the cross-validation prediction error gives you an estimate of how large the prediction error will be in the future.  At this point, you would run your procedure over the full dataset and use that as the final model.  In general, I would advise <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/a/20856/7290\">against</a> this, but that would be the protocol.</p>\n<p>If you want to use cross-validation to determine the <span class=\"math-container\">$F$</span>-value to use as a cutoff for your modeling procedure, you need to do more.  In that case, you would use a <em>nested</em> cross-validation scheme.  In the outer loop, you would partition the data into <span class=\"math-container\">$k$</span> folds and set one aside.  Then you would perform another cross-validation loop on the remaining folds.  In the inner loop, you would use some means to search over possible <span class=\"math-container\">$F$</span>-values; for instance, you could use a grid search over a series of possible <span class=\"math-container\">$F$</span> cutoffs.  For each possible <span class=\"math-container\">$F$</span>, there would be a average out of sample predictive accuracy score.  You would take the cutoff that performed best and use it on the entire (nested) dataset to get a model.  That model would be used to make predictions on the top level set that had been set aside, and from that you would get an estimate of the out of sample performance of a model that is selected in this manner.  Then you would set the second fold aside, and perform the inner loop cross-validation and <span class=\"math-container\">$F$</span> cutoff selection again, etc.  After having done all this <span class=\"math-container\">$k$</span> times, you could average those and get an average estimate of the out of sample performance of models selected in this manner.  After that, you can repeat the search procedure that you had used in the inner loop on the outer loop alone (i.e., there wouldn't be an inner loop this time).  That will give the model slightly more data to work with to select your final cutoff.  Finally, you would fit your intended model using that cutoff on the whole dataset to get your final model, and you would have an estimate of how well a model of that type, selected in that manner, will perform out of sample.  In short, the larger protocol is this:</p>\n<ol>\n<li>Run nested cross-validation, selecting a cutoff on the inner loop and then using it in the outer loop, to get an estimate of out of sample performance.</li>\n<li>Run cross-validation to select the cutoff to be used for the final model.</li>\n<li>Fit your model to the full dataset using the cutoff selected.</li>\n</ol>\n<p>To get more detail, try reading: <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/q/65128/\">Nested cross validation for model selection</a> and <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/q/11602/\">Training on the full dataset after cross-validation?</a>.  Again, I wouldn't recommend you use stepwise selection, even in this case because the parameters will still be biased (and the constituent hypothesis tests will still be garbage), but the out of sample estimate of the predictive performance of a model fitted in this manner should be OK.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2023-03-21T18:24:59.740000", "posts_rownum": "posts_403550", "provsql": "add11306-1828-43a7-bb88-a4ee94e18163"}, "posts_403626": {"id": 610322, "owneruserid": 28500, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 610263, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>You would also have to add in the <code>(Intercept)</code> value to your calculation to get the type of estimate that you seek. The <code>(Intercept)</code> value holds the key here, as its value of 0.031 represents a situation in which <code>Intervention = 0</code> and <code>grade_level = "elementary"</code>. Yet the plot presents a value on the order of -0.025.</p>\n<p>I suspect that the discrepancy has to do with how the plotting software is handling the data values associated with other predictors (the <code>perc_</code> coefficients), each of which is a necessarily non-negative value with a negative regression coefficient. The software is presumably using some average over the data in your model or is otherwise centering some aspect of your data. Software-specific questions are off-topic here, so you might enquire of the package author if that's not clear from the manual.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2023-03-22T14:45:15.570000", "posts_rownum": "posts_403626", "provsql": "2dae13ce-6bfc-444e-9580-ad03a25ca433"}, "posts_895": {"id": 914, "owneruserid": null, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 913, "ownerdisplayname": "user88", "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>What you are looking for is called regression; there are a lot of methods you can do it, both statistical and machine learning ones. If you want to find f, you must use statistics; in that case you must first assume that f is of some form, like f:y=a*x+b and then use some regression method to fit the parameters.<br>\nThe plot suggests there are a lot of outliers (elements that does not follow f(x)); you may need robust regression to get rid of them.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-28T16:21:41.483000", "posts_rownum": "posts_895", "provsql": "f18f327f-6f0e-45e9-a3bb-a69236703aee"}, "posts_408309": {"id": 616126, "owneruserid": 22047, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 616112, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Analysis of variance compares means and variability about those means of an outcome or response variable, given information on one more other variables, which are often, but not necessarily, categorical.</p>\n<p>Whether you call that outcome <em>dependent</em> and the other variable(s) <em>independent</em> is a matter of taste. For other reasons, many statistical people find those terms overloaded and try to use more evocative terms. (It's not trivial that many beginners get muddled on which is which.)</p>\n<p>How you -- or whether you can -- interpret the results in terms of causation, process, mechanism or whatever else is a key question, but I call it a different question.</p>\n<p>Even in simple exercises the chain of causation and process can be hard to think about. If I compare say males and females on mathematics scores, that doesn't mean that I think or am hypothesising that anatomy or physiology determines or even influences mathematics scores. In the first instance I am checking to see if there are different means in statistical terms. If I find that there are different means, then I stop describing and have to wonder what else lies behind it, in this case quite possibly social or cultural or educational factors. If the example seems contentious, that is the point. We may need very detailed discussion of what is behind any pattern and it is usually the more difficult part of the analysis.</p>\n<p>Crudely, both you and your colleague have good points, but your ways of looking at analysis of variance are just different.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2023-05-17T11:35:34.260000", "posts_rownum": "posts_408309", "provsql": "d957ac19-941c-420e-9f9e-cab57e4a937c"}, "posts_412434": {"id": 621328, "owneruserid": 390971, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 621321, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>You're proposing the following model:\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$h^{(i)}(t)=h_0(t)e^{\\beta x_i},$$</span>\nwhere <span class=\"math-container\">$h^{(i)}(t)$</span> is the hazard function for patient <span class=\"math-container\">$i$</span> at time <span class=\"math-container\">$t$</span>, <span class=\"math-container\">$h_0(t)$</span> is the baseline hazard function at time <span class=\"math-container\">$t$</span>, and <span class=\"math-container\">$x_i$</span> is the transplant time of patient <span class=\"math-container\">$i$</span> as you have defined it.</p>\n<p>Under this model, <span class=\"math-container\">$e^{\\beta d}$</span> is the hazard ratio comparing the hazard function of a patients who received a transplant <span class=\"math-container\">$d$</span> days apart. You've (implicitly) assumed that the hazard ratio comparing the hazard function of a patient who received a transplant at time <span class=\"math-container\">$t$</span> to that of a patient who never received a transplant is <span class=\"math-container\">$e^{\\beta(t+1)}$</span>. Another implication is that the hazard rate of a patient who received a transplant at time 0 is <span class=\"math-container\">$e^\\beta$</span> times that of a patient who didn't receive a transplant -- and the hazard rate of a patient who received a transplant at time <span class=\"math-container\">$t$</span> is also <span class=\"math-container\">$e^\\beta$</span> times that of a patient who received a transplant at time <span class=\"math-container\">$t-1$</span>. Is that (very strong) assumption reasonable? I would guess no, according to the authors you mention.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2023-07-13T15:32:09.363000", "posts_rownum": "posts_412434", "provsql": "65188994-e423-45b5-9f8c-53592e44fcfa"}, "posts_342": {"id": 360, "owneruserid": null, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 173, "ownerdisplayname": "user88", "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Does it really need some advanced model? Based on what I know about TB, in case there is no epidemy the infections are stochastic acts and so the count form month N shouldn't be correlated with count from month N-1. (You can check this assumption with autocorrelation). If so, analyzing just the distribution of monthly counts may be sufficient to decide if some count is significantly higher than normal.<br>\nOn the other hand you can look for correlations with some other variables, like season, travel traffic, or anything that you can imagine that may be correlated. If you would found something like this, it could be then used for some data normalization.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-20T23:56:33.933000", "posts_rownum": "posts_342", "provsql": "d7ef052b-0423-4842-a764-123484abdb5a"}, "posts_548": {"id": 558, "owneruserid": 39, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Comprehensive overview of loss functions?", "tags": "<references><loss-functions>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I am trying to get a global perspective on some of the essential ideas in machine learning, and I was wondering if there is a comprehensive treatment of the different notions of loss (squared, log, hinge, proxy, etc.).  I was thinking something along the lines of a more comprehensive, formal presentation of John Langford’s excellent post on <a href=\"http://hunch.net/?p=269\">Loss Function Semantics</a>.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-23T16:15:33.137000", "posts_rownum": "posts_548", "provsql": "0840a9d7-0de6-4fae-8851-4219dc08ce0c"}, "posts_1047": {"id": 1083, "owneruserid": 603, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 95, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Generally, by not allowing for assymetry, you expect the effect of shocks to last longers: i.e. the half-life increases (the half life is the number of units of time, after a 1 S.D. shock to $\\epsilon_{t-1}$ for $\\hat{\\sigma}<em>t|I</em>{t-1}$ to come back to the its unconditional value.) </p>\n\n<p>Here is a code snipped that downloads stock data, fits (e)Garch and computes half lifes, in R:</p>\n\n<pre><code>install.packages(\"rgarch\",repos=\"http://R-Forge.R-project.org\")\ninstall.packages(\"fGarch\")\ninstall.packages(\"fImport\")\nlibrary(rgarch)\nlibrary(fImport)\nlibrary(fGarch)\nd1<-yahooSeries(symbols=\"ibm\",nDaysBack=1000,frequency=c(\"daily\"))[,4]\ndprice1<-diff(log(as.numeric(d1[length(d1):1])))\nspec1<-ugarchspec(variance.model=list(model=\"eGARCH\",garchOrder=c(1,1)),mean.model=list(armaOrder=c(0,0),include.mean=T))\nspec2<-ugarchspec(variance.model=list(model=\"fGARCH\",submodel=\"GARCH\",garchOrder=c(1,1)),mean.model=list(armaOrder=c(0,0),include.mean=T))\nfit1<-ugarchfit(data=dprice1,spec=spec1)\nfit2<-ugarchfit(data=dprice1,spec=spec2)\nhalflife(fit1)\nhalflife(fit2)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>The reason for this is that generally speaking, negative spells tend to be more persistent.\nIf you don't control for this, you will generally bias the $\\beta$ (i.e. persistance parameters) downwards.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-01T11:56:51.260000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1047", "provsql": "681314ee-0778-424a-af29-cd1c17461077"}, "posts_8204": {"id": 8809, "owneruserid": 449, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 8795, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I'm pretty sure the answer is <strong>yes</strong>, the standard binomial 'fair coin' test <em>is</em> still valid: if you wish to test whether two of the three probabilities of a <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinomial_distribution\" rel=\"nofollow\" rel=\"nofollow\">multinomial distribution</a> are the same but you're not interested in any hypotheses about the third probability, you can analyse the numbers of the corresponding two outcomes as if they were drawn from a <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_distribution\" rel=\"nofollow\" rel=\"nofollow\">binomial distribution</a>.</p>\n\n<p>In fact this seems to make quite a nice exercise about sufficient statistics and conditional likelihood:</p>\n\n<p>You can think of this as a multinomial distribution with three possible outcomes and hence two estimable parameters (as the three probabilities must sum to 1). But you're not interested in the probability of the 'middle' outcome, so you can take this to be the <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuisance_parameter\" rel=\"nofollow\" rel=\"nofollow\">nuisance parameter</a>, and the difference between the number of 'top' and 'bottom' outcomes to be the parameter of interest. </p>\n\n<p>It's straightforward to show (using the <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufficient_statistic#Fisher.E2.80.93Neyman_factorization_theorem\" rel=\"nofollow\" rel=\"nofollow\">Fisher–Neyman factorization theorem</a>) that the numbers of 'top' and 'bottom' outcomes together form a (two-dimensional) <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufficient_statistic\" rel=\"nofollow\" rel=\"nofollow\">sufficient statistic</a> for the parameter of interest, i.e. the number of 'middle' outcomes doesn't provide any additional information about the value of the parameter of interest. The number of 'middle' outcomes is clearly a sufficient statistic for the nuisance prameter. If we condition on the latter, I think (haven't checked properly) that the resulting <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_likelihood#Conditional_likelihood\" rel=\"nofollow\" rel=\"nofollow\">conditional likelihood</a> will end up the same as the likelihood for the binomial distribution, i.e. the coin-tossing problem.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-03-26T22:13:15.587000", "posts_rownum": "posts_8204", "provsql": "fe3ef673-ba02-4078-9351-a2598a6bafb6"}, "posts_17270": {"id": 18942, "owneruserid": 2669, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 18937, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I doubt there is much that will help with the idiosyncratic, jagged shape of temperature, but with rainfall there are data-transformations you can try.  You can search for that tag on this site and you'll come up with many useful posts.  (Note that \"normalization\" is defined differently from \"data-transformation\" and it is the latter that you want in order to create something closer to a bell curve.)  </p>\n\n<p>The first thing I would try would be to take the square root of each value.  The result may still be skewed, but probably a lot less so.  In other words, it would probably not \"pass\" a normality test (those are pretty unreliable anyway), but it would likely be a more workable variable for most purposes.  As many on this site have reminded us, in multivariate analysis it is typically the residuals, rather than the univariate distributions, that must be close to normal in order to satisfy the normality assumption.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-11-25T14:42:55.577000", "posts_rownum": "posts_17270", "provsql": "df2872c9-cdaa-4f46-8c5a-7def01e900e7"}, "posts_27442": {"id": 30954, "owneruserid": 12158, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Binary classification and ROC curve area less than .5", "tags": "<logistic><auc>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Both my independent and dependent variables are binary. k)=\\frac{k}{\\lambda}\\left(\\frac{x}{\\lambda}\\right)^{k-1}\\text{exp}\\left\\{-\\left(\\frac{x}{\\lambda}\\right)^k\\right\\}$</p>\n\n<p>Then </p>\n\n<p>$L(\\lambda|x_1,\\dots, x_n)\\propto If it's not too bad then just use what you have.  Your series of parallel lines with negative slopes is hard to imagine as well.  It does sound like there's some pattern happening in the data that your regression isn't explaining.  Without seeing your actual figures it's hard to tell if you have any problem at all.</p>\n\n<p>Time variables often have tails out to the right.  Often a useful transform is rate.  Right now you might have the time it took something to occur in seconds.  Let's say it took 2s for something to occur.  The rate would be 0.5 occurrences / second.  The transform is just 1/t.  That might fix your qq-plot but it would just change the parallel lines, not eliminate them.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2012-10-02T05:06:39.500000", "posts_rownum": "posts_32817", "provsql": "98d73b7c-562b-410d-ab36-461fa78854b4"}, "posts_33286": {"id": 39025, "owneruserid": 7828, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 39024, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>The problem with dimensionality reduction and number of variables >> number of observations is that the $k$ observations that you have define an at most $k-1$ dimensional hyperplane on which the objects perfectly are located on.</p>\n\n<p>So yes, anything more than 9 dimensions still has proven redundancies.</p>\n\n<p>Many dimension reduction techniques - in particular PCA, SVD, but probably also MDS etc. - will essentially try to preserve this hyperplane.</p>\n\n<p>Don't you have a way to reduce the number of dimensions <strong>that uses domain information that you have</strong>? I.e. if you know that your dimensions are <em>expected</em> to be highly correlated, remove dimensions that are the most correlated (pairwise is probably best). But note that even correlation is not very stable to compute when you have just 10 observations. You lose one degree of freedom for the mean, for example, which you can't really afford.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2012-10-09T16:54:20.357000", "posts_rownum": "posts_33286", "provsql": "a9b05b55-38ee-4960-8473-0774724c8b37"}, "posts_53352": {"id": 67212, "owneruserid": 14860, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 67106, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I haven't yet used <a href=\"http://dirk.eddelbuettel.com/code.html\" rel=\"nofollow\">RcppArmadillo</a> package but you may look into it. This package is useful if C++ has been decided as the language of choice. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2013-08-13T00:03:36.180000", "posts_rownum": "posts_53352", "provsql": "b54cf6f4-0183-4882-9f13-293fd866368a"}, "posts_40377": {"id": 49737, "owneruserid": 9136, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Generating data using grf and plotting its variogram- Result intrepretation", "tags": "<r><spatial>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I have a question about the semivariogram plot:</p>\n\n<p>Suppose I generated 50 data points from Gaussian random field (using grf function in R), and assumed that we have exponential covariance model with $\\sigma^2 = 1$ and $\\phi=0.5$, and $\\phi$ here represents the range which can be defind as \"The distance in which the difference of the variogram from the sill becomes negligible\".</p>\n\n<p>So when we plot the semivariogram for the generated data, we would assume that the range is going to be around 0.5, but it is not!</p>\n\n<p>Here is code I'm using. Can someone explain what's going on, or I'm missing something? Thanks!</p>\n\n<pre><code>![grd <- expand.grid(seq(0, 1, l=5), seq(0, 1, l=5))\nsdata <- grf(50, grid=\"reg\", cov.pars=c(1, 0.5), cov.model=\"exponential\")\nplot(sdata)][1]\n</code></pre>\n", "creationdate": "2013-02-11T14:13:30.717000", "posts_rownum": "posts_40377", "provsql": "6aa97a58-b790-4df3-a636-cd1c40546c76"}, "posts_44854": {"id": 56522, "owneruserid": 11187, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 56516, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>In a machine learning context (i.e. \"kernel methods\"), the key requirement for a kernel is that it must be symmetric and positive-definite, that is, if $K$ is a kernel matrix, then for any (column) vector $x$ of the appropriate length, $x^{T}Kx$ must be a positive real number. This restriction is in place mostly due to requirements of optimization processes that operate downstream on this matrix.</p>\n\n<p>To answer your question, certain basic operations preserve positive-definiteness, and some don't. You can use the definition of positive-definiteness above to decide whether an operation preserves that property or not. The product operation does not always preserve positive definiteness (it does preserve it in the case where their product is commutative). The square operation however does preserve it. For a real positive number $r$, $rK$ is positive definite, and the sum of any two positive definite matrices is also positive definite.</p>\n\n<p>So in your examples, $K_3$ and $K_4$ may or may not be proper kernel matrices (to use your terminology) and $K_5$ is definitely a proper kernel matrix.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2013-04-18T19:56:29.013000", "posts_rownum": "posts_44854", "provsql": "2855c8ec-a58c-437e-a91d-6935e8f17da4"}, "posts_46724": {"id": 59018, "owneruserid": 16362, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 59024, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to forecast hourly data in R", "tags": "<r><time-series><forecasting>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I have hourly login data for a web site.
