null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I would not make an automatic choice. Sometimes you want a more parsimonious model, sometimes you want a less parsimonious model. Sometimes you want a model that is less parsimonious than either AIC or BIC recommends.</p>\n\n<p>In almost all cases you will want to look at several models and see which is the most useful to you, for your particular purposes, with your knowledge of the substantive area, with the amount of data you have. </p>\n\n<p>Attempts to automate these decisions are ways of saying to your boss \"Don't pay me so much, the computer does my thinking\".</p>\n\n<p>:-)</p>\n", "creationdate": "2013-05-14T18:54:26.863000", "posts_rownum": "posts_46727", "provsql": "3fa79ba9-58da-4d56-bc3d-22a438648f67"}, "posts_59091": {"id": 74639, "owneruserid": 32337, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Transfer functions in R (TSA package)", "tags": "<r><time-series><arima>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>In Time Series models’ transfer functions there is a decay parameter in the\nformula (let’s call it b). In TSA package that decay parameter is not mentioned. When I used other software before (such as SAS) I used to determine b after analyzing ‘prewhitened series’. But\nin TSA package in R there is no need to specify the decay parameter once you analyze CCF?</p>\n\n<p>If not how am I going to know when the decay starts?</p>\n\n<p>I understand CCF is used after prewhitening to determine how to\nfilter the outputs but where b comes into the picture?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2013-11-05T14:10:31.143000", "posts_rownum": "posts_59091", "provsql": "93c30ec2-eeee-4357-967e-9bd788fe84c7"}, "posts_69640": {"id": 90394, "owneruserid": 3277, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 90380, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<ul>\n<li><strong>Why are there negative values in the range of the plot?</strong> Because the input contingency table of positive values (e.g. frequencies) was\nstandardized by the analysis in a special way relative the central\npoint.</li>\n<li><strong>How is the center of the plot (i.e., the 0.0  point) found?</strong> It is the weighted mean row profile and the weighted mean column profile.\nIt is thus the locus of \"perfectly typical\" or predominant hair and eye colour.\nAccording to your data, brown hair and hazel eyes are the closest\ncandidates to be called \"typical\" of the population.</li>\n<li><strong>How did the black-brown points end up in the third quadrant of the plot?</strong> What quadrant - it doesn't matter. Row and column points\nwhich are close together tend to co-occure in the population. Blach\nhair and brown eyes normally go together, as blond hair and blue\neyes. Brown hair is also not uncommon with brown eyes; however, brown\nhair occurs very often in the population so it also is often seen with\ncombination with some other eyes, mostly hazel.</li>\n<li><strong>Why are red, hazel, & brown positive on the y-axis and negative on the x-axis?</strong> As said already, positive/negative sign doesn't matter\nitself. The general moral following from your map is that Dimension X\ncorresponds to blond vs brown/black opposition, and weaker (less\ndiscriminative of the population) Dimension Y corresponds to \"colourful\"\nvs \"plain\" opposition. Note that in simple correspondence analysis you are allowed to rotate the axes as you wish if it facilitates interpretation.</li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2014-03-18T08:24:51.273000", "posts_rownum": "posts_69640", "provsql": "7b792d5f-dd96-483c-b2d7-8518e99094c8"}, "posts_97875": {"id": 134924, "owneruserid": 67430, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Tests for lognormal distribution", "tags": "<lognormal-distribution>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I have some data in the following manner.\n10\n3\n4\n5\n6\n9\n...</p>\n\n<p>I have to check that the difference between returns is log normal by doing ln(return/previous return).</p>\n\n<p>I know some tests for normality if i do (return - previous return) such as chi square test, kolmogorov-smirnov test, qq test.</p>\n\n<p>I was wondering if there are any similar tests for the lognormal, or perhaps if I could apply the normality tests in the same way</p>\n", "creationdate": "2015-01-26T01:46:06.837000", "posts_rownum": "posts_97875", "provsql": "ca4a58f5-9c7c-4afc-b0fe-b9d3a2dc469d"}, "posts_107310": {"id": 148507, "owneruserid": 61826, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 136087, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>The std deviations given in the summary for a linear mixed model are not the std deviation for the variance estimates, they are just the estimates for the std deviation of the effects themselves, that is the square-roots of the variance estimates.\nThus, even if you calculate the std deviation of the fixed-effects variance estimate, you will not be able to compare the fixed and random variances on a graph using the random std deviations given by the summary. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2015-04-27T13:39:23.447000", "posts_rownum": "posts_107310", "provsql": "84b64b67-f219-445d-900b-67dd962a5e50"}, "posts_112342": {"id": 156886, "owneruserid": 21072, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 71946, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Is there any model, leave aside logistic regression, that it is not possible to overfit? </p>\n\n<p>Overfitting arises fundamentally because you fit to a sample & not the whole population. Artifacts of your sample can seem like features of the population and they are not and hence overfitting hurts. </p>\n\n<p>It is akin to a question of external validity. Using only the sample you are trying to get a model that gives you the best performance on the real population which you cannot see. </p>\n\n<p>Sure, some model forms or procedures are more likely to overfit than others but no model is ever truly immune from overfitting, is it? </p>\n\n<p>Even out-of-sample validation, regularization procedures etc. can only guard against over-fitting but there's no silver bullet. In fact, if one were to estimate one's confidence in making a real world prediction based on a fitted model one must always assume that some degree of overfitting has indeed happened. </p>\n\n<p>To what extent might vary, but even a model validated on a hold out dataset will rarely yield in-wild performance that matches what was obtained on the hold-out dataset. And overfitting is a big causative factor. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2015-06-14T07:34:51.983000", "posts_rownum": "posts_112342", "provsql": "3e7549d2-b560-4128-b224-df037de9bee9"}, "posts_119368": {"id": 168040, "owneruserid": 83751, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Requirement on data distribution when using certain data mining classifiers", "tags": "<distributions><data-mining><weka>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am a little bit confused on whether data mining classifiers make any assumptions about the distribution of the data.\nI myself have a computer science background, but when I have discussions with an economist, he asks whether these classifiers do not make any assumptions of the distribution of the data (e.g. normal distribution).</p>\n\n<p>As far as I know, you can make a distinction between parametric and non-parametric classifiers in which the first is based on the statistical probability distribution of each class and the non-parametric classifier is used in case of an unknown density function.\nWhen I look at <a href=\"http://www.mecs-press.org/ijitcs/ijitcs-v4-n7/IJITCS-V4-N7-6.pdf\" rel=\"nofollow\">this paper</a> I find some classifiers being parametric (Bayes, Decision Trees, SVM) and some being non-parametric (Multilayer Perceptron).\n(Oddly enough, <a href=\"http://www.ise.bgu.ac.il/faculty/liorr/hbchap9.pdf\" rel=\"nofollow\">this paper</a> claims that decision trees are non-parametric.)</p>\n\n<p>However, <a href=\"http://weka.8497.n7.nabble.com/Normal-distribution-td810.html\" rel=\"nofollow\">here</a> I find that it is not necessary to test whether the data is normally distributed when using data mining tools.</p>\n\n<p>Do the data mining classifiers (esspecially in WEKA) require the input features and the feature that will be predicted to follow a certain distribution?\nIf so, do you know some references on which classifiers (J48,Naive Bayes, SVM,Random Forest, Multilayer Perceptron etc.) require which distribution?\nIf not, why isn't this necessary? </p>\n", "creationdate": "2015-08-20T12:36:26.750000", "posts_rownum": "posts_119368", "provsql": "15fe7164-8fca-444b-88f6-41fa1231d068"}, "posts_290199": {"id": 437015, "owneruserid": 892, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 437001, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I think an improvement over what you have done is to compute for each user the vector of differences of word usage in the 70 categories, before and after the intervention. Thus, each user would be characterised by a vector of dimension 70. Next, I would perform a cluster analysis to show if some users separate from others in a consistent way; the results of that analysis will suggest, I expect, ways to proceed.</p>\n\n<p>You have to decide what distance to use between the 70-dimensional vectors, as I suspect some word catgegories may be much more populated than others. But surely you can come out with something reasonable.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2019-11-20T10:08:12.093000", "posts_rownum": "posts_290199", "provsql": "cddf47cf-cffc-4206-a554-5a2f618ebfe4"}, "posts_141812": {"id": 203933, "owneruserid": 4253, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 203929, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>To externally validate a regression model, don't refit the model.  All model parameters should be \"frozen\".  Start with a rigorous full-resolution smooth nonparametric calibration plot to check absolute predictive accuracy.  There are various tests for calibration accuracy, the most powerful of which is probably Spiegelhalter's.  Both these methods and many more, including indexes of predictive discrimination, are automatically done by the R <code>rms</code> package's <code>val.prob</code> function.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2016-03-27T12:05:03.300000", "posts_rownum": "posts_141812", "provsql": "8fc39c40-bcc0-45c1-8fb2-75e87463dc68"}, "posts_133056": {"id": 189248, "owneruserid": 93788, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 189245, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>If you are assuming the treatment effect size and the sd of the outcome are the same in all three sites, then you don't need to account for center in your power calculation.</p>\n\n<p>This doesn't mean that the stratified randomization isn't likely to be improving your power in actual practice. Stratified randomization, matched randomization, minimization, and other forms of restricted randomization all increase your power through balancing (among the treatment arms) the distribution of covariates that are predictive of the outcome. However in your case, you are already accounting for this benefit if you are assuming a common sd for the outcome within each site. The sensibility of that assumed sd is what will largely drive the sensibility of your power calculation.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2016-01-04T21:24:19.380000", "posts_rownum": "posts_133056", "provsql": "67cb39e5-a9bf-4f62-98fa-abcad8a56654"}, "posts_148647": {"id": 214739, "owneruserid": 86652, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 214724, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>The difference is that with ABC you do not need an analytic expression for $P(x|\\theta)$ and instead approximate it by simulating data and seeing for which values of $\\theta$ simulated data most often (approximately) matches the observed data (with proposed values e.g. drawn randomly from the prior). For simple cases, such as a single binomial random variable with a not too large sample size you can even require an exact match and in those cases, there really is absolutely nothing you could not do with these posterior samples that you could not also do with standard MCMC samples. For more complex situations with continuous (even for multivariate discrete outcomes) and potentially multivariate outcomes requiring an exact match is no longer feasible. </p>\n\n<p>There are in fact MCMC versions of ABC, which addresses the issue that if you have a prior that does not closely resemble the posterior (e.g. because the prior is very uninformative) sampling by drawing from the prior is extremly inefficient, because you very rarely will get a close match between the observed and the simulated data.</p>\n\n<p>When $P(x|\\theta)$ is analytically available, I assume it will nearly always be preferrable to use a standard MCMC. I suppose it is conceivable that somehow the evaluation of $P(x|\\theta)$ is so incredibly computationally expensive that ABC performs better. Perhaps someone knows an example of this. In contrast I would consider ABC or MCMC-ABC (or one of the many other ABC variants) primarily when a standard MCMC approach is not an option, because $P(x|\\theta)$ is not analytically available. Of course there may be some other possible options in such cases (e.g. INLA, quadratic approximations to likelihoods etc.) that may be more efficient/successful for particular problems. In a way, any limitations in what you can do with posterior samples from ABC come from only requiring an aproximate match between the actual and the simulated data (if you could require an exact match, there would be no issues, at all). There are several good introductory papers e.g. this paper by <a href=\"http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/s11222-011-9288-2\">Marin et al. (2012)</a>. At least one of the co-authors (@Xi'an) is an active contributor here and I'd love to here his thoughts, too - I believe he may be able to say a lot more on the testing topic.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2016-05-26T07:39:08.687000", "posts_rownum": "posts_148647", "provsql": "a85209df-0c95-4c00-8991-320373d540a0"}, "posts_156692": {"id": 229245, "owneruserid": 5739, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 229240, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>This is a partial answer since the question is wa-a-a-ay too broad.</p>\n\n<p>Maximum likelihood is an estimation method, not an imputation method, although some variations can be applied to missing data problems. It does not naturally produce imputations of any kind.</p>\n\n<p>Survey statisticians are usually very cautious working with heavily-model-dependent methods, such as any GLM-type models or even MI, as far as establishment surveys are concerned, because the data are usually very highly skewed. So on one hand, transformations towards normality seem like a knee-jerk reaction, but on the other hand, the imputed data have to satisfy a lot of accounting constraints. E.g., total revenue must equal the sum of total compensation, total cost of inputs, net interest payments, and profit... and I am sure I am forgetting something since I am not an accountant. If one or more of these is imputed from say a lognormal model, there is no guarantee that the accounting inequalities would hold.</p>\n\n<p>A <a href=\"http://rads.stackoverflow.com/amzn/click/047090304X\" rel=\"nofollow\">recent handbook on business surveys</a> has a chapter on editing and imputation that may help.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2016-08-10T18:51:04.377000", "posts_rownum": "posts_156692", "provsql": "e1c4e9ce-817e-4b8d-b0c5-528d16a4abbb"}, "posts_158155": {"id": 231322, "owneruserid": 28500, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 231260, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Regression coefficients in a Cox model are calculated from events, based on the covariate values of the individual having an event and the covariate values of all those still at risk at that time. With no events in the lowest-risk group of the 3 groups you thus have no ability to calculate the Cox coefficient for the lowest-risk group or its associated hazard ratio. That's different from a situation where some <em>combination</em> of covariates leads to quasi-separation, or where there are some events in a low-risk group but they all occur after those in another group.</p>\n\n<p>So your wall is insurmountable and impenetrable if you need a hazard ratio representing the lowest-risk category, based on a binned continuous marker, from your data. This is yet another reason to avoid binning a continuous marker, as frequently recommended on this site. Using the marker as a continuous predictor would give you a way to simply walk around the wall.</p>\n\n<p>If binning is necessary, you might be able to use the highest-risk group as the reference factor level and calculate the hazard ratio of the middle-risk group against that reference. But I see no way to get a corresponding hazard ratio for the lowest-risk group if it has no events.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2016-08-23T17:06:09.537000", "posts_rownum": "posts_158155", "provsql": "3023e1b7-f94c-419d-8eb4-c920c2bd887a"}, "posts_190603": {"id": 279749, "owneruserid": 131391, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 279752, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Which neural network package should i use?", "tags": "<neural-networks><nnet>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm looking at running a neural network to predict the probability of a turtle becoming entangled in a fishing net. My input variables are fishing net characteristics that include continuos and categorical values (that i have scaled between 0 and 1) and my output is either 1(present) or 0 (absent).</p>\n\n<p>My question is:\nAm i correct in saying this is a classification problem and i should be using the 'nnet' package, since 'neuralnet' only deals with regression? </p>\n\n<p>Thanks for your time</p>\n\n<p>UPDATE: Here is some code i used for cross validating</p>\n\n<p>`ControlParameters<-trainControl(method=\"cv\",number=10, classProb=FALSE)</p>\n\n<p>parameterGrid<- expand.grid(layer1=1:5,layer2=1:5,layer3=1:5) </p>\n\n<p>Model1<-train(Turtles~Twine+Mesh+Black+Blue+Green+Red+Orange‌​+Yellow+Synthetic+Br‌​aided+Mono+Multi+X1+‌​X2+X3+X4+X5+X16,data‌​=train_Hypep,method=‌​'neuralnet', preProc = c(\"center\", \"scale\"),trControl=ControlParameters) `</p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-05-15T18:59:32.707000", "posts_rownum": "posts_190603", "provsql": "1ae34ecf-0b65-4228-9458-c13168294fa4"}, "posts_194083": {"id": 284963, "owneruserid": 11060, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Correlation in Distances of Points Within a Circle from Centre and One Other Point", "tags": "<correlation><spatial>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p><strong>Background</strong></p>\n\n<p>The travel cost method, a method used in economics to estimate the value of parks and other recreational sites, requires (as one step) estimating the relation between $VR_i$, the visit rate to the site for the $i$'th individual (or sometimes zone of origin), and $TC_i$, the corresponding travel cost to the site.  Travel cost is often roughly proportional to distance. Sometimes the visit rate is influenced by a second site, so that the true regression equation is of the form:</p>\n\n<p>$$VR_i = B_0 + B_1TC_i + B_2TCS_i$$</p>\n\n<p>where $TCS_i$ is the travel cost to the second site.  Regression theory implies that if the variable $TCS_i$ is omitted when estimating the relation between $VR_i$ and $TC_i$, then the estimates of $B_0$ and $B_1$ are likely to be biased, and that the amount and direction of bias will depend partly on the sign and magnitude of correlation between $TC_i$ and $TCS_i$. </p>\n\n<p><strong>Question</strong></p>\n\n<p>Abstracting from the above, suppose $A$ is the centre of a circle of radius $r$, and $B$ is a point at distance $d$ from $A$ ($d < r$).  Suppose a large number of points, indexed by $i$, are uniformly distributed by area within the circle.  Define random variables $X$ and $Y$ as the distances from $A$ and $B$ respectively to $i$.  What is the correlation coefficient $\\rho$ between $X$ and $Y$?  Either an exact formula or a good approximation would be useful.</p>\n\n<p><strong>What I Have Done</strong></p>\n\n<p>Starting from the formula:</p>\n\n<p>$$\\rho = \\frac{cov(X,Y)}{\\sigma_X\\sigma_Y}$$</p>\n\n<p>I calculated $\\mu_X$ and hence $\\sigma_X$ as follows:</p>\n\n<p>$$\\mu_X = \\int_0^r z.(2\\pi z/\\pi r^2) dz = \\int_0^r 2z^2/r^2 dz = \\bigg[ 2z^3/3r^2 \\bigg]_0^r = 2r/3$$</p>\n\n<p>$$\\sigma^2_X = \\int_0^r [z - (2r/3)]^2(2\\pi z/\\pi r^2) dz = \\int_0^r [z^2 - 4rz/3 + 4r^2/9](2z/r^2) dz$$\n$$\\sigma^2_X = \\frac{1}{r^2} \\int_0^r [2z^3 - 8rz^2/3 + 8r^2z/9] dz = \\frac{1}{r^2} \\bigg[\\frac{z^4}{2} - \\frac{8rz^3}{9} + \\frac{4r^2z^2}{9} \\bigg]_0^r$$\n$$\\sigma^2_X = \\frac{1}{r^2}\\bigg[\\frac{r^4}{2} - \\frac{8r^4}{9} + \\frac{4r^4}{9}\\bigg] = \\frac{r^2}{18}$$\n$$\\sigma_X = \\frac{r}{3\\sqrt{2}} \\approx 0.236r$$</p>\n\n<p>However, I'm not sure how to proceed to find $cov(X,Y)$ and $\\sigma_Y$, which appear to need more sophisticated applications of calculus.</p>\n\n<p>Intuitively, I can see that there will be a positive correlation when $d$ is much smaller than $r$, so that A and B are relatively close together, but I'm not sure whether the correlation will become negative for larger $d$.</p>\n\n<p><strong>Update 14/6/2017</strong></p>\n\n<p>Prompted by whuber's comment I estimated $\\rho$ for the case with $B$ on the edge of the circle by an approximate method. A distribution of 120 points within the circle was defined as follows. The circle was imagined divided into 10 concentric rings of equal width. Numbering the rings from the centre, their areas are in the ratio $1:3:5:...:2n-1:...:19$. Along the middle of each ring, 12 points were positioned at intervals of 30 degrees relative to the line $AB$. The distance of each point from $B$ was found using the cosine rule. In calculating $\\rho$, values associated with points were weighted by the areas of their respective rings (this is equivalent to having the number of points in each ring proportional to its area). This gave the following results (rounded to 3 significant figures):</p>\n\n<p>$$\\sigma_X = 0.235r$$</p>\n\n<p>$$\\sigma_Y = 0.470r$$</p>\n\n<p>$$cov(X,Y) = 0.0175r^2$$</p>\n\n<p>$$\\rho = 0.158$$</p>\n\n<p>This estimate of $\\rho$ is reasonably close to whuber's 0.164. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-06-12T15:58:54.837000", "posts_rownum": "posts_194083", "provsql": "428af291-e093-4aaf-a290-28cfbed4e055"}, "posts_175105": {"id": 255868, "owneruserid": 60621, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 257305, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to include in a regression two factors where one level of one factor is necessarily nested with one level of another factor?", "tags": "<regression><categorical-data><fixed-effects-model>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I've got a situation where I have a series of individuals who have two factors describing their health.  Factor A has 3 levels while factor B has 4 levels.  Biologically, level 1 of factor A appears if and only if factor B is level 1.  Therefore, I have data structured like this:</p>\n\n<pre><code>ID   Factor A  Factor B   Score\n1      a        alpha       0.1\n2      a        alpha       0.2\n3      b        beta        0.3\n4      b        gamma       0.4\n5      b        delta       0.5\n6      c        beta        0.6\n7      c        gamma       0.7\n8      c        delta       0.8\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>I'm interested in studying the effects of both factors, but I'm struggling with how to properly code this.  Giving each factor their own full set of dummy codes is rank deficient and leaving out a level of either factor creates a model with impossible combinations (ie level <em>a</em> ONLY occurs with level <em>alpha</em>, and vice versa).  <strong>How could I code these fixed effects so that I can investigate the impact of both factors on our score?  Additionally, how would I interpret this coding scheme?</strong></p>\n\n<p>EDIT:  To give some further context on how this happens, Factor A is series of related diseases (each phenotypically similar, but genetically different) while Factor B is severity of that diseased state.  So <em>a</em> is the control group while <em>alpha</em> is healthy severity.  These two occur contemporaneously by necessity (ie a healthy severity must be a control while a control can be nothing but healthy).</p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-01-12T15:31:55.227000", "posts_rownum": "posts_175105", "provsql": "0939f72b-d635-4b3a-9e71-178cf5b27873"}, "posts_183324": {"id": 268357, "owneruserid": 153643, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 268419, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What hypothesis test should I use to test if a binary variable is dependent on an ordinal value?", "tags": "<hypothesis-testing><mathematical-statistics><categorical-data><ordinal-data><binary-data>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I have a number of finishes in football which are labeled either goal or miss. What test should I use?</p>\n\n<pre><code>total shots: 30331\ngoals: 3674\nconversion: 12.11 %\n\n#for each gamestate\n   shots  conv_rate  goals   Gamestate\n0   8339  0.111164    927     -1\n1  14032  0.115522   1621      0\n2   7960  0.141457   1126      1\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Below is the data uncategorized:</p>\n\n<pre><code>    shots  conv_rate  goals    Gamestate\n0       6  0.166667      1         -7\n1      10  0.000000      0         -6\n2      24  0.166667      4         -5\n3     140  0.121429     17         -4\n4     535  0.104673     56         -3\n5    1977  0.109762    217         -2\n6    5647  0.111918    632         -1\n7   14032  0.115522   1621          0\n8    5252  0.136519    717          1\n9    1849  0.149270    276          2\n10    605  0.157025     95          3\n11    163  0.165644     27          4\n12     60  0.133333      8          5\n13     18  0.166667      3          6\n14     13  0.000000      0          7\n</code></pre>\n", "creationdate": "2017-03-18T22:22:36.303000", "posts_rownum": "posts_183324", "provsql": "657ad2eb-d197-4d87-b527-973c3f2e6427"}, "posts_184093": {"id": 269533, "owneruserid": 102189, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 123272, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>From what I have understood, in the cubist algorithm a linear model is made per decision node, and that model is then extended each node further down the tree. This should result in a more continuous predicted value whereas M5P might suffer from discontinuities when jumping from one leaf node to the other by crossing a decision node. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-03-24T09:15:34.927000", "posts_rownum": "posts_184093", "provsql": "33a73fa7-83be-4ea5-aaed-3029946bc756"}, "posts_187348": {"id": 274591, "owneruserid": 142002, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to compare two group means with multiple measures", "tags": "<regression><statistical-significance><mixed-model><random-effects-model>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Suppose we have $N$ patients and two groups. For each patient, he can have one or two measures. Theses measures are classified by the group. Therefore one patient can contribute to both groups. \n  My purpose is to compare the difference between the group means. However, there exist correlation across the multiple measures for each patient, so the group means are correlated. I want to use the mixed effect model:</p>\n\n<p>$Y_{ij}=Group_{ij}*\\beta$ + $Group_{ij}*U_i$ + $\\epsilon_{ij}$</p>\n\n<p>Where Group is a 1 by 2 design matrix and $U_i$ is a vector with two random variables, $var(U_i)$=[$\\sigma_{ij}$], $U_i$ and $\\epsilon_{ij}$ are i.i.d.. Therefore</p>\n\n<p>$cov(Y_{i1},Y_{i2'})=\\sigma_{Group_1,Group_2}$</p>\n\n<p>and</p>\n\n<p>$cov(Y_{ij},Y_{i'j'})=0$</p>\n\n<p>I've tried to use SAS and R to fit the above model. However SAS will give me \"Did not converge\" and R will say \"the random-effects parameters and the residual variance (or scale parameter) are probably unidentifiable\"</p>\n\n<p>Here is my R code for simulation:</p>\n\n<pre><code>getdata<-function(n){\n  set.seed(1)\n  groupMean=c(1,2)\n  data=c()\n  sig=matrix(data=c(1,0.5,0.5,1),nrow = 2)\n  for(i in 1:n){\n    rndEffect=mvrnorm(1,c(0,0),sig)\n    repeatNum=sample(1:2,1)\n    for(j in 1:repeatNum){\n      group=sample(1:2,1)\n      y=groupMean[group]+rndEffect[group]+rnorm(1)\n      data=rbind(data,c(y,group,i))\n    }\n\n  }\n  data=as.data.frame(data)\n  names(data)=c(\"y\",\"group\",\"id\")\n  data$group=as.factor(data$group)\n  return(data)\n}\n\nmydata=getdata(10)\nmodel <- lmer(y ~ group-1 + (0+group|id),mydata)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>I know there are several existing answers related to this question, but none of them can solve my problem, the most related one is here:</p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/95676/how-to-compare-two-sides-of-patients-with-multiple-measures-per-patient\">How to compare two sides of patients with multiple measures per patient?</a></p>\n\n<p>Unfortunately, their suggestion is the same as mine and the answer doesn't have the model or the code.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-04-19T15:07:19.723000", "posts_rownum": "posts_187348", "provsql": "d455040e-9d7e-47e0-9492-508f02f24747"}, "posts_200554": {"id": 297015, "owneruserid": 100048, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 296955, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'd say the distinction between engineering and learning is subjective. This is how I differentiate them,</p>\n\n<p><strong>Feature Engineering:</strong></p>\n\n<p>Handcrafting new variables from the existing ones.</p>\n\n<p>eg: BMI, when the weight and the height are available</p>\n\n<p><strong>Feature Learning:</strong></p>\n\n<p>Letting your system figure out what are the best features for the problem at hand.</p>\n\n<p>The <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feature_learning\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">wikipedia page</a> is a good resource to read more. There's a huge interest in the field of ML to automatically learn new features and <a href=\"http://www.iclr.cc/doku.php?id=ICLR2017:main&redirect=1\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">ICLR</a> is a one conference that you may find many directions.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-08-09T12:23:14.937000", "posts_rownum": "posts_200554", "provsql": "7e722ee7-fa5b-45f7-9d2c-a54d3801139f"}, "posts_206465": {"id": 306175, "owneruserid": 179347, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 305860, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>You can use TADPOLE [a]</p>\n\n<p>You CAN you k-means. The convergence in not guaranteed, but in practice it works.</p>\n\n<p>However, I agree that with a small data-set, HAC makes sense</p>\n\n<p>[a] Accelerating Dynamic Time Warping Clustering with a Novel Admissible Pruning Strategy\n<a href=\"http://www.cs.ucr.edu/~eamonn/Speeded%20Clustering%20Paper%20Camera%20Ready.pdf\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">http://www.cs.ucr.edu/~eamonn/Speeded%20Clustering%20Paper%20Camera%20Ready.pdf</a></p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-10-04T01:23:04.883000", "posts_rownum": "posts_206465", "provsql": "1b320a88-7212-4d8f-a54d-3831bb4caadb"}, "posts_244865": {"id": 367530, "owneruserid": 221014, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 367434, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Yes, the numbers they give produce a p-value of <code>0.000402</code>. They probably made a typo in their publication. </p>\n\n<p>The <a href=\"https://www.socscistatistics.com/pvalues/chidistribution.aspx\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">site</a> I used to compute the p-value.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2018-09-18T21:53:57.243000", "posts_rownum": "posts_244865", "provsql": "fa19b728-75f1-4cdb-8c09-2fc0478f1f8d"}, "posts_245281": {"id": 368157, "owneruserid": 219255, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 368159, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Determine AR term from PACF plot", "tags": "<time-series><mathematical-statistics><arima><acf-pacf>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I have the a time series data, the acf and pacf for which have been displayed below:\n<a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/WyEol.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/WyEol.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a></p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/cBUo5.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/cBUo5.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a></p>\n\n<p>I get that MA term is 1. But I'm confused about AR term since it is geometrically decaying from 7th lag. Do I need to transform the data again to eliminate this?</p>\n\n<p>PS: This data has already been differenced once.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2018-09-22T11:19:55.817000", "posts_rownum": "posts_245281", "provsql": "0d0ae02a-4d1b-4160-a1fc-0f568c7c4144"}, "posts_249376": {"id": 374517, "owneruserid": 225264, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 357162, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>You didn't mention you train strategy, assuming that you use pretrained ImageNet weights:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>You should first freeze everything but your last added dense layer\nand train it for some epochs (say 10).  </li>\n<li>Then you might want to train only 1/2 or 1/4 of all layers counting\nfrom the last one. Especially if your data is natural images. The\ngoal is to fine-tune abstract layers without overfitting the\nnetwork.</li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>Even if you train it from the scratch, from provided log it's quite clear that your model just overfits the training data without learning generalizable features.</p>\n\n<p>To prevent that:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>Use heavy data augmentation</li>\n<li>Add weight decay to all layers and set it to ~ 1e-4 or 1e-5</li>\n<li>As mentioned above, decrease the number of trainable layers,\nfreezing them from left to right if you use pre-trained weights.</li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2018-10-30T21:25:46.520000", "posts_rownum": "posts_249376", "provsql": "f0f69a9c-6dae-43f7-b00c-a5a7472900c2"}, "posts_252717": {"id": 379829, "owneruserid": 11887, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 87336, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Partially answered in comments:</p>\n\n<p>Clearly <span class=\"math-container\">$(x−a)/(b−a)$</span> maps <span class=\"math-container\">$x \\in [a,b]$</span> to <span class=\"math-container\">$[0,1]$</span>. logit(x) maps (0,1) to (−∞,∞). – Nick Cox</p>\n\n<p>indeed the inverse of any continuous-strictly-monotonic-cdf-on-(−∞,∞) maps (0,1) to (−∞,∞). There's uncountable infinities of choices. – Glen_b   </p>\n", "creationdate": "2018-12-01T21:59:44.927000", "posts_rownum": "posts_252717", "provsql": "8b09f0d9-a2cf-42ce-a76a-1b0b13e72432"}, "posts_253954": {"id": 381633, "owneruserid": 226981, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "PROC GENMOD Negative Binomial doesn't predict zeros", "tags": "<regression><sas><negative-binomial-distribution><poisson-regression>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I am using PROC GENMOD with time series data, I have tried to work with Negative Binomial, Poisson, GEE and Zero Inflated Poisson, but in each case when I score my validation dataset, I am getting predicted values which are never zero.</p>\n\n<p>E.g. A customer might buy fuel every 4 weeks, the model does not predict the weeks in between fuel fills as zeros.</p>\n\n<p>Is there a better way of predicting the weeks with zero fuel fills? I assumed Negative Binomial would be able to do this, but the lack of predicted zero outcomes, which represent 78% of the fuel filling weeks (by customer) has made this model ineffective.</p>\n\n<p>Thanks in advance!!</p>\n", "creationdate": "2018-12-12T11:08:20.800000", "posts_rownum": "posts_253954", "provsql": "a7acb866-ef13-410c-9c5a-4ec5d22c3ea0"}, "posts_256788": {"id": 386716, "owneruserid": 232372, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "When does my autoencoder start to overfit?", "tags": "<neural-networks><overfitting><unsupervised-learning><autoencoders><stochastic-gradient-descent>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I am working on anomaly detection using an <strong>autoencoder</strong> neural network with <span class=\"math-container\">$1$</span> hidden layer. This is an <strong>unsupervised</strong> setting, as I do not have previous examples of anomalies. The input data has patterns but also varies a lot, hence, is partly stochastic in nature.</p>\n\n<p>For understanding purposes, I trained a (complete) autoencoder with dimensions input = <span class=\"math-container\">$500$</span>, hidden = <span class=\"math-container\">$500$</span>, output = <span class=\"math-container\">$500$</span> and sigmoid functions in the hidden and output layer. My training data has dimension <span class=\"math-container\">$X\\in[0,1]^{5000\\times500}$</span> (500 variables, 5000 samples). I used <span class=\"math-container\">$3$</span> algorithms, with learning rate <span class=\"math-container\">$0.01$</span>, mini batch size <span class=\"math-container\">$64$</span>, and pretty much the standard algo-parameters in Keras/TensorFlow:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>standard stochastic gradient descent (SGD)</li>\n<li>advanced/extended SGD with Nesterov momentum <span class=\"math-container\">$0.9$</span> and learning rate decay <span class=\"math-container\">$10^{-8}$</span></li>\n<li>Adam optimizer (<span class=\"math-container\">$\\beta_1=0.9$</span>, <span class=\"math-container\">$\\beta_2=0.999$</span>, learning rate decay <span class=\"math-container\">$0$</span>)</li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>The image below shows the corresponding error curves. In my case both keep decreasing (except for Adam) so I would say \"keep training\". On the other hand I know intuitively that I should not train so long because there must be some overfitting going on. So how do I know when to stop training, how would you interpret the result below? Would I be right, to just take Adam and use 250 epochs (even though it has a wide bias between training/validation sets)?</p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/qL2fH.png\" rel=\"noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/qL2fH.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a></p>\n", "creationdate": "2019-01-11T14:38:02.043000", "posts_rownum": "posts_256788", "provsql": "db5979f4-3c58-490e-ab8d-cfb54a031222"}, "posts_257513": {"id": 387743, "owneruserid": 209784, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Determining variance of UMVUE", "tags": "<mathematical-statistics><estimation><unbiased-estimator>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Let <span class=\"math-container\">$X_1,...,X_n$</span> be iid with pdf given by <span class=\"math-container\">$f(x;\\theta)=\\frac{log\\theta}{\\theta^{x-1}}I(x>1)$</span>. My task is to determine if the <span class=\"math-container\">$\\mu=E[X]=1+\\frac{1}{log\\theta}$</span> can be estimated efficiently, i.e. if the UMVUE for <span class=\"math-container\">$\\mu$</span> achieves the Cramer-Rao lower bound. Here's my work:</p>\n\n<p>The pdf <span class=\"math-container\">$f(x;\\theta)$</span> is a member of the one-parameter exponential family, so <span class=\"math-container\">$T=T(X)=\\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$</span> is complete-sufficient for <span class=\"math-container\">$\\theta$</span>, i.e. for <span class=\"math-container\">$\\mu$</span>. Furthermore, <span class=\"math-container\">$g(T)=\\frac{T}{n}$</span> is unbiased for <span class=\"math-container\">$\\mu$</span>, so by Lehmann-Scheffe, <span class=\"math-container\">$g(X)=\\bar X$</span> is the UMVUE. </p>\n\n<p>To see if <span class=\"math-container\">$\\bar X$</span> attains the Cramer-Rao lower-bound, we must calculate its variance, where <span class=\"math-container\">$V[\\bar X]=\\frac{V[X]}{n}$</span>. Here is where I'm stuck. To get <span class=\"math-container\">$V[X]$</span>, how should I calculate <span class=\"math-container\">$E[X^2]$</span>? Should I simply use the integration method? I believe it would require integration by parts twice, and I end up with very strange expression. Is there some other route I could take? </p>\n", "creationdate": "2019-01-17T15:28:31.027000", "posts_rownum": "posts_257513", "provsql": "41163de7-be81-430b-b904-a3bd1b93d3a5"}, "posts_260772": {"id": 392478, "owneruserid": 1352, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 392475, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>The first thing to look at is what happened in months 10 and 11: where did the large increases come from? Has the product reached a plateau? If so, essentially forecast a flat line on the level of sales in months 11-17. Or is another increase of a similar magnitude likely? Or was this a one-time push that saturated the market, so that future sales will drop down to the level in months 1-9?</p>\n\n<p>Forecasting 36 months based on 18 months history is very hard.</p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>with the best fitting curve (an exponential curve)</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>In-sample fit is not a good proxy for out-of-sample predictive accuracy. Fitting an exponential curve to 18 months of history and extrapolating 36 months out invites disaster. You should not be expending more than two parameters on only 18 observations.</p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>the MSE, MAD and MAPE are too high</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>What is \"too high\"? Your series may simply be hard to forecast. <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/q/222179/1352\">How to know that your machine learning problem is hopeless?</a></p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>and the residual plots suggest correlation. </p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>Given the upward trend, this does not surprise me. The important thing is to understand where that trend came from, and whether the driver is likely to continue.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2019-02-14T12:53:29.463000", "posts_rownum": "posts_260772", "provsql": "127682f0-bf85-48ea-8f5a-f8708526ac81"}, "posts_265353": {"id": 399319, "owneruserid": 242367, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Find a vector that satisfies the following: i) it has a given correlation with a second vector and ii) it is orthogonal to a set of vectors", "tags": "<correlation><orthogonal>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I would like to generate a vector <span class=\"math-container\">$\\vec{u}$</span> of dimension <span class=\"math-container\">$n$</span>, so that i) it has a given correlation <span class=\"math-container\">$r$</span> with a second vector <span class=\"math-container\">$\\vec{v}$</span> and ii) it is orthogonal to a set of <span class=\"math-container\">$m$</span> vectors <span class=\"math-container\">$A = \\{\\vec{w}_1, \\vec{w}_2, \\dots, \\vec{w}_k\\}$</span>. I would like to do it in R. Any idea?</p>\n\n<p>thanks a lot!</p>\n\n<p>PS: Solving <span class=\"math-container\">$A \\times x = 0$</span> would fix ii). Also, satisfiying i) is relatively straightforward. However I have not been able to find a way to to ensure both i) and ii).</p>\n", "creationdate": "2019-03-25T14:37:00.407000", "posts_rownum": "posts_265353", "provsql": "3091bd8a-0264-4b71-a8bf-7e5c881cbe94"}, "posts_266538": {"id": 401072, "owneruserid": 212689, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 401035, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>If you genuinely have a small population and you manage to sample more than 5% of it, you can apply the finite population correction, where you multiply your standard error by: <span class=\"math-container\">$FPC=\\sqrt{\\frac{N-n}{N-1}}$</span>, where N is your population size and n is your sample size.</p>\n<p>However, I would urge caution on a few points, as I'm not convinced that you will meet the assumptions required to use the finite population correction:</p>\n<ol>\n<li><p>You need a random sample of your population, will you achieve that?</p>\n</li>\n<li><p>1% of a large population is still a large number.</p>\n</li>\n<li><p>You presumably want to make inferences about people with the condition in future, e.g. those who have not been born yet. So your population may actually be larger than you think. Even though that doesn't help you with recruitment for your study!</p>\n</li>\n</ol>\n<p>The difference you are trying to detect is quite small (and potentially very small relative to the expected population variance, which you don't give) which is probably why the software estimates that you need a large sample size.</p>\n<p>Others may have helpful suggestions for how to mitigate the effects of your small sample size.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2019-04-03T22:56:10.780000", "posts_rownum": "posts_266538", "provsql": "e51f192c-f078-4743-8313-31429d42e3a3"}, "posts_297274": {"id": 447319, "owneruserid": 153364, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 447303, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>If I'm reading your question correctly you are simply asking about <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_comparisons_problem\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">multiple comparison</a> in statistics which is a well known phenomena. To remedy this, you can correct your significance using something like a <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonferroni_correction\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Bonferroni-correction</a>, although many types of correction methods exist.</p>\n\n<p>Note that you also need to consider the implication of your analysis. Is it something that will dictate how your company or medical department operates? Then you should probably take it more seriously than if your study is simply to pave way and direct future research. Multiple comparison and how we address it, is in essence just a dance between type-1 and type-2 errors.</p>\n\n<p>EDIT: After reading your edit.</p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>This may be my main point: does significance at the regression\n  coefficient level mean anything in this case?</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>The coefficient tells you both the direction and size of the impact your covariates have on the dependent variable, with respect to the model as a whole. If the p-value of a covariate is significant, but the model contains enough individual covariates with no pre-determined hypothesis, that you suspect the unadjusted p-values may be erroneous, the coefficient and the CI may be inflated, even if truly significant. Another important part with respect to coefficients is how well you have controlled for confounders as these can dramatically change the coefficients in your model. <a href=\"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23583358\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Related literature</a> on this topic.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-01-31T18:33:43.840000", "posts_rownum": "posts_297274", "provsql": "dcd1ee6c-4aa6-4e35-88e9-b1f9c6d093bd"}, "posts_308620": {"id": 465408, "owneruserid": 203570, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 465399, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Hi you can train in self supervised way your 4D time series. \nYou can use a convolutionnal network you will have 4 inputs channels.\nYou will use then a MSE loss between your input let's says last 2048 points and prediction set at the 256 points for example.\nIn order to achieve a good accuracy you can train a convolutionnal VAE autoencodeur and use the encoder in your convolutionnal network for prediction.\nLike :\nInput -> Encode -> feedForward -> prediction</p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-05-09T13:10:08.897000", "posts_rownum": "posts_308620", "provsql": "929df6ad-7e61-4e11-b128-7340ef142171"}, "posts_313635": {"id": 472618, "owneruserid": 1352, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 472610, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>The most reliable way of understanding the capabilities of a package is, as always its CRAN page. In the specific case of <a href=\"https://cran.r-project.org/package=fable\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">the <code>fable</code> package</a>, we find <a href=\"https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/fable/fable.pdf\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">its reference manual</a> and two different vignettes, <a href=\"https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/fable/vignettes/fable.html\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">one introduction</a> and <a href=\"https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/fable/vignettes/transformations.html\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">one vignette on forecasting with transformations</a>.</p>\n<p>The reference manual in particular looks helpful. For instance, I see no less than ten <code>fitted.*()</code> functions:</p>\n<pre><code>> library(dplyr)\n> ls(getNamespace("fable"), all.names=TRUE) %>%\n+ grep(pattern="fitted",value=TRUE)\n[1] "fitted.AR"         "fitted.ARIMA"      "fitted.croston"   \n[4] "fitted.ETS"        "fitted.model_mean" "fitted.NNETAR"    \n[7] "fitted.RW"         "fitted.TSLM"       "fitted.VAR"\n</code></pre>\n<p>True, not all of them are very different (<code>fitted.AR()</code> vs. <code>fitted.ARIMA()</code>), but there are quite a few more than you mention (e.g., <code>fitted.NNETAR()</code>, <code>fitted.fable_theta()</code> or <code>fitted.croston()</code>).</p>\n<p>Also note that <code>fable</code> is the successor package to <code>forecast</code>, so over time, it will likely accumulate more models.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-06-17T05:44:41.513000", "posts_rownum": "posts_313635", "provsql": "2cf0bc8b-7899-43af-8a56-50efd918af84"}, "posts_316866": {"id": 477352, "owneruserid": 69508, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 230752, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>This is only a partial answer because it doesn't meet the accuracy requirements, however I'll explain where the answer comes from. As has been pointed out by <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/users/919/whuber\">whuber♦</a> above in the comments and in this <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/26988/probability-of-finding-a-particular-sequence-of-base-pairs\">post</a>, the specific content of the strings influence the true probability of the event described in the OP.</p>\n<p>Instead of analytically working out these many details, one might try a simulated approach. The following is an implementation in Python of an algorithm that simply generates k-mers of length 9 and 500 sequences of length 1000, counts occurrences of the k-mer in the other sequences, and puts the resulting count into a list. There are improvements that can be made to this code to improve the time and space requirements, but I think this simpler example communicates the process adequately.</p>\n<pre class=\"lang-py prettyprint-override\"><code>from random import choice\nimport numpy as np\n\ndef randseq(n):\n    return ''.join([choice(['A', 'T', 'C', 'G']) for i in range(n)])\n\ncounts = []\ni = 0\nwhile len(counts) < 5 or 3 * np.std(counts) / np.sqrt(i) > 0.0001:\n    i += 1\n    kmer = randseq(9)\n    kcount = 0\n    for j in range(500):\n        seq = randseq(1000)\n        if kmer in seq:\n            kcount += seq.count(kmer)\n    counts.append(kcount)\n    print(i, kcount, np.mean(counts), 3 * np.std(counts) / np.sqrt(i))\n</code></pre>\n<p>Using the above, I found that a sample of <span class=\"math-container\">$n=14199$</span> iterations of the 'experiment' yielded a mean of <span class=\"math-container\">$1.8833016409606311 \\pm 0.03492470125969519$</span> (3 times standard error). I stopped the calculations at this point because I realized that the mean would converge very slowly. The standard error of the mean is <span class=\"math-container\">$$s_{\\bar{x}} = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{n}} \\sqrt{\\frac{(\\sum x_i - \\bar{x})^2}{n}} = \\frac{s_x}{\\sqrt{n}}$$</span></p>\n<p>where <span class=\"math-container\">$n$</span> is the sample size, <span class=\"math-container\">$x_i$</span> is an instance of the random variable representing the number of occurrences of the k-mer in the other sequences, and <span class=\"math-container\">$\\bar{x}$</span> is the estimate of the mean of this random variable.</p>\n<p>Since the mean and standard deviation are consistent estimators, we need only have a sufficiently large <span class=\"math-container\">$n$</span> to reach an arbitrary precision in <span class=\"math-container\">$\\bar{x}$</span> as calculated in terms of <span class=\"math-container\">$s_{\\bar{x}}$</span>. Thinking in terms of confidence intervals, perhaps we'd be satisfied with <span class=\"math-container\">$3 s_{\\bar{x}} = 10^{-4}$</span> being a way of declaring whether we've met the accuracy requirement, giving us:</p>\n<p><span class=\"math-container\">$$\\frac{s_x}{\\sqrt{n}} = \\frac{10^{-4}}{3}$$</span></p>\n<p>Given that my data had <span class=\"math-container\">$s_x = 1.387203975627196$</span> at <span class=\"math-container\">$n=14199$</span>, we'll use that value for a ball-park estimate. Substituting for <span class=\"math-container\">$s_x$</span>, and solving for <span class=\"math-container\">$n$</span>, I would expect that the required sample size using this approach would be <span class=\"math-container\">$n=1731901383$</span>. My approach here doesn't work to answer the question in a reasonable amount of time, but would <em>eventually</em> yield the correct answer.</p>\n<h3 id=\"update-8aqg\">Update</h3>\n<p>I re-ran the simulations and obtained a closer <span class=\"math-container\">$3 \\sigma$</span> estimate of <span class=\"math-container\">$\\bar{x} = 1.8897422883888795 \\pm 0.0043822154484445775$</span> where <span class=\"math-container\">$n=886650$</span>.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-07-15T19:31:39.497000", "posts_rownum": "posts_316866", "provsql": "c2b84162-0dd1-439e-a665-d7697dd45405"}, "posts_317062": {"id": 477629, "owneruserid": 163146, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 477627, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Basically, you reduce the input (dimension) by reducing the neurons per layer. This is the encoder part.\nAfterwards, based on that very low dimensional representation, the entire data is broken down to only important features.\nThis is what you finally wanna' have: A meaningful, low dimensional data representation.\nTo train and validate this encoder function, you decode this data by mostly using the same topology in a reversed manner.\nNow there are two options:</p>\n<ol>\n<li>Either you use the encoder + decoder: So you wanna' be able to restore all your data again only based on these few features. This would be something like a nonlinear PCA.</li>\n<li>Or you detach the encoder part and use it for new data.</li>\n</ol>\n<p>A good example, e.g., is the use for mobile communication which breaks down/encodes the data so that only a significant part of your speech remains, then this data is transfered and at the receiver side it is decoded.\nDespite from that concept the handling and so on is quite the same like for every neural network (train, validate, minimize error function and so on..).</p>\n<p><a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/ScCqO.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/ScCqO.png\" alt=\"AE\" /></a></p>\n<p><a href=\"https://lilianweng.github.io/lil-log/2018/08/12/from-autoencoder-to-beta-vae.html\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Image source</a></p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-07-17T11:07:59.030000", "posts_rownum": "posts_317062", "provsql": "f8e8d65d-8521-48be-92ed-8578bbb0b015"}, "posts_317063": {"id": 477630, "owneruserid": 291597, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Fitting Joint Model with GLMM", "tags": "<r><mixed-model><survival><glmm>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I'm looking to fit a joint survival model (<a href=\"https://www.r-bloggers.com/an-introduction-to-joint-modeling-in-r/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">example</a>). For those who are unfamiliar, joint survival models are Cox proportional hazard models where the covariates are allowed to be time-varying and are actually predictions from a mixed effects model. Typically these are fit by fitting an linear mixed effects model and survival model separately, and then putting the outputs into a joint modeling function. Example using <code>library(JM)</code> taken from <a href=\"https://aurora-mareviv.github.io/talesofr/2018/02/intro-joint-modeling-r/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">this online example</a>:</p>\n<pre><code>library(JM)\n# Animation example \n# Mixed-effects model fit\nlmeFit.p1 <- lme(log(pro) ~ time + time:treat, data = prothro,\n    random = ~ time | id)  \n\n# Cox survival model fit\nsurvFit.p1 <- coxph(Surv(Time, death) ~ treat, data = prothros, x = TRUE)  \n\n# Joint model\njointFit.p1 <- jointModel(lmeFit.p1, survFit.p1, timeVar = "time",\n    method = "piecewise-PH-aGH")\n</code></pre>\n<p>However, in the case of my particular research question, my covariates are not normally distributed (they are rates, and are therefore Poisson distributed). I assume that this means that I'll need to be using a GLMM to estimate the time-varying predictors/covariates instead of a simple LMM.</p>\n<p>I'll be running my analyses in <code>R</code>, so am looking for packages that will accommodate GLMMs in the mixed model, but everything that I seem to find online only uses a <a href=\"https://www.annalsthoracicsurgery.org/article/S0003-4975(12)00409-2/pdf\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">linear mixed effect model</a> (e.g. from <code>lme</code>).</p>\n<p>Does anyone have any recommendations for extending the joint model to include GLMMs and/or any package recommendations to do so? I know that there are lots of GLMM packages out there that fit GLMMs, but is there anything that is analogous to the above code but using GLMMs instead of LMMs?</p>\n<p>As an aside, I also am looking into if transformations of the covariate is appropriate. However, I'm hoping to not lose interpretability on this particular covariate.</p>\n<p>Thank you!</p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-07-17T11:08:16.017000", "posts_rownum": "posts_317063", "provsql": "2b582478-6091-4430-bdfc-fb3b1ac9bae2"}, "posts_320522": {"id": 483263, "owneruserid": 294173, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to decide if categorical variable is significant in cox regression, SPSS", "tags": "<multiple-regression><survival><spss><cox-model>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I performed univariate analysis to identify predictors of survival in a cohort. In a second step I performed multiple cox regression of the factors significant in univariate analysis.\nOne variable is categorical with 4 categories. I am trying to decide whether I should consider this variable as significant in cox regression or not. So kind of a global p-value for this variable is needed. SPSS shows four p-values: one for the reference value (marked black) and one for each of the other values (vs. the reference value).</p>\n<p>Is this marked p value kind of a global p-value for this variable? Or do I have to perform some other test ?</p>\n<p>The variables significant on cox-regression will be incorporated in a predictive score, so a decision needs to be made whether the "whole" variable is considered significant.</p>\n<p><a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/pdVa6.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/pdVa6.png\" alt=\"x\" /></a></p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-08-16T20:09:45.947000", "posts_rownum": "posts_320522", "provsql": "33ccd674-f5a4-42ca-bfef-e09417455f4a"}, "posts_323873": {"id": 487966, "owneruserid": 208417, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 487974, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Interaction and nested structure in symbolic formulae", "tags": "<mathematical-statistics><mixed-model><lme4-nlme>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I am using the following two structures, one simpler and one more complex, in <code>lme4</code> format which, as you can see, have an interaction term in the fixed effects as well as a nested structure with varying intercepts per dyad/participant and after that in the interaction per electrode.</p>\n<p><code>Signal ~ Repetition * Predictor + (1 | Dyad/Participant)</code></p>\n<p>My take on the 1st one is:\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$\nY_{i}=\\beta _{0}+\\beta _{1}Repetition\\times Predictor+\\varepsilon _{Dyad\\mid Participant}+\\varepsilon _{i }\n$$</span></p>\n<p><code>Signal ~ Repetition * Predictor + (1 | Dyad/Participant) + (1 + Repetition * Predictor || Electrode)</code></p>\n<p>My take on the 2nd one:\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$\nY_{i}=\\beta _{0}+\\beta _{1}Repetition\\times Predictor+\\varepsilon _{Dyad\\mid Participant}+\\varepsilon _{Repetition\\times Predictor\\parallel Electrode}+\\varepsilon _{i }\n$$</span></p>\n<p>I would appreciate some cross validation or correction.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-09-17T15:04:46.750000", "posts_rownum": "posts_323873", "provsql": "4d07523f-56ca-4626-b9cf-6c0dd913db8a"}, "posts_324363": {"id": 488717, "owneruserid": 215932, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 488709, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>When you have an equation like (1) with a constraint which requires minimization or maximization it suggests that Lagrange multipliers could be used (the lambda notation also suggest Lagrange multipliers were used).</p>\n<p>But in ridge regression the constraint is not an equality, meaning the generalization of Lagrange multipliers is needed—the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions. This gets you from (1) to (2).</p>\n<p>The blue circle represents the constraint for the case of two covariates in your regression model. The solution (betas) has to be somewhere in the blue circle. The contours are local minima, hopefully someone else can explain how the contour plot is as it is.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-09-23T05:01:13.543000", "posts_rownum": "posts_324363", "provsql": "9725d97c-3861-4309-8e9b-003393988530"}, "posts_326368": {"id": 491671, "owneruserid": 297766, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 491391, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I will then answer my own question. The PMF is correct, because:</p>\n<ul>\n<li>all probabilities sum to 1</li>\n<li><span class=\"math-container\">$E[Z]$</span> gives the result I expected</li>\n<li>I generalized the PMF to <span class=\"math-container\">$n$</span> random variables with a nonlinear transformation and the expected value is still correct (I checked it by sampling 1 million times)</li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2020-10-12T23:48:26.663000", "posts_rownum": "posts_326368", "provsql": "fc4f5106-96f4-46d3-9357-2e1ea5079b92"}, "posts_327392": {"id": 493123, "owneruserid": 143489, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 492836, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>You are interested in the distribution of number of successes, that is how many dice out of an initial <span class=\"math-container\">$x$</span> will be left in the game after three rolls, given the rules. You estimated <span class=\"math-container\">$E[X]=np=20 \\cdot 0.11=2.2$</span>, this is the expected number of dies that remain in the game at the end. The variance is <span class=\"math-container\">$Var[X]=np(1-p)=20 \\cdot 0.11(1-0.11)=1.958$</span>.</p>\n<p>Your question, at the least the last one, is how many dice would you have to roll, such that you decrease the variance enough that 90 % of outcomes are within one standard deviation of the expected value. So if the expected value is 2.2, 90 % of outcomes would have to be between 1 and 3.</p>\n<p>This cannot be done. In fact, what you will find is that, by increasing the number of dice, while keeping the probability the same, the variance actually increases (so you would have to decrease the number of dice to decrease the variance). I think you got this idea from the distribution of the mean, where increasing the sample size decreases the variance of the distribution, that is the distribution gets narrower.</p>\n<p>In your case the only way you can decrease the variance is by changing the probability of success (which is related to changing the number of rolls, which is the question in your title but not in the actual text). This is actually a rule which is sometimes used when estimating the sample size, the variance is greatest at probability 0.5, and then decreases as you move towards the extremes 0 and 1.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-10-22T06:14:59.507000", "posts_rownum": "posts_327392", "provsql": "7547e465-9331-4176-b8a7-77f5b6e025fa"}, "posts_330803": {"id": 498103, "owneruserid": 1352, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 498101, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>The most balanced partition would be the one that has equal mass in all bins. So we should compare each partition to the equal-mass one.</p>\n<p>The most natural comparison metric would be the <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_mover%27s_distance\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Earth Mover's Distance</a> (EMD), which calculates how much mass needs to be shifted how far to turn one distribution to another one. In your case, Partition 1 will have a smaller EMD to the uniform partition than Partition 2.</p>\n<p>The EMD is also known as the <a href=\"/questions/tagged/wasserstein\" class=\"post-tag\" title=\"show questions tagged 'wasserstein'\" rel=\"tag\">wasserstein</a> metric. You may want to look through the tag.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-11-26T06:50:22.050000", "posts_rownum": "posts_330803", "provsql": "4088a45b-4d12-4dcb-9f8a-9e3758b29e5b"}, "posts_331210": {"id": 498679, "owneruserid": 221384, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 498646, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Note: This is just a comment but to quote a long code, I put it here.</p>\n<blockquote>\n<pre><code>for (ite in 2:NSim){\n#Full conditional for pi\n\n pi[ite]=rbeta(1, sum(delta[ite-1,])+0.5, sum(1-delta[ite-1,])+0.5)\n\n #Full conditional for delta\n for(j in 1:4){\n  p1=pi[ite]*exp(-beta[ite-1,j]^2/(20))\n  p0=((1-pi[ite])*10^3)*exp(-500*beta[ite-1,j]^2)\n  cat('\\n',ite,j,(p1/(p0+p1)))\n  delta[ite,j]=rbinom(1, 1,prob=(p1/(p0+p1)))\n  }\n</code></pre>\n</blockquote>\n<p>The error says that maybe <span class=\"math-container\">$p1$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$p0$</span> are NAs. My experience when checking this type of error is that. Instead of for loop, just give <span class=\"math-container\">$ite=2$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$j=1$</span>. Compute p1 and p0 as your formulas. Check carefully if they are NAs or not. If the codes are symmetric with regard to <span class=\"math-container\">$iter$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$j$</span>, and if you can correct the error for this case, it will pass this.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-11-30T11:05:08.520000", "posts_rownum": "posts_331210", "provsql": "2e305911-e4cd-4543-b8df-a64ebb3586eb"}, "posts_335384": {"id": 505207, "owneruserid": 45971, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 505471, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How does forward stepwise regression select variables", "tags": "<regression><least-squares><stepwise-regression>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Suppose there are <span class=\"math-container\">$p = 3$</span> variables total and suppose the forward stepwise procedure selects the third variable. The forward stepwise procedure will assign it a positive coefficient if and only if the following two conditions are true:\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$X_3^Ty/||X_3||_2 \\geq \\pm X_1^Ty/||X_1||_2$$</span>\nand\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$X_3^Ty/||X_3||_2 \\geq \\pm X_2^Ty/||X_2||_2$$</span>\nwhere <span class=\"math-container\">$X_j$</span> is the <span class=\"math-container\">$j$</span>th column vector of the design matrix, <span class=\"math-container\">$X \\in \\mathbb{R}^{N \\times p}$</span>, and <span class=\"math-container\">$y\\in \\mathbb{R}^n$</span> is the response vector.</p>\n<p><strong>My question is: how does "the 3rd variable minimizes the residual sum error" translate to the above two conditions?</strong></p>\n<p>From my understanding, the procedure would select the third variable <span class=\"math-container\">$X_3$</span> if <span class=\"math-container\">$\\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - \\hat{\\beta}_3X_{3i})^2$</span> is smaller than  <span class=\"math-container\">$\\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - \\hat{\\beta}_1X_{1i})^2$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$\\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - \\hat{\\beta}_2X_{2i})^2,$</span> where <span class=\"math-container\">$\\hat{\\beta}_j = \\left(X_j^TX_j\\right)^{-1}X_j^Ty$</span> is the OLS estimate for the <span class=\"math-container\">$j$</span>th variable. How does this translate to the 2 conditions I've listed above? class=\"math-container\">$y$</span>.)</p>\n<p>Naively, we can do an MCMC on the jointly density <span class=\"math-container\">$p(x, y)$</span>, getting a joint vector <span (e.g. papers like <a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.7392\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">this</a> indicate that the complexity of MCMC sampling scales polynomially with dimension)</p>\n<p>Question: Are there better techniques to sample from <span class=\"math-container\">$p(x)$</span> when <span class=\"math-container\">$n \\gg m$</span>?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2021-05-04T07:20:22.743000", "posts_rownum": "posts_346193", "provsql": "9a934896-010f-4a59-9184-139a99b3a779"}, "posts_359760": {"id": 547886, "owneruserid": 337591, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 548659, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Dimensions in the PAM method", "tags": "<clustering>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I am just starting my adventure with data analysis. And I have a problem with understanding the results obtained in the PAM method. Could someone explain to me in a simple way what are these two dimensions Dim1 and Dim2 obtained in this method?\n<a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/girKc.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/girKc.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\" /></a></p>\n<p>Above I present an example visualization of the results of the PAM method in which my data has been divided into 5 clusters. I understand what mediodes are but unfortunately I don't understand what these Dim1 and Dim2 are.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2021-10-11T19:20:10.507000", "posts_rownum": "posts_359760", "provsql": "4f6e24cc-b986-4b21-843b-8e789a70f227"}, "posts_361904": {"id": 551145, "owneruserid": 919, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 550810, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p><strong>The answer is no:</strong> the univariate regressions can all have positive coefficients, yet the multiple regression can involve negative coefficients.</p>\n<p><strong>You ask for intuition.</strong>  One route to that is through the geometric interpretation of the Ordinary Least Squares solution, as expressed by the Normal equations: they state that the coefficients in the regression of a column of <span class=\"math-container\">$n$</span> data <span class=\"math-container\">$y$</span> on explanatory columns <span class=\"math-container\">$x_i$</span> are the coefficients of the orthogonal projection of the <em>vector</em> <span class=\"math-container\">$y$</span> onto the span of the <em>vectors</em> <span class=\"math-container\">$x_i$</span> in <span class=\"math-container\">$n$</span>-dimensional Euclidean space <span class=\"math-container\">$R^n.$</span></p>\n<p>Although <span class=\"math-container\">$n$</span> dimensions sounds like a lot, <strong>you don't need more than two dimensions to visualize useful examples:</strong> just limit yourself to <span class=\"math-container\">$2$</span> explanatory variables <span class=\"math-container\">$x_1$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$x_2.$</span>  <em>They</em> determine a plane (at least when they're not collinear) and we may suppose <span class=\"math-container\">$y$</span> is located in that very plane.</p>\n<p>Here, to illustrate, is a situation where <span class=\"math-container\">$y= x_1 - x_2.$</span>  As indicated at the bottom right, although these vectors "live" in <span class=\"math-container\">$R^n,$</span> we can draw them faithfully within the plane of the paper.</p>\n<p><a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/aMdFC.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/aMdFC.png\" alt=\"Figure\" /></a></p>\n<p>The gray area at the left is the locus of points whose projection onto <em>some</em> of the <span class=\"math-container\">$x_i$</span> has a negative coefficient.  It's the union of all the half-planes behind the <span class=\"math-container\">$x_i.$</span>  Provided <span class=\"math-container\">$y$</span> lies outside that gray area, its regression (<em>i.e.</em>, projection) onto any of the variables <span class=\"math-container\">$x_i$</span> <em>individually</em> is guaranteed to have a <em>positive</em> value.  Nevertheless, whenever <span class=\"math-container\">$y$</span> is outside the infinite wedge lying between the <span class=\"math-container\">$x_1$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$x_2$</span> direction (their positive cone <span class=\"math-container\">$\\{\\alpha x_1 + \\beta x_2\\mid \\alpha\\ge 0, \\beta\\ge 0 \\}$</span>), it (obviously) cannot have all its coefficients positive. Likewise, I know that the variance of the mean is equal to the variance over n.</p>\n<p>My question is: if the variances of the respective random variables are not the same, is the variance of the mean still an average of the variances?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2023-03-21T18:47:33.617000", "posts_rownum": "posts_403551", "provsql": "b6c3311e-11c0-47b6-9eb3-8a841000e04c"}, "posts_405208": {"id": 612274, "owneruserid": 385190, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 612281, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Prove that 2nd order polynomial kernel is positive semi-definite", "tags": "<machine-learning><self-study><kernel-trick><linear-algebra>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I'm trying to prove that the 2nd order polynomial kernel, <span class=\"math-container\">$K(x_i, x_j) = (x_i^Tx_j + 1)^2$</span> is a valid kernel which satisfies the following conditions:</p>\n<ol>\n<li>K is symmetric, that is, <span class=\"math-container\">$K(x_i, x_j) = K(x_j, x_i)$</span>.</li>\n<li>K is positive semi-definite, that is, <span class=\"math-container\">$\\forall v \\space\\space  v^TKv \\geq 0.$</span></li>\n</ol>\n<p>We can actually prove that second-order polynomial kernel function is a valid kernel by deriving the corresponding transformation function <span class=\"math-container\">$\\phi(x) = [1, \\sqrt{2}x_1, ..., \\sqrt{2}x_d, x_1x_1, x_1x_2, ..., x_1x_d, x_2x_1, ...x_dx_d]^T$</span> where <span class=\"math-container\">$d$</span> is the number of features (dimensionality). A related question can be found here about the normal assumption of the error (or more generally of the data if we do not have prior knowledge about the data).

Basically,

  1. It is mathematically convenient to use normal distribution. (It's related to Least Squares fitting and easy to solve with pseudoinverse)
  2. Due to Central Limit Theorem, we may assume that there are lots of underlying facts affecting the process and the sum of these individual effects will tend to behave like normal distribution. In practice, it seems to be so.

An important note from there is that, as Terence Tao states here, "Roughly speaking, this theorem asserts that if one takes a statistic that is a combination of many independent and randomly fluctuating components, with no one component having a decisive influence on the whole, then that statistic will be approximately distributed according to a law called the normal distribution".

To make this clear, let me write a Python code snippet

# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
"""
Illustration of the central limit theorem

@author: İsmail Arı, http://ismailari.com
@date: 31.03.2011
"""
 
import scipy, scipy.stats
import numpy as np
import pylab
 
#===============================================================
# Uncomment one of the distributions below and observe the result
#===============================================================
x = scipy.linspace(0,10,11)
#y = scipy.stats.binom.pmf(x,10,0.2) # binom
#y = scipy.stats.expon.pdf(x,scale=4) # exp
#y = scipy.stats.gamma.pdf(x,2) # gamma
#y = np.ones(np.size(x)) # uniform
y = scipy.random.random(np.size(x)) # random
 
y = y / sum(y);

N = 3
ax = pylab.subplot(N+1,1,1)
pylab.plot(x,y)

# Plotting details 
ax.set_xticks([10])
ax.axis([0, 2**N * 10, 0, np.max(y)*1.1])
ax.set_yticks([round(np.max(y),2)])
 
#===============================================================
# Plots
#===============================================================
for i in np.arange(N)+1:
    y = np.convolve(y,y)
    y = y / sum(y);    
 
    x = np.linspace(2*np.min(x), 2*np.max(x), len(y))
    ax = pylab.subplot(N+1,1,i+1)
    pylab.plot(x,y)
    ax.axis([0, 2**N * 10, 0, np.max(y)*1.1])
    ax.set_xticks([2**i * 10])
    ax.set_yticks([round(np.max(y),3)])
 
pylab.show()

As can be seen from the figures, the resulting distribution (sum) tends towards a normal distribution regardless of the individual distribution types. So, if we do not have enough information about the underlying effects in the data, normality assumption is reasonable.
