I fit an ARMA model with the differenced data, and the best fit I think was a model with one degree of differencing and first order auto-correlation at lag 2.</p>\n\n<p>My question is, what on earth can I use this model for? Time series always seems so useful in the textbooks when it's about hare populations and oil prices, but now I've done my own the result seems so abstract as to be completely opaque. The differenced scores correlate with each other at lag two, but I can't really advise everyone to be on high alert two days after a serious incident in all seriousness.</p>\n\n<p>Or can I?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-20T07:56:16.297000", "posts_rownum": "posts_229", "provsql": "6c752694-43fc-4253-91ae-4dfae922b0ad"}, "posts_262": {"id": 276, "owneruserid": 90, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 553, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How large should a sample be for a given estimation technique and parameters?", "tags": "<sample-size><estimation><least-squares><maximum-likelihood>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Is there a rule-of thumb or even any way at all to tell how large a sample should be in order to estimate a model with a given number of parameters? </p>\n\n<p>So, for example, if I want to estimate a least-squares regression with 5 parameters, how large should the sample be? </p>\n\n<p>Does it matter what estimation technique you are using (e.g. maximum likelihood, least squares, GMM), or how many or what tests you are going to perform? Should the sample variability be taken into account when making the decision?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-20T11:43:25.013000", "posts_rownum": "posts_262", "provsql": "e0614208-f983-458d-bfcc-48f4ef451f72"}, "posts_1216": {"id": 1266, "owneruserid": 253, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2338, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "A non-parametric repeated-measures multi-way Anova in R?", "tags": "<r><anova><repeated-measures><nonparametric><manova>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>The following question is one of those holy grails for me for some time now, I hope someone might be able to offer a good advice.</p>\n\n<p>I wish to perform a non-parametric repeated measures multiway anova using R.</p>\n\n<p>I have been doing some online searching and reading for some time, and so far was able to find solutions for only some of the cases: friedman test for one way nonparametric repeated measures anova, ordinal regression with {car} Anova function for multi way nonparametric anova, and so on.  The partial solutions is NOT what I am looking for in this question thread.  I have summarized my findings so far in a post I published some time ago (titled: <a href=\"http://www.r-statistics.com/2010/04/repeated-measures-anova-with-r-tutorials/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Repeated measures ANOVA with R (functions and tutorials)</a>, in case it would help anyone) </p>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p>If what I read online is true, this task might be achieved using a mixed Ordinal Regression model (a.k.a: Proportional Odds Model).</p>\n\n<p>I found two packages that seems relevant, but couldn't find any vignette on the subject:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><a href=\"http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/repolr/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/repolr/</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ordinal/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ordinal/</a></li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>So being new to the subject matter, I was hoping for some directions from people here.</p>\n\n<p>Are there any tutorials/suggested-reading on the subject?  Even better, can someone suggest a simple example code for how to run and analyse this in R (e.g: \"non-parametric repeated measures multiway anova\") ?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-04T20:01:07.787000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1216", "provsql": "ee90a0c7-4b1a-4f3d-a91c-62a2ca296885"}, "posts_1217": {"id": 1268, "owneruserid": 170, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1393, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "SVD dimensionality reduction for time series of different length", "tags": "<time-series><machine-learning><pca><data-transformation><multivariate-analysis>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I am using Singular Value Decomposition as a dimensionality reduction technique.</p>\n\n<p>Given <code>N</code> vectors of dimension <code>D</code>, the idea is to represent the features in a transformed space of uncorrelated dimensions, which condenses most of the information of the data in the eigenvectors of this space in a decreasing order of importance.</p>\n\n<p>Now I am trying to apply this procedure to time series data. The problem is that not all the sequences have the same length, thus I cant really build the <code>num-by-dim</code> matrix and apply SVD. My first thought was to pad the matrix with zeros by building a <code>num-by-maxDim</code> matrix and filling the empty spaces with zeros, but I'm not so sure if that is the correct way.</p>\n\n<p>My question is how do you the SVD approach of dimensionality reduction to time series of different length? Alternatively are there any other similar methods of eigenspace representation usually used with time series?</p>\n\n<p>Below is a piece of MATLAB code to illustrate the idea:</p>\n\n<pre><code>X = randn(100,4);                       % data matrix of size N-by-dim\n\nX0 = bsxfun(@minus, X, mean(X));        % standarize\n[U S V] = svd(X0,0);                    % SVD\nvariances = diag(S).^2 / (size(X,1)-1); % variances along eigenvectors\n\nKEEP = 2;                               % number of dimensions to keep\nnewX = U(:,1:KEEP)*S(1:KEEP,1:KEEP);    % reduced and transformed data\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>(I am coding mostly in MATLAB, but I'm comfortable enough to read R/Python/.. as well)</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-04T20:51:04.053000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1217", "provsql": "1918e1ca-883b-4606-8005-ab397f3a40bf"}, "posts_1507": {"id": 1576, "owneruserid": 776, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1579, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What are the differences between Factor Analysis and Principal Component Analysis?", "tags": "<pca><factor-analysis>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>It seems that a number of the statistical packages that I use wrap these two concepts together. However, I'm wondering if there are different assumptions or data 'formalities' that must be true to use one over the other. A real example would be incredibly useful. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-12T03:46:05.987000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1507", "provsql": "5b7bdd72-a634-4ca6-a07d-a774bb0ff6e2"}, "posts_1565": {"id": 1637, "owneruserid": 199, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1639, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "If the t-test and the ANOVA for two groups are equivalent, why aren't their assumptions equivalent?", "tags": "<distributions><regression><normality-assumption><t-test><anova>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I'm sure I've got this completely wrapped round my head, but I just can't figure it out.</p>\n\n<p>The t-test compares two normal distributions using the Z distribution. That's why there's an assumption of normality in the DATA.</p>\n\n<p>ANOVA is equivalent to linear regression with dummy variables, and uses sums of squares, just like OLS. That's why there's an assumption of normality of RESIDUALS.</p>\n\n<p>It's taken me several years, but I think I've finally grasped those basic facts. So why is it that the t-test is equivalent to ANOVA with two groups? How can they be equivalent if they don't even assume the same things about the data?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-13T09:41:13.160000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1565", "provsql": "c2e6dd85-2f5c-46ca-b3f4-d9fa01eb7653"}, "posts_1633": {"id": 1709, "owneruserid": 198, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1717, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to draw a probable outcome from a distribution?", "tags": "<distributions><data-visualization>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I have collected positional data. To visualize the data, I'd like to draw a 'typical' outcome of an experiment. </p>\n\n<p>The data comes from a few hundred experiments, where I identify a variable number of objects at different positions relative to the origin in 2D. Thus, I can calculate the average number of objects, as well as estimate the empirical distribution of the objects. A plot of the 'typical' outcome would then have the average (or possibly mode) number of objects, say, 5. What I'm not sure about is where to position these 5 objects.</p>\n\n<p>To simplify the problem, assume that the data follows a 2D normal distribution. If I were just to randomly draw 5 points from the distribution, I might get one point at [3,3], which would be a very rare outcome, and would thus not reflect the 'typical', or 'average' outcome. However, just drawing 5 points at [0,0] would also not make sense - even though [0,0] is the average position of the objects, 5 overlapping points are not an 'average' outcome of the process, either.</p>\n\n<p>In other words, how can I get a 'likely' draw from a distribution?</p>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p><strong>EDIT</strong> </p>\n\n<p>It looks like I should mention <em>why</em> I don't want to use the usual methods (like a 2D smoothed histogram, or plotting all the many points) to look at the 2D distribution. </p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>The objects (which are vesicles (i.e. little spheres) inside cells) vary in number, size and position (distribution of the distance from the cell center, amount of clustering). I would like to display all these features in one graph. Since there are several hundred cells containing many vesicles each, it is not very useful to combine them all in a single plot. I am well aware that I could use a multipanel graph showing the distributions of all parameters, but this would be a lot less intuitive. </li>\n<li>I would like to show a 'typical' cell that shows all the salient features that characterize a specific phenotype. This way, if I want to image a particular phenotype in a mixed population, I know what kind of cell I'm looking for.</li>\n<li>I think such a plot would be a cool way to display a lot of information at once, and I just want to try.</li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>Maybe it would be clearer If I said that I want to simulate a likely experimental result based on my measurements?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-15T14:30:23.597000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1633", "provsql": "9c3413f3-bd62-4ed7-9e74-9b6364db08fb"}, "posts_1799": {"id": 1881, "owneruserid": 582, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1901, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Analysis of cross correlation between point-processes", "tags": "<point-process><cross-correlation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I would like an advice on a analysis method I am using, to know if it it statistically sound.</p>\n<p>I have measured two point processes <span class=\"math-container\">$T^1 = t^1_1, t^1_2, \\ldots, t^1_n$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$T^2 = t^2_1, t^2_2, \\ldots, t^2_m$</span> and I want to determine if the events in <span class=\"math-container\">$T^1$</span> are somehow correlated to the events in <span class=\"math-container\">$T^2$</span>.</p>\n<p>One of the methods that I have found in the literature is that of constructing a cross-correlation histogram: for each <span class=\"math-container\">$t^1_n$</span> we find the delay to all the events of <span class=\"math-container\">$T^2$</span> that fall in a given window of time (before and after <span class=\"math-container\">$t^1_n$</span>), and then we construct an histogram of all these delays.</p>\n<p>If the two processes are not correlated I would expect a flat histogram, as the probability of having an event in <span class=\"math-container\">$T^2$</span> after (or before) an event in <span class=\"math-container\">$T^1$</span> is equal at all delays. On the other hand if there is a peak in the histogram, this suggests that the two point process are somehow influencing each other (or, at least, have some common input).</p>\n<p>Now, this is nice and good, but how do I determine whether the histograms do have a peak (I have to say that for my particular set of data they're clearly flat, but still it would be nice to have a statistical way of confirming that)?</p>\n<p>So, here what I've done: I've repeated the process of generating the histogram for several (1000) times keeping <span class=\"math-container\">$T^1$</span> as it is and using a "shuffled" version of <span class=\"math-container\">$T^2$</span>.\nTo shuffle <span class=\"math-container\">$T^2$</span> I calculate the intervals between all the events, shuffle them and sum them to reconstitute a new point process. In R I simply do this with:</p>\n<pre><code>times2.swp <- cumsum(sample(diff(times2)))\n</code></pre>\n<p>So, I end up with 1000 new histogram, that show me the density of events in <span class=\"math-container\">$T^{2*}$</span> compared to <span class=\"math-container\">$T^1$</span>.</p>\n<p>For each bin of these histogram (they're all binned in the same way) I calculate the density of 95% of the histogram. In other words I'm saying, for instance: at time delay 5 ms, in 95% of the shuffled point processes there is a probability x of finding an event in <span class=\"math-container\">$T^{2*}$</span> after an event in <span class=\"math-container\">$T^1$</span>.</p>\n<p>I would then take this 95% value for all of the time delays and use it as some "confidence limit" (probably this is not the correct term) so that anything that goes over this limit in the original histogram can be considered a "true peak".</p>\n<p><strong>Question 1</strong>: is this method statistically correct? If not how would you tackle this problem?</p>\n<p><strong>Question 2</strong>: another thing that I want to see is whether there is a "longer" type of correlation of my data. For instance there may be similar changes in the rate of events in the two point processes (note that they may have quite different rates), but I'm not sure how to do that. I thought of creating an "envelope" of each point process using some sort of smoothing kernel and then performing a cross-correlation analysis of the two envelopes. Could you suggest any other possible type of analysis?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-19T06:42:15.767000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1799", "provsql": "66c535b6-aa15-4790-96b3-87c6d4281511"}, "posts_1801": {"id": 1883, "owneruserid": 273, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Revolutions in statistics for the last 50 years?", "tags": "<history>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>What areas of statistics have been substantially revolutionised in the last 50 years? For example, about 40 years ago, Akaike with colleagues revolutionised the area of statistical model discrimination. About 10 years ago, Hyndman with colleagues revolutionised the area of exponential smoothing. About XX years ago, ... </p>\n\n<p>How do I possibly continue the list, with years and names please? By statistics I mean its all four types from Bartholomew's 1995 presidential address, Chambers's greater and lesser statistics together, as featuring in Hand's recent presidential address on 'Modern statistics' and so on - anything professionally relevant.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-19T07:00:53.840000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1801", "provsql": "b2ccb8e4-f77a-4684-8a6a-28344bdaec9e"}, "posts_2268": {"id": 2356, "owneruserid": 887, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Are there any examples where Bayesian credible intervals are obviously inferior to frequentist confidence intervals", "tags": "<bayesian><confidence-interval>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>A recent question on the difference between confidence and credible intervals led me to start re-reading Edwin Jaynes' article on that topic:</p>\n\n<p>Jaynes, E. T., 1976. `Confidence Intervals vs Bayesian Intervals,' in Foundations of Probability Theory, Statistical Inference, and Statistical Theories of Science, W. L. Harper and C. A. Hooker (eds.), D. Reidel, Dordrecht, p. 175; (<a href=\"http://bayes.wustl.edu/etj/articles/confidence.pdf\">pdf</a>)</p>\n\n<p>In the abstract, Jaynes writes:</p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>...we exhibit the Bayesian and orthodox solutions to six common statistical problems involving confidence intervals (including significance tests based on the same reasoning).  In every case, we find the situation is exactly the opposite, i.e. the Bayesian method is easier to apply and yields the same or better results.  Indeed, the orthodox results are satisfactory only when they agree closely (or exactly) with the Bayesian results. <strong>No contrary example has yet been produced.</strong></p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>(emphasis mine)</p>\n\n<p>The paper was published in 1976, so perhaps things have moved on. My question is, are there examples where the frequentist confidence interval is clearly superior to the Bayesian credible interval (as per the challenge implicitly made by Jaynes)?</p>\n\n<p>Examples based on incorrect prior assumptions are not acceptable as they say nothing about the internal consistency of the different approaches.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-03T18:23:44.087000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2268", "provsql": "8f472694-7cbc-4e18-bbac-39911dbfd18e"}, "posts_2408": {"id": 2516, "owneruserid": 666, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2519, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Are large data sets inappropriate for hypothesis testing?", "tags": "<hypothesis-testing><statistical-significance><dataset><sample-size><large-data>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>In a <a href=\"http://magazine.amstat.org/blog/2010/09/01/statrevolution/\">recent article</a> of <em>Amstat News</em>, the authors (Mark van der Laan and Sherri Rose) stated that \"We know that for large enough sample sizes, every study—including ones in which the null hypothesis of no effect is true — will declare a statistically significant effect.\".</p>\n\n<p>Well, I for one didn't know that. Is this true? Does it mean that hypothesis testing is worthless for large data sets?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-09T18:21:30.200000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2408", "provsql": "6daa06b2-ac06-431c-a46c-5039a918a4be"}, "posts_2450": {"id": 2563, "owneruserid": 1248, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2571, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What are some of the best ranking algorithms with inputs as up and down votes?", "tags": "<algorithms>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>What are some of the best ranking algorithms with inputs as up and down votes?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-11T13:15:03.890000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2450", "provsql": "816d8790-14a3-429f-995b-55e1bceb7631"}, "posts_2805": {"id": 2956, "owneruserid": 364, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Have I computed these likelihood ratios correctly?", "tags": "<r><anova><likelihood-ratio>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I'm the author of the <a href=\"http://cran.r-project.org/package=ez\" rel=\"noreferrer\">ez package</a> for R, and I'm working on an update to include automatic computation of likelihood ratios (LRs) in the output of ANOVAs. The idea is to provide a LR for each effect that is analogous to the test of that effect that the ANOVA achieves. For example, the LR for main effect represents the comparison of a null model to a model that includes the main effect, the LR for an interaction represents the comparison of a model that includes both component main effects versus a model that includes both main effects <em>and</em> their interaction, etc.</p>\n\n<p>Now, my understanding of LR computation comes from <a href=\"http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15732688\" rel=\"noreferrer\">Glover & Dixon</a> (<a href=\"http://www.thinkingaboutthinking.org/wp-content/uploads/2010/09/Glover-Dixon-2004-Likelihood-ratios-a-simple-and-flexible-statistic-for-empirical-psychologists.pdf\" rel=\"noreferrer\">PDF</a>), which covers basic computations as well as corrections for complexity, and the appendix to <a href=\"http://rads.stackoverflow.com/amzn/click/0521009138\" rel=\"noreferrer\">Bortolussi & Dixon</a> (<a href=\"http://www.thinkingaboutthinking.org/wp-content/uploads/2010/09/Dixon-Unknown-Evaluating-Evidence-Appendix-to-Psychonarratology.pdf\" rel=\"noreferrer\">appendix PDF</a>), which covers computations involving repeated-measures variables. To test my understanding, I developed <a href=\"https://spreadsheets.google.com/ccc?key=0Ap2N_aeyRMGHdHJxUnVNeEl5VGtvY1RVLVc5UjU4Vmc&hl=en\" rel=\"noreferrer\">this spreadsheet</a>, which takes the dfs & SSs from an example ANOVA (generated from a 2*2*3*4 design using fake data) and steps through the computation of the LR for each effect.</p>\n\n<p>I would really appreciate it if someone with a little more confidence with such computation could take a look and make sure I did everything correctly. For those that prefer abstract code, <a href=\"http://gist.github.com/590789\" rel=\"noreferrer\">here is the R code</a> implementing the update to ezANOVA() (see esp. lines 15-95).</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-21T23:40:39.317000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2805", "provsql": "87115163-5042-4321-bba5-bbfeb1515e85"}, "posts_2814": {"id": 2966, "owneruserid": 183, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2967, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Estimating latent performance potential based on a sequence of observations", "tags": "<time-series><bayesian><latent-variable><isotonic>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p><strong>Context</strong></p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>you have 200 observations of an individual's running time for the 100 metres measured once a day for 200 days.</li>\n<li>Assume the individual was not a runner before commencement of practice</li>\n<li>Based on the observed data and the 199 other observations, you want to estimate the latent time it would take the individual to run if they (a) applied maximal effort; and (b) had a reasonably good run for them (i.e., no major problems with the run; but still a typical run). Let's call this <strong>latent potential</strong>.</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>Of course, the actual data would not measure latent potential directly. The data would be noisy:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>Times would vary from run to run</li>\n<li>On some days the individual would be particularly slow because of one or more possible problems (e.g., tripping at the start, getting a cramp half way through, not putting in much effort). Such problems would result in  massive outliers</li>\n<li>On some days the individual would be slower than you'd expect, perhaps because of more minor issues.</li>\n<li>In general, with practice the runner would be expected to get faster in latent potential.</li>\n<li>In rare cases, it is possible for the runner to get slower in latent potential (e.g., injury)</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>The implications of this:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>The occasional slow time might provide minimal information on what the individual is capable of. </li>\n<li>A fast time for the individual suggests that the individual is capable of such a fast time, but a small amount of this fast time might be good fortune on the day (e.g., the right wind, a little luck on the start).</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p><strong>The question:</strong>\nThus, how could one estimate  latent potential at each of the 200 time points based on the available data and a few assumptions about the nature of running times?</p>\n\n<p><strong>Initial Thoughts:</strong> I imagine there would be some form of Bayesian approach that combined the available information and assumptions to form an estimate, but I'm not sure where to look for such models. I'm also not quite clear how the effectiveness of such a model would be evaluated.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-22T10:32:51.633000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2814", "provsql": "b1355018-733e-46a4-ac1d-077bb6be7418"}, "posts_3967": {"id": 4211, "owneruserid": null, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 4213, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": "user88", "title": "How to visualize 3D contingency matrix?", "tags": "<data-visualization><contingency-tables>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I have a data like this:</p>\n\n<pre><code>> table(A,B,C)\n, , C = FALSE\n\n       B\nA       FALSE TRUE\n  FALSE   177   42\n  TRUE      6    8\n\n, , C = TRUE\n\n       B\nA       FALSE TRUE\n  FALSE     5   31\n  TRUE      4   10\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>How can I plot this on a single graph, possibly without imposing any hierarchy?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-11-04T16:11:48.220000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3967", "provsql": "f4f69906-c0eb-4181-a13f-17264021fb52"}, "posts_4783": {"id": 5081, "owneruserid": 264, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Java library for Bayesian Networks", "tags": "<bayesian><bayesian-network><software><java>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>As the headline suggest, I am looking for a java library for learning and inference of Bayesian Networks. I have already found some, but I am hoping for a recommendation.</p>\n\n<p>Requirements in a quick overview:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>written in Java (my overlord tells me that this is no point of discussion)</li>\n<li>configuration is possible via code (and not solely via a GUI).</li>\n<li>source code available</li>\n<li>project is still maintained</li>\n<li>the more powerful, the better</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>Which one do you recommend?   </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-12-02T11:17:13.693000", "posts_rownum": "posts_4783", "provsql": "3ba1875c-2ec4-4b90-88d8-3516930554fd"}, "posts_3398": {"id": 3589, "owneruserid": 1118, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3605, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Correlation between two variables of unequal size", "tags": "<time-series><correlation><missing-data><finance>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>In a problem I am working on, I have two random variables, X and Y. I need to figure out how closely correlated the two of them are, but they are of different dimensions. The rank of the row space of X is 4350, and the rank of the row space of Y is substantially larger, in the tens of thousands. Both X and Y have the same number of columns.</p>\n\n<p>I need a measure of correlation between the two variables, and Pearson's r requires X and Y to have equal dimension (at least R requires the two r.v.'s to be). </p>\n\n<p>Do I have any hope of doing a correlation between these two, or should I find some way of pruning off observations from Y?</p>\n\n<pre><code> EDIT\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Adding information from the comments, which should be in the question.</p>\n\n<p>I suppose I forgot to mention this. X and Y are stock prices. Company X has been public for a much shorter time period than Y. I wanted to tell how correlated the prices of X and Y are. I could definitely get a correlation for the period of time that X and Y both exist. Sometimes the parameter of interest is the inverse of the data or the ratio of two variables.    </p>\n\n<p><strong>Examples:</strong> </p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>the ratio of two normally distributed variables:\n<ul>\n<li>data: mean and sd for percent nitrogen and percent carbon </li>\n<li>parameter: ratio of carbon to nitrogen.</li>\n</ul></li>\n<li>the inverse of a normally distributed variable:\n<ul>\n<li>data: mass/area</li>\n<li>parameter: area/mass</li>\n</ul></li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>My current approach is to use simulation:</p>\n\n<p>e.g. for a set of percent carbon and nitrogen data with means: xbar.n,c, variance: se.n,c, and sample size: n.n, n.c:</p>\n\n<pre><code>set.seed(1)\nper.c <- rnorm(100000, xbar.c, se.c*n.c) # percent C\nper.n <- rnorm(100000, xbar.n, se.n*n.n) # percent N\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>I want to parameterize ratio.cn = perc.c/perc.n</p>\n\n<pre><code># parameter of interest\nratio.cn <- perc.c / perc.n\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Then choose the best fit distributions with range $0 \\rightarrow \\infty$ for my prior </p>\n\n<pre><code>library(MASS)\ndist.fig <- list()\nfor(dist.i in c('gamma', 'lognormal', 'weibull')) {\n    dist.fit[[dist.i]] <- fitdist(ratio.cn, dist.i)\n}\n</code></pre>\n\n<p><strong>Question:</strong>\nIs this a valid approach? Are there other / better approaches?</p>\n\n<p>Thanks in advance!</p>\n\n<p><strong>Update:</strong> the Cauchy distribution, which is defined as the ratio of two normals with $\\mu=0$, has limited utility since I would like to estimate variance. \n</code></pre>\n\n<p>I tried to reproduce it, reading the code under prop.test. Here is a simplified way to get those two limits</p>\n\n<pre><code>ESTIMATE <- x/n\nYATES <- 0.5\nconf.level <- 0.95\nz <- qnorm((1 + conf.level)/2)\nYATES <- min(YATES, abs(x - n * p)) \nz22n <- z^2/(2 * n)\np.c <- ESTIMATE + YATES/n\n(p.c + z22n + z * sqrt(p.c * (1 - p.c)/n + z22n/(2 * n)))/(1 + 2 * z22n)\n[1] 0.5008409\np.c <- ESTIMATE - YATES/n\n(p.c + z22n - z * sqrt(p.c * (1 - p.c)/n + z22n/(2 * n)))/(1 + 2 * z22n)\n[1] 0.4196787\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Can you explain to me why the underlying probability of success (p) is used in line 5? or maybe you could suggest where can I find more info about this YATES correction that affects the ESTIMATE.</p>\n\n<p>Thank you</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-12-07T10:10:47.810000", "posts_rownum": "posts_4902", "provsql": "c116b095-3dd0-4177-8e60-1960e6fc8eae"}, "posts_5035": {"id": 5344, "owneruserid": 199, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 5345, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to choose nlme or lme4 R library for mixed effects models?", "tags": "<r><mixed-model><lme4-nlme>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I have fit a few mixed effects models (particularly longitudinal models) using <code>lme4</code> in <code>R</code> but would like to really master the models and the code that goes with them.</p>\n<p>However, before diving in with both feet (and buying some books) I want to be sure that I am learning the right library. My main criteria are:</p>\n<ol>\n<li>Easy to use (I'm a psychologist by training, and not particularly versed in statistics or coding, but I'm learning)</li>\n<li>Good features for fitting longitudinal data (if there is a difference here- but this is what I mainly use them for)</li>\n<li>Good (easy to interpret) graphical summaries, again not sure if there is a difference here but I often produce graphs for people even less technical than I, so nice clear plots are always good (I'm very fond of the <code>xyplot</code> function in <code>lattice()</code> for this reason).</li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2010-12-10T09:31:14.580000", "posts_rownum": "posts_5035", "provsql": "4ea58c37-1ce9-4833-8a01-7269153ef3e2"}, "posts_5375": {"id": 5700, "owneruserid": 2488, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 444148, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Finding the change point in data from a piecewise linear function", "tags": "<regression><change-point>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Greetings,</p>\n\n<p>I'm performing research that will help determine the size of observed space and the time elapsed since the big bang. There is a point at which the slope and intercept change, and I need to (write a program to) find this point.</p>\n\n<p>Thoughts?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-12-22T17:44:21.793000", "posts_rownum": "posts_5375", "provsql": "8d3a8530-c313-4f31-b519-7c03d98e7b55"}, "posts_5420": {"id": 5747, "owneruserid": 1329, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 5753, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "If A and B are correlated with C, why are A and B not necessarily correlated?", "tags": "<correlation><cross-correlation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I know empirically that is the case. It may be just a sign direction and nothing else.  </p>\n\n<p>Here is what I mean...  Let's say A and B both have a 0.5 correlation with C.  Given that, the correlation between A and B could well be 1.0.  I think it also could be 0.5 or even lower.  But, I think it is unlikely that it would be negative.  Do you agree with that?  </p>\n\n<p>Also, is there an implication if you are considering the standard Pearson Correlation Coefficient or instead the Spearman (rank) Correlation Coefficient?  My recent empirical observations were associated with the Spearman Correlation Coefficient.   </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-12-25T19:24:45.540000", "posts_rownum": "posts_5420", "provsql": "3fbb5800-e604-4f57-88a8-b7a1bc151e9b"}, "posts_5578": {"id": 5913, "owneruserid": 2616, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 5921, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Interpreting two-sided, two-sample, Welch T-Test", "tags": "<distributions><t-test><javascript>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I’m writing some code <em>(JavaScript)</em> to compare benchmark results. I’m using the <a href=\"http://frank.mtsu.edu/~dkfuller/notes302/welcht.pdf\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Welch T-test</a> because the variance and/or sample size between benchmarks is most likely different. The critical value is pulled from a T-distribution table at 95% confidence <em>(two-sided)</em>.</p>\n\n<p>The Welch formula is pretty straight-forward, but I am fuzzy on interpreting a significant result. I am not sure if the critical value should be divided by 2 or not. Help clearing that up is appreciated. Also should I be <a href=\"https://developer.mozilla.org/en/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Math/round\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">rounding</a> the degrees of freedom, <code>df</code>, to lookup the critical value or would <a href=\"https://developer.mozilla.org/en/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Math/ceil\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><code>Math.ceil</code></a> or <a href=\"https://developer.mozilla.org/en/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Math/floor\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><code>Math.floor</code></a> be more appropriate?</p>\n\n<pre><code>  /**\n   * Determines if the benchmark's hertz is higher than another.\n   * @member Benchmark\n   * @param {Object} other The benchmark to compare.\n   * @returns {Number} Returns `1` if higher, `-1` if lower, and `0` if indeterminate.\n   */\n  function compare(other) {\n    // use welch t-test\n    // http://frank.mtsu.edu/~dkfuller/notes302/welcht.pdf\n    // http://www.public.iastate.edu/~alicia/stat328/Regression%20inference-part2.pdf\n    var a = this.stats,\n        b = other.stats,\n        pow = Math.pow,\n        bitA = a.variance / a.size,\n        bitB = b.variance / b.size,\n        df = pow(bitA + bitB, 2) / ((pow(bitA, 2) / a.size - 1) + (pow(bitB, 2) / b.size - 1)),\n        t = (a.mean - b.mean) / Math.sqrt(bitA + bitB),\n        c = getCriticalValue(Math.round(df));\n\n    // check if t-statistic is significant\n    return Math.abs(t) > c / 2 ? (t > 0 ? 1 : -1) : 0;\n  }\n</code></pre>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p><strong>Update:</strong> Thanks for all the replies so far! My colleague <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/5913/interpreting-two-sided-two-sample-welch-t-test/5961#5961\">posted some more info here</a>, in case that affects the advice.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-01-03T13:17:49.960000", "posts_rownum": "posts_5578", "provsql": "8ed3a761-e84d-4b7f-9998-85fc590cd7cc"}, "posts_5583": {"id": 5918, "owneruserid": 2040, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 5988, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Cross Validation (error generalization) after model selection", "tags": "<machine-learning><model-selection><data-mining><cross-validation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Note: Case is n>>p</p>\n\n<p>I am reading Elements of Statistical Learning and there are various mentions about the \"right\" way to do cross validation( e.g. page 60, page 245). Specifically, my question is how to evaluate the final model (without a separate test set) using k-fold CV or bootstrapping when there has been a model search? It seems that in most cases (ML algorithms without embedded feature selection) there will be</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>A feature selection step</li>\n<li>A meta parameter selection step (e.g. the cost parameter in SVM).</li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>My Questions:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>I have seen that the feature selection step can be done where feature selection is done on the whole training set and held aside. Then, using k-fold CV, the feature selection algorithm is used in each fold (getting different features possibly chosen each time) and the error averaged. Then, you would use the features chosen using all the data (that were set aside) to train the final mode, but use the error from the cross validation as an estimate of future performance of the model. <em>IS THIS CORRECT?</em></li>\n<li>When you are using cross validation to select model parameters, then how to estimate model performance afterwards? <em>IS IT THE SAME PROCESS AS #1 ABOVE OR SHOULD YOU USE NESTED CV LIKE SHOWN ON PAGE 54 (<a href=\"http://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~elkan/291/dm.pdf\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">pdf</a>) OR SOMETHING ELSE?</em></li>\n<li>When you are doing both steps (feature and parameter setting).....then what do you do? complex nested loops?</li>\n<li>If you have a separate hold out sample, does the concern go away and you can use cross validation to select features and parameters (without worry since your performance estimate will come from a hold out set)?</li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2011-01-03T15:08:29.897000", "posts_rownum": "posts_5583", "provsql": "a4f3381e-6403-49a4-a7eb-a26506f1333c"}, "posts_5782": {"id": 6127, "owneruserid": 442, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 6128, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Which permutation test implementation in R to use instead of t-tests (paired and non-paired)?", "tags": "<r><t-test><nonparametric><permutation-test>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I have data from an experiment that I analyzed using t-tests. The dependent variable is interval scaled and the data are either unpaired (i.e., 2 groups) or paired (i.e., within-subjects). \nE.g. (within subjects):</p>\n\n<pre><code>x1 <- c(99, 99.5, 65, 100, 99, 99.5, 99, 99.5, 99.5, 57, 100, 99.5, \n        99.5, 99, 99, 99.5, 89.5, 99.5, 100, 99.5)\ny1 <- c(99, 99.5, 99.5, 0, 50, 100, 99.5, 99.5, 0, 99.5, 99.5, 90, \n        80, 0, 99, 0, 74.5, 0, 100, 49.5)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>However, the data are not normal so one reviewer asked us to use something other than the t-test. However, as one can easily see, the data are not only not normally distributed, but the distributions are not equal between conditions:\n<img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/5y0kx.png\" alt=\"alt text\"></p>\n\n<p>Therefore, the usual nonparametric tests, the Mann-Whitney-U-Test (unpaired) and the Wilcoxon Test (paired), cannot be used as they require equal distributions between conditions. Hence, I decided that some resampling or permutation test would be best.</p>\n\n<p><strong>Now, I am looking for an R implementation of a permutation-based equivalent of the t-test, or any other advice on what to do with the data.</strong>  </p>\n\n<p>I know that there are some R-packages that can do this for me (e.g., coin, perm, exactRankTest, etc.), but I don't know which one to pick. So, if somebody with some experience using these tests could give me a kick-start, that would be ubercool.</p>\n\n<p><strong>UPDATE:</strong> It would be ideal if you could provide an example of how to report the results from this test.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-01-10T12:10:29", "posts_rownum": "posts_5782", "provsql": "071d91bb-39cc-4058-b91a-69204df74b06"}, "posts_6223": {"id": 6601, "owneruserid": 2392, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 6605, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What is the hardest statistical concept to grasp?", "tags": "<teaching>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>This is a similar question to the one <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/155/what-is-your-favorite-laymans-explanation-for-a-difficult-statistical-concept\">here</a>, but different enough I think to be worthwhile asking.</p>\n\n<p>I thought I'd put as a starter, what I think one of the hardest to grasp is.  </p>\n\n<p>Mine is the difference between <em>probability</em> and <em>frequency</em>.  One is at the level of \"knowledge of reality\" (probability), while the other is at the level \"reality itself\" (frequency).  This almost always makes me confused if I think about it too much.</p>\n\n<p>Edwin Jaynes Coined a term called the \"mind projection fallacy\" to describe getting these things mixed up.</p>\n\n<p>Any thoughts on any other tough concepts to grasp?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-01-27T03:57:01.977000", "posts_rownum": "posts_6223", "provsql": "51b27398-ffb4-40fb-9d0c-a457cdff5d08"}, "posts_6840": {"id": 7308, "owneruserid": 1393, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 7629, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Can the empirical Hessian of an M-estimator be indefinite?", "tags": "<estimation><maximum-likelihood><econometrics><asymptotics>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Jeffrey Wooldridge in his <em>Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data</em> (page 357) says that the empirical Hessian \"is not guaranteed to be positive definite, or even positive semidefinite, for the particular sample we are working with.\".</p>\n\n<p>This seems wrong to me as (numerical problems apart) the Hessian must be positive semidefinite as a result of the definition of the M-estimator as the value of the parameter which minimizes the objective function for the given sample and the well-known fact that at a (local) minimum the Hessian is positive semidefinite.</p>\n\n<p>Is my argument right?</p>\n\n<p><strong>[EDIT: The statement has been removed in the 2nd ed. of the book. See comment.]</strong></p>\n\n<p>BACKGROUND\nSuppose that $\\widehat \\theta_N$ is an estimator obtained by minimizing\n$${1 \\over N}\\sum_{i=1}^N q(w_i,\\theta),$$\nwhere $w_i$ denotes the $i$-th observation.</p>\n\n<p>Let's denote the Hessian of $q$ by $H$,\n$$H(q,\\theta)_{ij}=\\frac{\\partial^2 q}{\\partial \\theta_i \\partial \\theta_j}$$</p>\n\n<p>The asymptotic covariance of $\\widehat \\theta_n$ involves $E[H(q,\\theta_0)]$ where $\\theta_0$ is the true parameter value. One way to estimate it is to use the empirical Hesssian</p>\n\n<p>$$\\widehat H=\\frac{1}{N}\\sum_{i=1}^N H(w_i,\\widehat \\theta_n)$$</p>\n\n<p>It is the definiteness of $\\widehat H$ which is in question.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-02-16T19:52:33.287000", "posts_rownum": "posts_6840", "provsql": "fd92ccaa-0c54-41c6-9415-85d65be903cf"}, "posts_6974": {"id": 7467, "owneruserid": 1381, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 7472, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Quality assurance and quality control (QA/QC) guidelines for a database", "tags": "<dataset><meta-analysis><quality-control><database>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p><strong>Background</strong></p>\n\n<p>I am overseeing the input of data from primary literature into a <a href=\"http://ebi-forecast.igb.illinois.edu/\" rel=\"nofollow\">database</a>. The data entry process is error prone, particularly because users must interpret experimental design, extract data from graphics and tables, and transform results to standardized units.</p>\n\n<p>Data are input into a MySQL database through a web interface. I need to run checks of the quality of not only the variable data, but also the data contained in lookup tables, such as the species associated with each data point, the location of the study, etc.  </p>\n\n<p>Data entry is ongoing, so QA/QC will need to be run intermittently. "posts_10510", "provsql": "63b3c025-ca20-4a8a-9d58-06eca093e6f7"}, "posts_10983": {"id": 11887, "owneruserid": 5003, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 15400, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What experimental design is this?", "tags": "<anova><repeated-measures><experiment-design>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I collect blood from <em>one</em> human (donor), separate leukocytes and put $2\\times10^6$ of them per each well of five:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>well 1: $2\\times10^6$ Lk (leukocytes)</li>\n<li>well 2: $2\\times10^6$ Lk    </li>\n<li>well 3: $2\\times10^6$ Lk    </li>\n<li>well 4: $2\\times10^6$ Lk  </li>\n<li>well 5: $2\\times10^6$ Lk</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>(Lk consists of a mix of different sets of cells and one of them are lymphocytes (Lph)).</p>\n\n<p>Then I incubated the cells under different conditions (with the following substances in the same concentration (with the exception of well #1, of course)):</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>well 1: saline (serves as a zero control)</li>\n<li>well 2: substance A (is a native compound) </li>\n<li>well 3: substance B (is a chemically modified analogue of A)</li>\n<li>well 4: substance C (is a chemically modified analogue' of A)</li>\n<li>well 5: substance D (is a chemically modified analogue'' of A)</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>Then I incubate the leucocytes for 24 hours.</p>\n\n<p>Then I run FACS and get percentages of lymphocytes expressing a receptor (CD69) of interest (Lph') (where the percentages is the ratio of Lph' to all Lph).</p>\n\n<p>Then I repeated the experiment 7 times: i.e. totally I collected blood from 8 different donors (so $n = 8$).</p>\n\n<p>With this experiment I want to know:<br>\nDoes a structure of a molecule affect the percentage/proportion of <em>activated</em> lymphocytes (Lph') (i.e. Lph bearing CD69 molecule)?</p>\n\n<p>My example data (<em>in percentages, %</em>) are:<br>\n<strong><pre>\nDonorID  cntrl  substanceA  substanceB  substanceC  substanceD</strong> \n20       5.1    12.42       10.10       9.58        8.54 \n21       4.07   9.96        14.12       10.79       12.24 \n22       3.94   4.92        13.04       15.96       9.37 \n25       0.60   3.24        8.94        0.61        3.62 \n26       1.72   13.96       2.48        3.44        3.12 \n27       0.53   3.36        1.40        4.00        0.81 \n28       0.97   3.88        2.33        3.77        3.31 \n31       0.15   4.05        1.45        2.44        1.47 \n32       0.58   1.92        2.47        2.33        4.92 \n33       1.02   6.03        4.40        4.80        3.88</pre></p>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p>SUMMARY:  </p>\n\n<p>So the experimental design can be characterized by the following terms:  </p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><em>ANOVA</em> as more than 2 groups are tested;  </li>\n<li><em>RM</em> as the statistical/experimental unit (\"Lph\") for every case is under different conditions;  </li>\n<li><em>one-way</em> there is one <em>fixed (within-subject) factor / independent variable</em> (\"conditioins\") with 5 levels; if I'm not mistaken in the light of linear mixed models the \"DonorID\" might be interpreted as an additional <em>random factor</em> (\"donor\").  </li>\n</ul>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p><em>Many thanks for the answers!</em></p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-06-14T01:07:19.033000", "posts_rownum": "posts_10983", "provsql": help identifing outliers in a pilot study to guide future hypothesis testing", "tags": "<outliers>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am looking to study a particular type of error on a cognitive test to evaluate for potential clinical implications.  As there is no existing research on this variable, I would like to run a pilot evaluation on a relatively large pool of subject data from our clinic (feasibly this would be about 200 subjects) to see if there are any trends to guide hypothesis testing in future studies (e.g., are patients from a particular clinical population more likely to make this type of error than those from another population).  The data is such that a patient could potentially make 0-15 of these errors, although it's likely that there will be a strong tendency toward the 0-5 range.  </p>\n\n<p>Essentially, I am looking to identify subjects from within this pool who are making a relatively higher rate of these errors.  Is there a recognized format for doing this type of pilot work?  Barring that, what would your recommendations be?  </p>\n\n<p>This is obviously very exploratory, so I feel like I would have some latitude in defining what constitutes an 'outlier' for the purposes of this study, but any references or suggestions would be much appreciated.  </p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-07-07T02:14:59.487000", "posts_rownum": "posts_11464", "provsql": "7fa6be83-cada-45c4-b5d1-9a4326edb053"}, "posts_12651": {"id": 13757, "owneruserid": 5647, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How do I weigh several variables at two levels to create an overall composite variable score?", "tags": "<correlation><latent-variable><composite>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<h3>Context</h3>\n\n<p>I am trying to find the <strong>correlation between two latent variables</strong>. Let's call them A and B. </p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>A has two dimensions. Let's call them Dimension 1 and 2. </li>\n<li>B also has two dimensions. Let's call them Dimension 3 and 4. </li>\n<li>The four dimensions (1, 2, 3 and 4) have several indicators each. Let's call them (a) and (b) for Dimension 1, (c), (d) and (e) for Dimension 2, (f) and (g) for Dimension 3 and (h), (i) and (j) for Dimension 4.</li>\n<li>I have measured the ten indicators (a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i and j) on a likert scale or else using cardinal numbers (e.g. one, two, three, four, etc.).</li>\n<li>I have then weighted the indicators using the likert scale codes that I created (e.g. 0 = not important, 1 = low importance, 2 = medium importance, 3 = high importance and 4 = absolute importance)</li>\n<li>I have then added the scores for all indicators to arrive at the dimension scores. This is my first weighting.</li>\n<li>I have then said that each dimension contributes 50% to the composite score of A or B and have standardised the dimension scores to 50% each. This is my second weighting. </li>\n<li>Finally I added the dimension scores to arrive at the composite score. </li>\n</ul>\n\n<p><strong>To give an example:</strong></p>\n\n<p>If I have a score of 2 for (a) and 3 for (b) then my total for Dimension 1 is 5. Similarly, if I have a score of 3 for (c), 4 for (d) and 2 for (e), then my total for Dimension 2 is 9. The score of 5 and 9 are the dimension scores, based on likert scale weights.</p>\n\n<p>As I said that each dimension contributes 50%, I have divided the obtained score by the total score for each dimension and multiplied it by 50%. So I have got the following:</p>\n\n<p>(2+3)/8 (remember this is based on two likert scale responses so the maximum score is 4 plus 4) x 50% = 0.31</p>\n\n<p>(3+4+2)/12 (remember this is based on three likert scale responses so the maximum score is 4 plus 4 plus 4) x 50% = 0.38</p>\n\n<p>I then added 0.31 and 0.38 and got 0.69. This is my composite score for Composite Variable A (which has 2 dimensions and 5 indicators; 2 for the first dimension and 3 for the second dimension). </p>\n\n<p>To make it comprehensible, I have multipled 0.69 by 100 to get 69 out of 100 scores. I want to run corrleation on the composite scores of A and B to see the relationship between them.</p>\n\n<p>As you would see, I have <strong>not done any complex statistical modeling</strong> using factor analysis etc but arrived at my final score using a system of subjective weighting based on relative importance (which is aligned to the likert scale coding in the first instance) and equal weighting in the second instance. I have used this approach to keep everything simple. I know it is subjecive weighting but I can justify it to some extent with theory and the rest with commonsense!</p>\n\n<h3>Questions</h3>\n\n<ul>\n<li><p>Am I doing this right? Is this approach robust enough? \n<strong>Remember, I don't want to complicate things!</strong> I am not statistically minded!</p></li>\n<li><p>Can I do correlation analysis on the composite scores of A and B? They are rank scores (based on weights) so is the Spearman Rank Correlation the way to go for the analysis? </p></li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2011-08-02T14:04:01.353000", "posts_rownum": "posts_12651", "provsql": "243b68ac-6e9d-46fe-bd4b-83d1ae7babdd"}, "posts_12779": {"id": 13902, "owneruserid": 5647, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How do I compare correlation coefficients of the same variables across different groups?", "tags": "<correlation><hypothesis-testing>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am testing the correlation between Variable A and Variable B by gender and marital status.</p>\n\n<p>So I have the coefficients for males and females and single, married and other.</p>\n\n<p>I want to compare the correlation coefficient of male with female.</p>\n\n<p>Similarly, I want to compare the correlation coefficient of single with marrried and with other.</p>\n\n<p>Finally, I want to compare the correlation coefficient of single male with single female, married male with married female and other male and other female. I have these coefficients too.</p>\n\n<p><strong>What is the easiest way of making this comparison?</strong></p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-08-05T12:25:06.180000", "posts_rownum": "posts_12779", "provsql": "d21c721e-7c48-43b1-9561-5f74e8526292"}, "posts_13065": {"id": 14219, "owneruserid": 3301, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How well does R scale to text classification tasks?", "tags": "<r><machine-learning><svm><text-mining><random-forest>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am trying to get upto speed with R. I eventually want to use R libraries for doing text classification. I was just wondering what people's experiences are with regard to R's scalability when it comes to doing text classification. </p>\n\n<p>I am likely to run into high dimensional data (~300k dimensions). I am looking at using SVM and Random Forest in particular as classification algorithms. </p>\n\n<p>Would R libraries scale to my problem size?</p>\n\n<p>Thanks.</p>\n\n<p>EDIT 1: Just to clarify, my data set is likely to have 1000-3000 rows (perhaps a bit more) and 10 classes.</p>\n\n<p>EDIT 2: Since I am very new to R, I will request the posters to be more specific where possible. For example, if you are suggesting a workflow/pipeline, please be sure to mention the R libraries involved in each step if possible. Some additional pointers (to examples, sample code etc.) would be icing on the cake.</p>\n\n<p>EDIT 3: First off, thanks everyone for your comments. And secondly, I apologize, perhaps I should have given more context for the problem. I am new to R but not so much to text classification. I have already done pre-processing (stemming, stopword removal, tf-idf conversion etc.) on my some part of my data using <a href=\"http://tm.r-forge.r-project.org/\">tm</a> package, just to get a feel for things. tm was so slow even on about 200docs that I got concerned about scalability. Then I started playing with FSelector and even that was really slow. And that's the point at which I made my OP.</p>\n\n<p>EDIT 4: It just occurred to me that I have 10 classes and about ~300 training documents per class, and I am in fact building the termXdoc matrix out of the entire training set resulting in very high dimensionality. But how about reducing every 1-out-of-k classification problem to a series of binary classification problems? That would drastically reduce the number of training documents (and hence dimensionality) at each of the k-1 steps considerably, wouldn't it? So is this approach a good one? How does it compare in terms of accuracy to the usual multi-class implementation?    </p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-08-13T16:52:34.583000", "posts_rownum": "posts_13065", "provsql": "25b08798-69a1-4d2a-abb4-2fab01f9fcf3"}, "posts_2322": {"id": 2410, "owneruserid": 253, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2411, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Can CART models be made robust?", "tags": "<regression><classification><robust><cart>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>A colleague in my office said to me today \"Tree models aren't good because they get caught by extreme observations\".</p>\n\n<p>A search here resulted in <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/1292/what-is-the-weak-side-of-decision-trees\">this thread</a> that basically supports the claim.</p>\n\n<p>Which leads me to the question - under what situation can a CART model be robust, and how is that shown?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-06T14:59:09.557000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2322", "provsql": "1f592b18-2281-46a7-8d4d-f4dd9aed0ea1"}, "posts_13080": {"id": 14237, "owneruserid": 5383, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 14283, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Normalisation for regression", "tags": "<regression><data-transformation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>First off, I know little about statistics, so some of this question may seem naive.</p>\n\n<p>I'm trying to perform linear regression to model the relationship between x and y where:</p>\n\n<p>-x is a company's daily stock volume on a date</p>\n\n<p>-y is variable that is taken from the same date, however is something unrelated to stock volume.  It is the volume of activity on that wikipedia for that company.</p>\n\n<p>I assume that the variables need normalising.  Specifically, x needs to be normalised as overall index volume fluctuates.  My first thoughts were to divide the daily volume by the total index volume.  I'll do the same with the y variable.  </p>\n\n<p>I just wondered if this seems sensible?  Thanks</p>\n\n<p>EDIT:</p>\n\n<p>I've just noticed a typo in the question, the Y variable description has changed.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-08-14T11:22:31.383000", "posts_rownum": "posts_13080", "provsql": "b21b27d9-34fe-4dc5-aa63-b1f8c702ae4d"}, "posts_13904": {"id": 15168, "owneruserid": 6096, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 15233, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Graphing effect size for coefficient of determination", "tags": "<data-visualization>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>If I have a significant correlation coefficient of r=.80 between Variable A and B, I can work out the effect size (coefficient of determination) by squaring it, which is 64%. </p>\n\n<p>I want to graph this in the simplest way possibe (given my non-statistical target audience). Can I use a 100% stacked bar graph for this purpose. This will show Variable B as 100% and on top of it would be Variable A which would be 64%. I can then graphically say that 64% of variance in Variable B can be attributed to Variable A. (Conversely, I can also graphically say that I am unsure of the remaining 36% of Variable B)  </p>\n\n<p>The appeal of this approach for me is that I can show the effect size between A and B on a number of variables (e.g. gender, age, education) in one graph. This will also make a colourful presentation (which is good for a non statistical target audience!).</p>\n\n<p>I have seen some textbooks showing two circles, each representing a variable (e.g. A and B). The part of the circles that overlaps illustrates the effect size. I thought doing a 100% stacked bar graph was a better way.</p>\n\n<p><strong>From the discussion below, it appears that the scatterplot is the way to go on this matter. However, how do I show 64% on a scatterplot?</strong></p>\n\n<p>I think the point is being missed in the discussion below. It is easy to illustrate the relationship through the scatterplot but how is the effect size illustrated i.e. the actual perecentage as above. I can't see this percentage figure in any of the diagrams below.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-09-04T01:27:19.153000", "posts_rownum": "posts_13904", "provsql": "b1bb1c7e-62e6-468f-8933-a202c1ce227c"}, "posts_14015": {"id": 15285, "owneruserid": 6191, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Problem with calculating $R^2$", "tags": "<modeling>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I believe I have rather simple question but I would like to make it right.<br>\nI have already asked question, however I am not sure whether I did everything correct or there is a mistake in the answer (probably the first one, but still I cannot find it).<br>\nTo make it short: \nI would like to check how well my model predicts outcome of a game between two players - and that is why I am trying to calculate R^2. What I have done is based on  <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/15281/optimizing-parameters-via-simple-visualisation-technique\">this answer</a>.<br>\nFirstly, I calculate ESS:</p>\n\n<pre><code>ess = 0\nfor each game in my database:\n   ess += (predictedOutcome - realOutcome)^2\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>The real outcome is either 1 (if win), 0.5 (if draw) or 0 (if lose). To calculate what was the average real outcome, I do:</p>\n\n<pre><code> averageRealOutcome = (wins + 1/2*draws)/(wins + draws + loses)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>The result is always about 0.5\nAnd then for each game I do a loop</p>\n\n<pre><code>tss = 0;\nfor each win\n   tss += (1 - averageRealOutcome)^2\nfor each draw\n   tss += (0.5 - averageRealOutcome)^2\nfor each lose\n   tss += (averageRealOutcome)^2\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Then, once more according to the previous answer, I try to calculate R^2:</p>\n\n<pre><code>R^2 = ESS/TSS\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Unfortunately the value that I get is above 1, while I believe it should be between 0 (very bad) to 1 (cool). Adjusting R^2 does not do the trick and i can see no difference at all. </p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>Does it in general make sense what I try to do?</li>\n<li>If it does, where is my mistake? Or maybe my interpretation is bad? If not, can you provide and resources where I can read what should I do?</li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2011-09-07T15:12:51.897000", "posts_rownum": "posts_14015", "provsql": "05b283c4-049a-4b4b-bc20-74e1dfde11a1"}, "posts_14212": {"id": 15501, "owneruserid": 5405, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Testing homoscedasticity with Breusch-Pagan test", "tags": "<r><heteroscedasticity>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>In these days I'm working with <strong>Breusch-Pagan</strong> to test homoscedasticity.</p>\n\n<p>I've tested the prices of two stocks with this method. This is the result:</p>\n\n<pre><code>> mod <- lm(prices[,1] ~ prices[,2])\n> bp <- bptest(mod)\n> bp\n\n    studentized Breusch-Pagan test\n\ndata:  prices[, 1] ~ prices[, 2] \nBP = 0.032, df = 1, p-value = 0.858\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Reading the result the series should be homoscedastic, but if I plot the residuals and the squares residuals it seems totally not! Take a look below:</p>\n\n<p><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/3Uubu.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></p>\n\n<p>the Residuals Vs FItted below:</p>\n\n<p><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/5NRzF.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></p>\n\n<p>How is it possible this series pass the test with a very high p-value?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-09-13T07:49:06.687000", "posts_rownum": "posts_14212", "provsql": "407c92e0-d6c7-4890-8a03-aedd011d1b01"}, "posts_14698": {"id": 16054, "owneruserid": 6544, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": "fred basset", "title": "Best algorithm for classifying time series motor data", "tags": "<time-series>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am working on a machine control project. The red trace shows the current from one motor, the blue trace the current from another.  I'd like to try and come up with an algorithm for identifying problems with machine behavior. Can anyone suggest a good algorithm for achieving this?  The only one I'm familiar with is a neural network.  I have put an Excel file of actual data at <a href=\"http://resplendid.com/motorcurrents.xlsx\" rel=\"noreferrer\">motor currents</a></p>\n\n<p><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/RQka3.png\" alt=\"Motor currents - good operation\">\n<img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/tOIpI.png\" alt=\"Motor currents - jam at end of operation\"></p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-09-25T01:49:55.263000", "posts_rownum": "posts_14698", "provsql": "c4c92c72-5ab9-42eb-acec-777b2dfa5dd2"}, "posts_2342": {"id": 2432, "owneruserid": 183, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2445, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "LOESS that allows discontinuities", "tags": "<r><regression><curve-fitting><change-point><loess>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<ul>\n<li>Is there a modelling technique like <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_regression\">LOESS</a> that allows for zero, one, or more discontinuities, where the timing of the discontinuities are not known apriori?</li>\n<li>If a technique exists, is there an existing implementation in R?</li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-07T03:24:59.747000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2342", "provsql": "0717cc56-8869-4b43-86fa-40615d5845e6"}, "posts_127": {"id": 138, "owneruserid": 142, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1213, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Free resources for learning R", "tags": "<r><references>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm interested in learning <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R_%28programming_language%29\">R</a> on the cheap. What ways exist to show the two methods are equivalent (or not).</p>\n\n<p>I'm thinking that plotting the results from a number of samples measured by both methods on a scatter graph is a good first step, but are there any good statistical methods ?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-22T21:15:52.347000", "posts_rownum": "posts_515", "provsql": "b13c90ad-5e4c-4826-bd84-4b7089e99f5a"}, "posts_1615": {"id": 1687, "owneruserid": 937, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1762, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Applied statistics to find the minimum load for power factor floor", "tags": "<probability><standard-deviation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>The problem I’m trying to solve is “How do I figure out how much gunpowder should I put into a cartridge so that I can give myself a good probability of making the minimum power factor?”</p>\n\n<p>I compete in USPSA/IPSC which requires that a competitors rounds make a minimum power factor. Power Factor is computed to be the FLOOR(average bullet velocity * bullet weight) / 1000) where velocity is in feet per second, and bullet weight is in grains. Note the use of FLOOR. No rounding is done. Only the integral part of the computation is used. The higher the power factor, the higher the felt recoil and harder it is to quickly do follow up shots. Since the sport is about firing shots as quickly and as accurately as possible, the lower the recoil the better.</p>\n\n<p>Different divisions within the sport have different power factor floors, but the particular division I compete in has a minimum of 165 Power Factor. The bullets I use are 180 gn bullets, and vary by about +/- 0.2 gn and is normally distributed. </p>\n\n<p>What makes this an interesting problem (and move it out of my meager stats and probability skills) is the testing procedure during a major match. Random sample of 8 rounds are collected. Of the 8 rounds, one is taken apart and the bullet is weighed for use in the formula above. Next, 3 rounds are fired and the average velocity is used. If the resulting power factor is below the minimum, then another 3 rounds are fired. The average of the 3 fastest velocities from the 6 rounds fired is now used to compute the power factor. If the resulting power factor is still below the floor, then the shooter has the option of having the last round taken apart and weighed or the last round fired. If the bullet is taken apart and it is heavier than the first bullet, the heavier weight is used to compute the power factor. If the last round is fired, the average of the 3 fastest velocities from the 7 rounds fired is used to compute the power factor.</p>\n\n<p>To add spice to this problem, not all chronographs used to measure bullet velocities are created equal. The chronograph industry acknowledges that there can be as much as +/- 4% variance between chronographs of different brands. Even more interesting is that the rules allow for the same chronograph used for a particular match to have +/- 4% variance over the duration of a match. I don’t know if either of these 4% variances are normally distributed or not.</p>\n\n<p>With my own chronograph, I test batches of a particular gunpowder load to get the average velocity and standard deviation. After statistical analyses of many different batches, I’ve confirmed that this data is normally distributed.</p>\n\n<p>The way I’m currently determining my minimum load is by finding the load the gives me 165 < FLOOR( target * 179.9 / 1000) where target =  (average velocity - standard deviation) * fudge factor. For fudge factor, I’ve unscientifically chosen 1.04. The 0.04 is the 4% variance between chronographs, but ignores the day-to-day allowable variance. I chose to just subtract just 1 standard deviation because it’ll only be 16% of the time that one bullet will be below the floor. In my mind, the probability of all the first 3 bullets all going below the floor is 0.16^3 which less than half a percent.</p>\n\n<p>My specific questions are: Am I going about computing the target the right way? Should my fudge factor include another 4% for the day-to-day variance allowed? Is the 1 standard deviation too much or too little? How should I write the formula for my target? </p>\n\n<p>Edit:\nAfter Srikant's initial response below let me add a couple of focusing questions and notes.</p>\n\n<p>I understand figuring out the error due to my measurements. Not much problem there unless I get really sloppy with quality control or maintenance. </p>\n\n<p>My grasp of probabilities is weak so please bear with me as I ask about computing probabilities:</p>\n\n<p>1) One of the key issues I need to deal with is figuring out how to correctly compute the probability for the testing process around the 7 rounds. It's pretty straight forward to me for the case of the first 3 rounds: (probability that the round is below the power flaw)^3. How do I account for the next 3 rounds and the last round?</p>\n\n<p>I can see computing the probabilities using combinations of bullets above or below the floor, but it's not quite a binary above or below. Let's assume that 6 rounds have been fired, and the average of the highest 3 rounds is 164.9. If the last round has at least 165.2, then the average of the highest 3 rounds out of 7 will be 165.</p>\n\n<p>2) The other issue I need to deal with is figuring out how to account for the 4% variance between my chrono and the match chrono, and how the match chrono is allowed to drift by 4% from day to day. Do I just assume the worst case and make sure that I'm at least 8% above 165 -- that is my rounds are shooting at least 179 power factor? Or do I try to assume some kind of normal distribution over the two 4% variances?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-14T14:00:16.297000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1615", "provsql": "86a7b72b-96ee-4852-b5c3-070743c0243d"}, "posts_1072": {"id": 1112, "owneruserid": 652, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1113, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to represent an unbounded variable as number between 0 and 1", "tags": "<normalization>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I want to represent a variable as a number between 0 and 1. Let x be a uniformly distributed random variable, i.e. p(x) = 0 if x < 0 and x ≥1; p(x) = 1 if 0 ≤ x <1.</p>\n\n<p>How would I compute the mean and variance of the variable x?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-09-20T17:34:55.513000", "posts_rownum": "posts_14484", "provsql": "7499a1f0-15c6-47ce-a340-5168fbcca1a8"}, "posts_1354": {"id": 1412, "owneruserid": 196, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1414, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Consequences of an improper link function in N alternative forced choice procedures (e.g. 2AFC)?", "tags": "<logistic><link-function>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Background:  In some cognitive psychology research areas N-alternative forced choice tasks are common.  The most common of these is a two alternative forced choice (2AFC).  This usually takes the form of participants being given a stimulus and asked to make one of two judgement, e.g. the target stimuli is present/absent, the stimulus on the left is the same/different than the the one on the right, etc.  Designs in which the experimental data is from a 2AFC but there is only one data point per subject are rare, but do exist, e.g. some eye-witness identification research.  Since the dependent variable (correct/incorrect) is binary, these experiments are reasonable places to use logistic regression.  </p>\n\n<p>My question is this:  since chance performance is 50% in a 2AFC trial, is it still reasonable to use the standard logistic link function?  Specifically, the logistic function has a minimum value approaching 0% correct, but in practice participants in a 2AFC should be correct at least 50% of the time due to chance.  I imagine the following case in which it may present a problem:  an independent variable is assessing the difficulty of the discrimination (e.g. difficulty 1, easy - 5, hard; please note this is introduced in ordinal terms only for ease of comprehension - for the sake of this discussion consider this variable as being interval) - participants got 50% correct at 5 and 4, 75% correct at 3, 85% correct at 2, and 99% correct at 1.  Would using a standard logistic link function cause us to underestimate the slope? [I think so, but please correct me if I'm wrong, see below]</p>\n\n<p>Edit:  Those who have answered my question so far have expressed that the way in which I set up the problem was unclear.  I'm providing the sample below to help clear things up.</p>\n\n<pre><code>library(psyphy)\nmake.data <- function(zero,one)\n    {\n        return(c(rep(0,zero),rep(1,one)))\n    }\ncenter <- function(x) {return(scale(x,scale=FALSE))}\nlogit.data <- data.frame(Score=c(make.data(50,50),make.data(50,50),make.data(25,75),make.data(15,85),make.data(1,99)), Difficulty=rep(5:1,each=100))\nlogit.data$Difficulty2 <- center(logit.data$Difficulty)^2\nstandard <- glm(Score~center(Difficulty),data=logit.data,family=binomial) #standard link function\nstandard.2 <- glm(Score~center(Difficulty)+Difficulty2,data=logit.data,family=binomial) #standard link function, but better with a quadradic\nrevised.link <- glm(Score~center(Difficulty),data=logit.data,family=binomial(mafc.logit(2)))\nAIC(base)\nAIC(base.2)\nAIC(revised.link)\ncoef(base)\ncoef(base.2)\ncoef(revised.link)\n#plot\nplot(diffs,plogis(coef(standard)[1] +coef(standard)[2]*center(diffs)),xlab=\"Difficulty\",ylab=\"Pr(Correct)\",ylim=c(0,1),col=\"blue\",type=\"l\");abline(.5,0,col=\"Orange\");lines(diffs,plogis(coef(standard.2)[1]+coef(standard.2)[2]*center(diffs)+coef(standard.2)[3]*center(diffs)^2),col=\"Cyan\");lines(diffs,(p2afc(coef(revised.link)[1]+coef(revised.link)[2]*center(diffs))),col=\"Green\");lines(5:1,c(.55,.60,.75,.85,.99),col=\"Black\")\n</code></pre>\n\n<p><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/elxVG.jpg\" alt=\"alt text\"></p>\n\n<p>In the above image the orange horizontal line marks 50% correct responses.  The jagged black line represents the data supplied to the estimation equation (note the values for 4 and 5 disappear behind the orange 50% marker).  The blue line is the equation produced by a standard logistic link.  Note that it estimates below 50% accuracy when discrimination is most difficult (5).  The cyan line is the standard logistic link with a quadratic term.  The green line is a non-standard link that takes into account that the data comes from a 2AFC experiment where performance is very unlikely to fall below 50%.\nNote that the AIC for a model fit using a non-standard link function is superior to the standard logistic link function.  Also note that the slope for the standard equation is less than the slope for the standard equation with the quadratic term (which more accurately reflects the real data).  Thus, using a logistic function blindly on 2AFC data does (at least) appear to underestimate the slope.</p>\n\n<p>Is there a problem with my demonstration that means that I am not seeing what I think I am seeing?  If I'm correct, then what other consequences (if any) are there of using the generic logistic function with 2AFC data [presumably extensible to NAFC cases]?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-08T18:10:40.850000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1354", "provsql": "d8ac92df-4931-4547-b287-1f58539072de"}, "posts_95": {"id": 97, "owneruserid": 114, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 104, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What are good basic statistics to use for ordinal data?", "tags": "<descriptive-statistics><ordinal-data><likert><faq>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I have some <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinal_scale#Ordinal_scale\">ordinal data</a> gained from survey questions.
