We estimate $p$ using, let's say, density estimator, to be $\\tilde{p}$. Now, again, we know some properties about the mode, such that, for some function $F(z_{mode}) = 0$. Then, (perhaps?) it is better to find the mode of $\\tilde{p}(z)$ while constraining $F(z)$ to be $0$, instead of just finding the mode of $\\tilde{p}$ without this constraint.</p></li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>My question is: are there any known results about incorporating this kind of prior knowledge (if it is true)? I am interested in reading more about this.</p>\n\n<p>Thanks.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-07-11T14:08:51.303000", "posts_rownum": "posts_11867", "provsql": "b251b7b9-6d80-483e-a354-e06d9b082055"}, "posts_11995": {"id": 13022, "owneruserid": 2848, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 13027, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to decide whether difference between two conditions is significant?", "tags": "<hypothesis-testing>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm trying to analyse an experiment I performed. I executed 9 <strike>tests</strike> measurements, at two different settings (A and B); I expect it to be normal distributed.  I had the following hypotheses:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>$H_0:\\; \\mu_A = \\mu_B$</li>\n<li>$H_1:\\; \\mu_A \\neq \\mu_B$</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>I got the following results for my measurements</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>A: n=9, mean = 1.66, sd = 1.12</li>\n<li>B: n=9, mean = 2.48, sd = 1.16</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>I would like to know whether this difference is significant (say at 95%), but I get a bit stuck - I only learned how to do this when I know $\\mu_A$ or $\\sigma_A$ (or have a very good estimate of it due to a large sample), but I only have a sample standard deviation for A.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-07-14T07:36:53.777000", "posts_rownum": "posts_11995", "provsql": "d6712f26-8986-40b0-b120-8622eb59d363"}, "posts_12082": {"id": 13112, "owneruserid": 5240, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 13115, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What is the correct way to test for significant differences between coefficients?", "tags": "<regression><hypothesis-testing><multiple-regression>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm hoping someone can help straighten out a point of confusion for me. Say I want to test whether 2 sets of regression coefficients are significantly different from each other, with the following set up:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>$y_i = \\alpha + \\beta x_i + \\epsilon_i$, with 5 independent variables.</li>\n<li>2 groups, with roughly equal sizes $n_1, n_2$ (though this may vary)</li>\n<li>Thousands of similar regression will be done simultaneously, so some kind of multiple hypothesis correction has to be done.</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>One approach that was suggested to me is to use a Z-test:</p>\n\n<p>$Z = \\frac{b_1 - b_2}{\\sqrt(SEb_1^2 + SEb_2^2)}$</p>\n\n<p>Another I've seen suggested on this board is to introduce a dummy variable for grouping and rewrite the model as:</p>\n\n<p>$y_i = \\alpha + \\beta x_i + \\delta(x_ig_i) + \\epsilon_i$, where $g$ is the grouping variable, coded as 0, 1.</p>\n\n<p>My question is, how are these two approaches different (e.g. different assumptions made, flexibility)? "<correlation><statistical-significance><multiple-comparisons>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I have computed a correlation matrix of a data set which contains 455 data points, each data point containing 14 characteristics. So the dimension of the correlation matrix is 14 x 14.</p>\n\n<p>I was wondering whether there is a threshold for the value of the correlation coefficient which points out that there is a significant correlation between two of those characteristics.</p>\n\n<p>I have value ranging from -0.2 to 0.85, and I was thinking that the important ones are those which are above 0.7. </p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>Is there a general value for the correlation coefficient which should be considered for the threshold or is just context dependent to the data type which I am investigating? </li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2011-08-03T15:56:20.387000", "posts_rownum": "posts_12697", "provsql": "c2fe47f5-0923-4629-a85e-cdd3ca48b9f4"}, "posts_13231": {"id": 14399, "owneruserid": 5191, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 14491, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to draw a random sample from distribution of prediction?", "tags": "<r><regression><predictive-models>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>For my microsimulation, I want to use R to predict values and draw a random sample based on this prediction.</p>\n\n<p>To clarify my point: I want to simulate the number of chronic conditions people suffer from ($y_t$) at a certain point in time. I have a few waves of panel data available to estimate a relation between age, sex, number of chronic conditions in the previous observation period (plus some others that I might include in later stages).</p>\n\n<p>Suppose my regression model is $y_t = β_0 + β_1 age + β_2 sex + β_3y_{t-1} +u $.   </p>\n\n<p>Since R provides me with coefficients for the betas, it is easy to predict $y_t$ given the independent variables. However, this is not what I want to do. Instead, I want my population of about 1300 individuals to resemble the variance in the possible outcomes of $y_t$ (otherwise after a few steps my simulated population won’t include those unlucky ones with much more chronic conditions than the average).   </p>\n\n<p>I believe what I have to do is to draw a random sample from the distribution of the predicted value $y_t$, conditional on the independent variables. I further believe this can be done by drawing random numbers with mean $β$ and variance $var(β)$, multiplied by the actual values of the independent variables.  </p>\n\n<p>So my question is: Is this the correct approach? Will this produce reliable values? Or do I need to take possible covariation of the independent variables etc. into consideration?</p>\n\n<p><strong>Edit</strong>: Another point came to my mind. Does it make a difference whether $y_t$ or $y_t - y_{t-1}$ is my left hand side variable?</p>\n\n<p>Thank you for your ideas.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-08-17T13:00:55.600000", "posts_rownum": "posts_13231", "provsql": "26267eb0-dc8e-4706-ba25-5d8501f35e8e"}, "posts_13499": {"id": 14721, "owneruserid": 5509, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 20515, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How is the bayesian framework better in interpretation when we usually use uninformative or subjective priors?", "tags": "<bayesian><interpretation><prior><likelihood><posterior>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>It is often argued that the bayesian framework has a big advantage in interpretation (over frequentist), because it computes the probability of a parameter given the data - $p(\\theta|x)$ instead of $p(x|\\theta)$ as in the frequentist framework. So far so good.</p>\n\n<p>But, the whole equation it is based on:</p>\n\n<p>$p(\\theta|x) = {p(x|\\theta) . p(\\theta) \\over p(x)}$</p>\n\n<p>looks to me little suspicious for 2 reasons:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li><p>In many papers, usualy uninformative priors (uniform distributions) are used and then just $p(\\theta|x) = p(x|\\theta)$, so bayesians get the same result as frequentists get - so how is then bayesian framework better in interpretation, when bayesian posterior and frequentists likelihood are the same distributions? It just yields the same result.</p></li>\n<li><p>When using informative priors, you get different results, but the bayesian is affected by the subjective prior, so the whole $p(\\theta|x)$ has the subjective tinge too.</p></li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>In other words, the whole argument of $p(\\theta|x)$ being better in interpretation than $p(x|\\theta)$ builds on a presumption that $p(\\theta)$ is kind of \"real\", which normally is not, it is just a starting point we somehow choose to make the MCMC run, a presumption, but it is not a description of reality (it can't be defined I think).</p>\n\n<p>So how can we argue that bayesian is better in interpretation?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-08-23T19:16:57.777000", "posts_rownum": "posts_13499", "provsql": "1ff876fb-d033-4a0c-94b1-afc4bd4a65a8"}, When I teach, I tend to use the following standard examples to illustrate this point:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>number of storks and birth rate in Denmark;</li>\n<li>number of priests in America and alcoholism;</li>\n<li>in the start of the 20th century it was noted that there was a strong correlation between 'Number of radios' and 'Number of people in Insane Asylums'</li>\n<li>and my favorite: <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File%3aPiratesVsTemp%28en%29.svg\">pirates cause global warming</a>.</li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>However, I do not have any references for these examples and whilst amusing, they are obviously false.</p>\n\n<p>Does anyone have any other good examples?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-19T19:31:47.363000", "posts_rownum": "posts_33", "provsql": "b22390f1-431f-4a65-b0c1-d45f4e4fe576"}, "posts_114": {"id": 124, "owneruserid": 131, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Statistical classification of text", "tags": "<classification><information-retrieval><text-mining>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I'm a programmer without statistical background, and I'm currently looking at different classification methods for a large number of different documents that I want to classify into pre-defined categories. (This is in the vein of the Stack Overflow question <em><a href=\"https://stackoverflow.com/questions/84556/whats-your-favorite-programmer-cartoon\">What’s your favorite “programmer” cartoon?</a></em>.)</p>\n<p>P.S. Do not hotlink the cartoon without the site's permission please.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-21T15:13:21.493000", "posts_rownum": "posts_406", "provsql": "2cd3ae45-ddd1-4c30-9d12-3bcb9d4dba04"}, "posts_470": {"id": 485, "owneruserid": 183, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Mathematical Statistics Videos", "tags": "<mathematical-statistics><references>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>A question previously sought recommendations for <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/414/intro-to-statistics-for-mathematicians\">textbooks on mathematical statistics</a></p>\n\n<p>Does anyone know of any good online <strong>video lectures</strong> on <strong>mathematical statistics</strong>?\nThe closest that I've found are:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><a href=\"http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UzxYlbK2c7E&feature=PlayList&p=A89DCFA6ADACE599&index=0\" rel=\"noreferrer\">Machine Learning</a> </li>\n<li><a href=\"http://economistsview.typepad.com/economics421/\" rel=\"noreferrer\">Econometrics</a> </li>\n</ul>\n\n<p><strong>UPDATE:</strong> A number of the suggestions mentioned below are good statistics-101 type videos.\nHowever, I'm specifically wondering whether there are any videos that provide a rigorous mathematical presentation of statistics.\ni.e., videos that might accompany a course that use a textbook mentioned in this <a href=\"https://mathoverflow.net/questions/31655/statistics-for-mathematicians\">discussion on mathoverflow</a></p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-22T10:08:10.067000", "posts_rownum": "posts_470", "provsql": "fdce5a46-21de-46c9-9591-b1cd6b260f23"}, "posts_475": {"id": 6814, "owneruserid": null, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": "user3016", "title": "Kullback-Leibler divergence - interpretation", "tags": "<kullback-leibler>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I have a question about the Kullback-Leibler divergence.</p>\n\n<p>Can someone explain why the \"distance\" between the blue density and the \"red\" density is smaller than the distance between the \"green\" curve and the \"red\" one?</p>\n\n<p><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/Zrm76.jpg\" alt=\"Graph of three pdfs\"></p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-02-02T15:07:42.593000", "posts_rownum": "posts_475", "provsql": "9a167d0a-a1a6-41b0-859c-f914cc9f6ed9"}, "posts_522": {"id": 534, "owneruserid": 159, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 538, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Under what conditions does correlation imply causation?", "tags": "<correlation><causality>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>We all know the mantra \"correlation does not imply causation\" which is drummed into all first year statistics students. There are some nice examples <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/36/correlation-does-not-mean-causation\">here</a> to illustrate the idea.</p>\n\n<p>But sometimes correlation <em>does</em> imply causation. The following example is taking from this <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation_does_not_imply_causation#Determining_causation\" rel=\"noreferrer\">Wikipedia page</a></p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>For example, one could run an experiment on identical twins who were known to consistently get the same grades on their tests. One twin is sent to study for six hours while the other is sent to the amusement park. If their test scores suddenly diverged by a large degree, this would be strong evidence that studying (or going to the amusement park) had a causal effect on test scores. In this case, correlation between studying and test scores would almost certainly imply causation.</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>Are there other situations where correlation implies causation?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-23T01:56:02.517000", "posts_rownum": "posts_522", "provsql": "78044620-a63b-4e62-b462-0569fb477780"}, "posts_620": {"id": 631, "owneruserid": null, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 28567, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": "user88", "title": "Standard deviation of standard deviation", "tags": "<estimation><standard-deviation><normality-assumption>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>What is an estimator of standard deviation of standard deviation if normality of data can be assumed?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-26T16:10:45.817000", "posts_rownum": "posts_620", "provsql": "d801cb0e-403b-4888-a692-94faafffa553"}, "posts_782": {"id": 798, "owneruserid": 476, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 862, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Calculating optimal number of bins in a histogram", "tags": "<rule-of-thumb><histogram>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm interested in finding as optimal of a method as I can for determining how many bins I should use in a histogram. My data should range from 30 to 350 objects at most, and in particular I'm trying to apply thresholding (like Otsu's method) where \"good\" objects, which I should have fewer of and should be more spread out, are separated from \"bad\" objects, which should be more dense in value. A concrete value would have a score of 1-10 for each object. I'd had 5-10 objects with scores 6-10, and 20-25 objects with scores 1-4. I'd like to find a histogram binning pattern that generally allows something like Otsu's method to threshold off the low scoring objects. However, in the implementation of Otsu's I've seen, the bin size was 256, and often I have many fewer data points that 256, which to me suggests that 256 is not a good bin number. With so few data, what approaches should I take to calculating the number of bins to use?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-27T15:21:48.417000", "posts_rownum": "posts_782", "provsql": "c9e7e8d3-830e-4de7-a377-576025bb320c"}, "posts_868": {"id": 880, "owneruserid": 223, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Cross validation in very high dimension (to select the number of used variables in very high dimensional classification)", "tags": "<machine-learning><classification><cross-validation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>My question is about cross validation when there are many more variables than observations. To fix ideas, I propose to restrict to the classification framework in very high dimension (more features than observation).</p>\n\n<p><strong>Problem:</strong> Assume that for each variable $i=1,\\dots,p$ you have a measure of importance $T[i]$ than exactly measure the interest of feature $i$ for the classification problem. The problem of selecting a subset of feature to reduce optimally the classification error is then reduced to that of finding the number of features. </p>\n\n<p><strong>Question:</strong> What is the most efficient way to run cross validation in this case (cross validation scheme)? My question is not about how to write the code but on the version of cross validation to use when trying to find the number of selected feature (to minimize the classification error) but how to deal with the high dimension when doing cross validation (hence the problem above may be a bit like a 'toy problem' to discuss CV in high dimension). </p>\n\n<p><strong>Notations:</strong>  $n$ is the size of the learning set, p the number of features (i.e. the dimension of the feature space).  By very high dimension I mean p>>n (for example $p=10000$ and $n=100$). </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-28T08:15:40.827000", "posts_rownum": "posts_868", "provsql": "0cd6f3c8-239e-4e4b-a4c2-3c7edf24b028"}, "posts_999": {"id": 1028, "owneruserid": 608, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to interpret KL divergence quantitatively?", "tags": "<distributions><kullback-leibler><information-geometry>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I am comparing two distributions with KL divergence which returns me a non-standardized number that, according to what I read about this measure, is the amount of information that is required to transform one hypothesis into the other. I have two questions:</p>\n\n<p>a) Is there a way to quantify a KL divergence so that it has a more meaningful interpretation, e.g. like an effect size or a R^2? Any form of standardization?</p>\n\n<p>b) In R, when using KLdiv (flexmix package) one can set the 'esp' value (standard esp=1e-4) that sets all points smaller than esp to some standard in order to provide numerical stability. I have been playing with different esp values and, for my data set, I am getting an increasingly larger KL divergence the smaller a number I pick. What is going on? I would expect that the smaller the esp, the more reliable the results should be since they let more 'real values' become part of the statistic. No? I have to change the esp since it otherwise does not calculate the statistic but simply shows up as NA in the result table ... </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-30T00:55:20.603000", "posts_rownum": "posts_999", "provsql": "a5566769-dd48-4033-95da-190c3e8415be"}, "posts_1124": {"id": 1169, "owneruserid": 364, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1171, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "CI for a difference based on independent CIs", "tags": "<confidence-interval>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I'm looking to check my logic here. </p>\n\n<p>Say you measure a quantity in group A, and find the mean is 2 and your 95% confidence interval ranges from 1 to 3. Then you measure the same quantity in group B and find a mean of 4 with a 95% confidence interval that ranges from 3.5 to 4.5. Assuming that A & B are independent, what is the 95% confidence interval for the difference between the groups? Presumably you can compute this using standard t-statistics, but I'd like to know if it's also possible to compute an estimate based on the CI's alone.</p>\n\n<p>I reason that the lower bound of the CI of the difference should be the minimum credible difference between A & B; that is, the lower bound of the interval for B (3.5) minus upper bound of the interval for A (3), which yields a lower bound for the difference of 0.5. Similarly, the upper bound of the CI of the difference should be the maximum credible difference between A & B; that is, the upper bound of the interval for B (4.5) minus lower bound of the interval for A (1), which yields a lower bound for the difference of 3.5. This reasoning thus yields a confidence interval for the difference that ranges from 0.5 to 3.5.</p>\n\n<p>Does that make sense, or is this a case where logic and statistics diverge?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-03T12:20:09.890000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1124", "provsql": "4dfdd420-2d1b-4c3b-97e7-79dd8f760cfa"}, "posts_4048": {"id": 4298, "owneruserid": 226, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 4314, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Use of kernel density estimate in Naive Bayes Classifier?", "tags": "<bayesian><kde>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>This question is a follow up to my earlier question <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/4220/probability-distribution-over-1-is-ok\">here</a> \nand is also related, in intent, to <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/3316/statistical-similarity-of-time-series\">this question</a>.</p>\n\n<p>On <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naive_Bayes_classifier\" rel=\"noreferrer\">this wiki page</a> <em>probability density values</em> from an assumed normal distribution for the training set are used to calculate a Bayesian posterior rather than actual probability values. However, if a training set is not normally distributed would it be equally as valid to use a <em>density value</em> taken from the <em>kernel density estimate</em> of the training set to calculate a Bayesian posterior? </p>\n\n<p>In its intended application this <em>kernel density estimate</em> would be taken from a theoretically ideal empirical data set generated by MC techniques. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-11-07T21:23:52.657000", "posts_rownum": "posts_4048", "provsql": "9a50ef64-543e-4697-9c45-fb6d2d2c3935"}, "posts_1237": {"id": 1289, "owneruserid": 760, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Visualizing multiple \"histograms\" (bar-charts)", "tags": "<pca><data-visualization><histogram><barplot>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I am having difficulties to select the right way to visualize data. Let's say we have <strong>bookstores</strong> that sells <strong>books</strong>, and every book has at least one <strong>category</strong>.</p>\n<p>For a bookstore, if we count all the categories of books, we acquire a histogram that shows the number of books that falls into a specific category for that bookstore.</p>\n<p>I want to visualize the bookstore behavior, I want to see if they favor a category over other categories. I don't want to see if they are favoring sci-fi all together, but I want to see if they are treating every category equally or not.</p>\n<p>I have ~1M bookstores.</p>\n<p>I have thought of 4 methods:</p>\n<ol>\n<li><p>Sample the data, show only 500 bookstore's histograms. Show them in 5 separate pages using 10x10 grid. Example of a 4x4 grid:</p>\n<p><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/LAOjc.png2.\" alt=\"multiple histograms 1\" /></p>\n</li>\n<li><p>Same as #1. But this time sort x axis values according to their count desc, so if there is a favoring it will be seen easily.</p>\n</li>\n<li><p>Imagine putting the histograms in #2 together like a deck and showing them in 3D. Something like this:<br />\n<img src=\"https://web.archive.org/web/20170712133139/https://www.statsoft.com/textbook/popups/popup110.gif\" alt=\"3D histogram\" /></p>\n</li>\n<li><p>Instead of using third axis suing color to represent colors, so using a heatmap (2D histogram):\n<img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/rHxg1.png\" alt=\"2D histogram\" /><br />\nIf generally bookstores prefer some categories to others it will be displayed as a nice gradient from left to right.</p>\n</li>\n</ol>\n<p>Do you have any other visualization ideas/tools to represent multiple histograms?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-05T10:03:34.997000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1237", "provsql": "b63cac93-b8ea-41b9-be3c-31b1c00f888b"}, "posts_1266": {"id": 1324, "owneruserid": 1356, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1326, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Parametric techniques for n-related samples", "tags": "<repeated-measures>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>The title is quite self-explanatory - I'd like to know if there's any other parametric technique apart from repeated-measures ANOVA, that can be utilized in order to compare several (more than 2) repeated measures?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-05T22:16:20.007000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1266", "provsql": "0c15ab06-1c3b-4907-bafa-521b547c6240"}, "posts_1328": {"id": 1385, "owneruserid": 438, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1404, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Techniques for Handling Incomplete/Missing Data", "tags": "<missing-data>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>My question is directed to techniques to deal with <em>incomplete</em> data during the classifier/model training/fitting.</p>\n\n<p>For instance, in a dataset w/ a few hundred rows, each row having let's say five dimensions and a class label as the last item, most data points will look like this:</p>\n\n<p>[0.74, 0.39, 0.14, 0.33, 0.34, 0]</p>\n\n<p>A few might look something like this:</p>\n\n<p><strong>[0.21, 0.68, ?, 0.82, 0.58, 1]</strong></p>\n\n<p>So it's those types of data points that are the focus of this Question.</p>\n\n<p>My initial reason for asking this question was a problem directly in front of me; however, before posting my Question, i thought it might be more useful if i re-phrased it so the answers would be useful to a larger portion of the Community.</p>\n\n<p>As a simple heuristic, let's divide these data-handling techniques based on when during the processing flow they are employed--before input to the classifier or during (i.e., the technique is inside the classifier).</p>\n\n<p>The best example i can think of for the latter is the clever 'three-way branching' technique used in Decision Trees.</p>\n\n<p>No doubt, the former category is far larger. The techniques i am aware of all fall into one of the groups below. </p>\n\n<p>While recently reviewing my personal notes on \"missing data handling\" i noticed that i had quite an impressive list of techniques. I just maintain these notes for general peace of mind and in case a junior colleague asks me how to deal with missing data. In actual practice, i don't actually use any of them, except for the last one.</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li><p><strong>Imputation</strong>: a broad rubric for a set of techniques which whose common\ndenominator (i believe) is that the\nmissing data is supplied directly by\nthe same data set--substitution\nrather than estimation/prediction.</p></li>\n<li><p><strong>Reconstruction</strong>: estimate the missing data points using an\nauto-associative network (just a\nneural network in which the sizes of\nthe input and output layers are\nequal--in other words, the output\nhas the same dimension as the\ninput); the idea here is to train\nthis network on complete data, then\nfeed it incomplete patterns, and\nread the missing values from the\noutput nodes.</p></li>\n<li><p><strong>Bootstrapping</strong>: (no summary necessary i shouldn't think, given\nit's use elsewhere in statistical\nanalysis).</p></li>\n<li><p><strong>Denial</strong>: quietly remove the data points with missing/corrupt elements\nfrom your training set and pretend\nthey never existed.</p></li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-07T05:07:27.083000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1328", "provsql": "8dfc605a-aa66-48e4-8b58-6e4bd7afe05a"}, "posts_1388": {"id": 1444, "owneruserid": 159, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1446, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How should I transform non-negative data including zeros?", "tags": "<data-transformation><large-data>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>If I have highly skewed positive data I often take logs. But what should I do with highly skewed non-negative data that include zeros? I have seen two transformations used:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>$\\log(x+1)$ which has the neat feature that 0 maps to 0.</li>\n<li>$\\log(x+c)$ where c is either estimated or set to be some very small positive value.</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>Are there any other approaches? Are there any good reasons to prefer one approach over the others?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-09T13:57:51.753000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1388", "provsql": "00c9a927-01a4-46ad-981b-5a00e15c8c66"}, "posts_1523": {"id": 1595, "owneruserid": 890, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1632, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Python as a statistics workbench", "tags": "<r><spss><stata><python>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Lots of people use a main tool like Excel or another spreadsheet, SPSS, Stata, or R for their statistics needs. They might turn to some specific package for very special needs, but a lot of things can be done with a simple spreadsheet or a general stats package or stats programming environment.</p>\n\n<p>I've always liked Python as a programming language, and for simple needs, it's easy to write a short program that calculates what I need. Matplotlib allows me to plot it.</p>\n\n<p>Has anyone switched completely from, say R, to Python? R (or any other statistics package) has a lot of functionality specific to statistics, and it has data structures that allow you to think about the statistics you want to perform and less about the internal representation of your data. Python (or some other dynamic language) has the benefit of allowing me to program in a familiar, high-level language, and it lets me programmatically interact with real-world systems in which the data resides or from which I can take measurements. But I haven't found any Python package that would allow me to express things with \"statistical terminology\" – from simple descriptive statistics to more complicated multivariate methods.</p>\n\n<p>What can you recommend if I wanted to use Python as a \"statistics workbench\" to replace R, SPSS, etc.?</p>\n\n<p>What would I gain and lose, based on your experience?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-12T10:46:45.407000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1523", "provsql": "f0cf2e24-cb61-49cf-8ca0-41df062fbd2a"}, "posts_1605": {"id": 1676, "owneruserid": 110, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "I just installed the latest version of R. What packages should I obtain?", "tags": "<r>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p><strong>Duplicate thread:</strong> <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/73/what-r-packages-do-you-find-most-useful-in-your-daily-work\">What R packages do you find most useful in your daily work?</a></p>\n\n<p>Are there any R packages that are just plain good to have, regardless of the type of work you are doing? If so, what are these packages? If not, what packages do you find the most useful?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-14T01:39:23.253000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1605", "provsql": "ab972e33-4234-4861-8083-735c5ed84b06"}, "posts_1685": {"id": 1761, "owneruserid": 253, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Statistics/Probability Videos for Beginners", "tags": "<references>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>There was already <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/485/mathematical-statistics-videos\">a request for Mathematical Statistics Videos</a>,  but it explicitly asked from people for</p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>videos that provide a rigorous\n  mathematical presentation of\n  statistics. i.e., videos that might\n  accompany a course that use a textbook\n  mentioned in this discussion on...</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>So at the same time I am wondering, <strong>what recommendation do you have for stat/prob - 101  - video courses?</strong></p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-17T02:52:02.637000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1685", "provsql": "20bce63f-ba2a-4d47-a9da-ca37467e5567"}, "posts_1719": {"id": 1799, "owneruserid": 835, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Recommendations - or best practices - for analyzing non-independent data. Specific example relating to pain perception data provided", "tags": "<non-independent>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I am seeking recommendations and/or best practices for analyzing non-independent data. In particular, I am curious about non-independent data that does not reflect typical repeated-measures time-based data in which data for the same question(s) or stimuli are collected at different time points. Rather the data collected is elicited from similar (but not identical) questions or stimuli that are known to be related. A specific example follows.</p>\n\n<p>I have pain perception data for two groups (group A, group B) that can be further divided by gender (i.e., A-women; A-men; B-women; B-men). The pain perception dependent variables include 3 thermal threshold tests (i.e., detection, pain, tolerance) and pain magnitude estimates for a range of specific temperatures (temp X1, X2, X3, X4, X5). These pain perception variables are collected for both heat and cold stimuli (e.g., heat pain tolerance; cold pain tolerance; heat temp X1; cold temp X1). It should be expected (and indeed it is observed) that the various pain perception variables for a given individual are not independent.</p>\n\n<p>The purpose of the analysis is to look for between group differences based on group membership (group A vs. group B) and sex (women vs men). It is desirable to find interactions between group membership and sex. It is also desirable to find interactions between specific pain perception variables (or types of variables; i.e., \"cold stimuli\") and group membership and/or sex. I have tried running a series of repeated-measures ANOVAs separately for each of the different groupings of pain perception variables (i.e., heat stimuli threshold tests; cold stimuli threshold tests; heat pain magnitude estimates; cold pain magnitude estimates); however this solution does not feel optimal or adequate. My specific questions are:</p>\n\n<p>1) is it appropriate to analyze data elicited from related (but not identical) questions/stimuli using repeated measures?</p>\n\n<p>2) Is it appropriate to analyze chunks of the data (e.g., cold pain magnitude estimates; cold stimuli threshold tests) separately?</p>\n\n<p>2) Would a different strategy (such as multilevel analysis / profile analysis / or some type of multivariate repeated measures ANOVA) be more appropriate?</p>\n\n<p>3) General recommendations and/or best practices for analyzing data such as this.</p>\n\n<p>Thank you for your feedback and input</p>\n\n<p>Patrick Welch</p>\n\n<p>note: I already searched the site for related questions (i.e., <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/859/anova-with-non-independent-observations\">ANOVA with non-independent observations</a> ; <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/1324/parametric-techniques-for-n-related-samples\">Parametric techniques for n-related samples</a>) but believe the current question to be different enough to warrant unique consideration.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-17T20:00:59.700000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1719", "provsql": "6b4ff86c-d4d0-4183-a4e1-65af604f0b2a"}, "posts_1733": {"id": 1815, "owneruserid": 174, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Recommended books on experiment design?", "tags": "<references><experiment-design>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>What are the panel's recommendations for books on design of experiments?</p>\n\n<p>Ideally, books should be still in print or available electronically, although that may not always be feasible. If you feel moved to add a few words on what's so good about the book that would be great too.</p>\n\n<p>Also, aim for one book per answer so that voting can help sort the suggestions.</p>\n\n<p>(Community Wiki, please edit the question if you can make it better!)</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-18T08:54:23.650000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1733", "provsql": "9a913c28-8f90-494c-abb0-9e3dc462df4f"}, "posts_1762": {"id": 1844, "owneruserid": 25, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2053, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What are the pros and cons of using the logrank vs. the Mantel-Haenszel method for computing the Hazard Ratio in survival analysis?", "tags": "<survival><hazard>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>One way to summarize the comparison of two survival curves is to compute the hazard ratio (HR). There are (at least) two methods to compute this value. </p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>Logrank method. As part of the Kaplan-Meier calculations, compute the number of observed events (deaths, usually) in each group ($Oa$, and $Ob$), and the number of expected events assuming a null hypothesis of no difference in survival ($Ea$ and $Eb$). The hazard ratio then is:\n$$\n    HR= \\frac{(Oa/Ea)}{(Ob/Eb)}\n$$</li>\n<li>Mantel-Haenszel method. First compute V, which is the sum of the hypergeometric variances at each time point. Then compute the hazard ratio as:\n$$\n HR= \\exp\\left(\\frac{(Oa-Ea)}{V}\\right)\n$$\nI got both these equations from chapter 3 of  Machin, Cheung and Parmar, <a href=\"http://rads.stackoverflow.com/amzn/click/0470870400\" rel=\"noreferrer\">Survival Analysis</a>. That book states that the two methods usually give very similar methods, and indeed that is the case with the example in the book. </li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>Someone sent me an example where the two methods differ by a factor of three. In this particular example, it is obvious that the logrank estimate is sensible, and the Mantel-Haenszel estimate is far off. My question is if anyone has any general advice for when it is best to choose the logrank estimate of the hazard ratio, and when it is best to choose the Mantel-Haenszel estimate? Does it have to do with sample size? Number of ties? Ratio of sample sizes?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-18T15:47:15.627000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1762", "provsql": "c2f1ca69-359d-4800-a926-acc404dea2a4"}, "posts_1924": {"id": 2002, "owneruserid": null, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": "Think Blue Crew", "title": "How do I decide what span to use in LOESS regression in R?", "tags": "<r><regression><loess>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I am running LOESS regression models in R, and I want to compare the outputs of 12 different models with varying sample sizes. I can describe the actual models in more details if it helps with answering the question. </p>\n\n<p>Here are the sample sizes: </p>\n\n<pre><code>Fastballs vs RHH 2008-09: 2002\nFastballs vs LHH 2008-09: 2209\nFastballs vs RHH 2010: 527 \nFastballs vs LHH 2010: 449\n\nChangeups vs RHH 2008-09: 365\nChangeups vs LHH 2008-09: 824\nChangeups vs RHH 2010: 201\nChangeups vs LHH 2010: 330\n\nCurveballs vs RHH 2008-09: 488\nCurveballs vs LHH 2008-09: 483\nCurveballs vs RHH 2010: 213\nCurveballs vs LHH 2010: 162\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>The LOESS regression model is a surface fit, where the X location and the Y location of each baseball pitch is used to predict sw, swinging strike probability. However, I'd like to compare between all 12 of these models, but setting the same span (i.e. span = 0.5) will bear different results since there is such a wide range of sample sizes.</p>\n\n<p>My basic question is how do you determine the span of your model? A higher span smooths out the fit more, while a lower span captures more trends but introduces statistical noise if there is too little data. I use a higher span for smaller sample sizes and a lower span for larger sample sizes. </p>\n\n<p>What should I do? What's a good rule of thumb when setting span for LOESS regression models in R? Thanks in advance!</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-22T02:24:24.947000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1924", "provsql": "2eac5d59-ec1a-45ba-92c8-dab9b74c6968"}, "posts_2002": {"id": 2086, "owneruserid": 840, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2087, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Quickly evaluate (visually) correlations between ordered categorical data in R?", "tags": "<r><correlation><categorical-data><data-visualization>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I'm looking for correlations between the answers to different questions in a survey (\"umm, let's see if answers to question 11 correlate with those of question 78\"). All answers are categorical (most of them range from \"very unhappy\" to \"very happy\"), but a few have a different set of answers. Most of them can be considered ordinal so let's consider this  case here.</p>\n\n<p>Since I don't have access to a commercial statistics program, I must use R.</p>\n\n<p>I tried <a href=\"http://rattle.togaware.com/\">Rattle</a> (a freeware data mining package for R, very nifty) but unfortunately it doesn't support categorical data. One hack I could use is to import in R the coded version of the survey which has numbers (1..5) instead of \"very unhappy\" ... \"happy\" and let Rattle believe they are numerical data.</p>\n\n<p>I was thinking to do a scatter plot and have the dot size proportional to the number of numbers for each pair. After some googling I found <a href=\"http://www.r-statistics.com/2010/04/correlation-scatter-plot-matrix-for-ordered-categorical-data/\">http://www.r-statistics.com/2010/04/correlation-scatter-plot-matrix-for-ordered-categorical-data/</a> but it seems very complicated (to me).</p>\n\n<p>I'm not a statistician (but a programmer) but have had some reading in the matter and, if I understand correctly, <em>Spearman's rho</em> would be appropriate here. </p>\n\n<p>So the short version of the question for those in a hurry: <strong>is there a way to quickly plot \nSpearman's rho in R</strong>? A plot is preferable to a matrix of numbers because it's easier to eye ball and also can be included in materials.</p>\n\n<p>Thank you in advance. </p>\n\n<p>PS I pondered for a while whether to post this on the main SO site or here. After searching both sites for R correlation, I felt this site is better suited for the question.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-25T03:16:23.030000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2002", "provsql": "e2c8cb63-11c7-44ae-9d5a-945198e7dfbf"}, "posts_2163": {"id": 2245, "owneruserid": 5, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2251, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Statistics and causal inference?", "tags": "<causality>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>In his 1984 paper <a href=\"http://www-unix.oit.umass.edu/~stanek/pdffiles/causal-holland.pdf\">\"Statistics and Causal Inference\"</a>, Paul Holland raised one of the most fundamental questions in statistics:</p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>What can a statistical model say about\n  causation?</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>This led to his motto:</p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>NO CAUSATION WITHOUT MANIPULATION</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>which emphasized the importance of restrictions around experiments that consider causation. \nAndrew Gelman makes <a href=\"http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~cook/movabletype/archives/2010/08/no_understandin.html\">a similar point</a>:</p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>\"To find out what happens when you change something, it is necessary to change it.\"...There are things you learn from perturbing a system that you'll never find out from any amount of passive observation.</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>His ideas are summarized in <a href=\"http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/causalreview4.pdf\">this article</a>.</p>\n\n<p>What considerations should be made when making a causal inference from a statistical model?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-31T19:13:04.883000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2163", "provsql": "33c782fa-5519-48d6-aea6-d0a2397b4e71"}, "posts_2313": {"id": 2401, "owneruserid": 364, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2409, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Is it appropriate to treat n-point Likert scale data as n trials from a binomial process?", "tags": "<binomial-distribution><likert><scales><psychometrics><psychology>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I've never liked how people typically analyze data from Likert scales as if error were continuous & Gaussian when there are reasonable expectations that these assumptions are violated at least at the extremes of the scales. What do you think of the following alternative:</p>\n\n<p>If the response takes value $k$ on an $n$-point scale, expand that data to $n$ trials, $k$ of which have the value 1 and $n-k$ of which have the value 0. Thus, we're treating response on a Likert scale as if it is the overt aggregate of a covert series of binomial trials (in fact, from a cognitive science perspective, this is actually an appealing model for the mechanisms involved in such decision making scenarios). With the expanded data, you can now use a mixed effects model specifying respondent as a random effect (also question as a random effect if you have multiple questions) and using the binomial link function to specify the error distribution.</p>\n\n<p>Can anyone see any assumption violations or other detrimental aspects of this approach?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-06T00:58:21.607000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2313", "provsql": "5fc56aec-d815-4be2-a5e8-e8a944b6ef96"}, "posts_2391": {"id": 2492, "owneruserid": 795, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2498, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Is normality testing 'essentially useless'?", "tags": "<hypothesis-testing><normality-assumption><philosophical>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>A former colleague once argued to me as follows: </p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>We usually apply normality tests to the results of processes that,\n  under the null, generate random variables that are only\n  <em>asymptotically</em> or <em>nearly</em> normal (with the 'asymptotically' part dependent on some quantity which we cannot make large); In the era of\n  cheap memory, big data, and fast processors, normality tests should\n  <em>always</em> reject the null of normal distribution for large (though not insanely large) samples. And so, perversely, normality tests should\n  only be used for small samples, when they presumably have lower power\n  and less control over type I rate.</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>Is this a valid argument? Is this a well-known argument? Are there well known tests for a 'fuzzier' null hypothesis than normality?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-08T17:47:21.820000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2391", "provsql": "9d0d1a63-566b-4826-b9ad-edd06742cdfb"}, "posts_2502": {"id": 2615, "owneruserid": 1250, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2664, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Analytical solutions to limits of correlation stress testing", "tags": "<correlation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Suppose I have some initial correlation matrix. I want to stress each correlation in the matrix by the same constant simultaneously (except the diagonal; lets call this global parallel stress since it affects the entire matrix by the same constant at the same time). I start with adding 0.01% to each correlation and check if the matrix is still PSD. I continue increasing the stress levels by small increments. Eventually I encounter a stress level above which the matrix would no longer be PSD. Let's call this the upper stress boundary. I repeat the same procedure for negative stresses and find the lower stress boundary.</p>\n\n<p>My general observation was that the minimum eigenvalue initial correlation matrix is roughly equal to the upper stress boundary. <strong>Is there an analytical solution for this problem?</strong></p>\n\n<p>Generally, I am more interested in the upper stress boundary. I stress the entire matrix at the same time because it is a simple way to reduce diversification benefit across all market variables. However, from a theoretical point of view it would be interesting to find out how to analytically calculate both lower and upper stress boundaries.</p>\n\n<p>EDIT: please see a previous thread, which might be relevant here (some brilliant idea's from kwak): <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/2572/correlation-stress-testing\">Correlation stress testing</a></p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-13T13:35:11.777000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2502", "provsql": "13b0e160-8b6f-486d-8d15-f7ac118644b6"}, "posts_2621": {"id": 2746, "owneruserid": 1250, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2750, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to efficiently generate random positive-semidefinite correlation matrices?", "tags": "<random-generation><correlation-matrix>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I would like to be able to efficiently generate positive-semidefinite (PSD) correlation matrices. My method slows down dramatically as I increase the size of matrices to be generated.</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>Could you suggest any efficient solutions? If you are aware of any examples in Matlab, I would be very thankful.</li>\n<li>When generating a PSD correlation matrix how would you pick the parameters to describe matrices to be generated? An average correlation, standard deviation of correlations, eigenvalues?</li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-16T20:39:00.603000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2621", "provsql": "728d1f46-b42d-4b19-b876-b676dd678265"}, "posts_2771": {"id": 2917, "owneruserid": 1381, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Are these formulas for transforming P, LSD, MSD, HSD, CI, to SE as an exact or inflated/conservative estimate of $\\hat{\\sigma}$ correct?", "tags": "<multiple-comparisons><variance><data-transformation><meta-analysis>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<h2>Background</h2>\n\n<p>I am conducting a meta-analysis that includes previously published data. Often, differences between treatments are reported with P-values, least significant differences (LSD), and other statistics but provide no direct estimate of the variance.</p>\n\n<p>In the context of the model that I am using, an overestimate of variance is okay.</p>\n\n<h2>Problem</h2>\n\n<p>Here is a list of transformations to $SE$ where $SE=\\sqrt{MSE/n}$ <a href=\"http://eskes.psychiatry.dal.ca/Files/2003_-_Saville_-_Basic_statistics_and_the_inconsistency_of_m.pdf\" rel=\"noreferrer\">(Saville 2003)</a> that I am considering, feedback appreciated; below, I assume that $\\alpha=0.05$ so $1-^{\\alpha}/_2=0.975$  and variables are normally distributed unless otherwise stated:</p>\n\n<h2>Questions:</h2>\n\n<ol>\n<li><p>given $P$, $n$, and treatment means $\\bar X_1$ and $\\bar X_2$ \n$$SE=\\frac{\\bar X_1-\\bar X_2}{t_{(1-\\frac{P}{2},2n-2)}\\sqrt{2/n}}$$</p></li>\n<li><p>given LSD <a href=\"http://apsjournals.apsnet.org/doi/abs/10.1094/PHYTO.2004.94.9.1013\" rel=\"noreferrer\">(Rosenberg 2004)</a>, $\\alpha$, $n$, $b$ where $b$ is number of blocks, and $n=b$ by default for RCBD\n$$SE = \\frac{LSD}{t_{(0.975,n)}\\sqrt{2bn}}$$</p></li>\n<li><p>given MSD (minimum significant difference) <a href=\"http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/etc.5620190113/full\" rel=\"noreferrer\">(Wang 2000)</a>, $n$, $\\alpha$, df = $2n-2$\n$$SE = \\frac{MSD}{t_{(0.975, 2n-2)}\\sqrt{2}}$$</p></li>\n<li><p>given a 95% Confidence Interval <a href=\"http://eskes.psychiatry.dal.ca/Files/2003_-_Saville_-_Basic_statistics_and_the_inconsistency_of_m.pdf\" rel=\"noreferrer\">(Saville 2003)</a> (measured from mean to upper or lower confidence limit), $\\alpha$, and $n$ $$SE = \\frac{CI}{t_{(\\alpha/2,n)}}$$</p></li>\n<li><p>given Tukey's HSD, $n$, where $q$ is the 'studentized range statistic', $$SE = \\frac{HSD}{q_{(0.975,n)}}$$</p></li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>An R function to encapsulate these equations:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li><p>Example Data: </p>\n\n<pre><code>data <- data.frame(Y=rep(1,5), \n                   stat=rep(1,5), \n                   n=rep(4,5), \n                   statname=c('SD', 'MSE', 'LSD', 'HSD', 'MSD') \n</code></pre></li>\n<li><p>Example Use:</p>\n\n<pre><code>transformstats(data)    \n</code></pre></li>\n<li><p>The <code>transformstats</code> function:</p>\n\n<pre><code>transformstats <- function(data) {\n  ## Transformation of stats to SE\n  ## transform SD to SE\n  if (\"SD\" %in% data$statname) {\n    sdi <- which(data$statname == \"SD\")\n    data$stat[sdi] <- data$stat[sdi] / sqrt(data$n[sdi])\n    data$statname[sdi] <- \"SE\"\n      }\n  ## transform MSE to SE\n  if (\"MSE\" %in% data$statname) {\n    msei <- which(data$statname == \"MSE\")\n    data$stat[msei] <- sqrt (data$stat[msei]/data$n[msei])\n    data$statname[msei] <- \"SE\"\n  }\n  ## 95%CI measured from mean to upper or lower CI\n  ## SE = CI/t\n  if (\"95%CI\" %in% data$statname) {\n    cii <- which(data$statname == '95%CI')\n    data$stat[cii] <- data$stat[cii]/qt(0.975,data$n[cii])\n    data$statname[cii] <- \"SE\"\n  }\n  ## Fisher's Least Significant Difference (LSD)\n  ## conservatively assume no within block replication\n  if (\"LSD\" %in% data$statname) {\n    lsdi <- which(data$statname == \"LSD\")\n    data$stat[lsdi] <- data$stat[lsdi] / (qt(0.975,data$n[lsdi]) * sqrt( (2 * data$n[lsdi])))\n    data$statname[lsdi] <- \"SE\"\n  }\n  ## Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference (HSD),\n  ## conservatively assuming 3 groups being tested so df =2\n  if (\"HSD\" %in% data$statname) {\n    hsdi <- which(data$statname == \"HSD\" & data$n > 1)\n    data$stat[hsdi] <- data$stat[hsdi] / (qtukey(0.975, data$n[lsdi], df = 2))\n    data$statname[hsdi] <- \"SE\"\n  }              \n  ## MSD Minimum Squared Difference\n  ## MSD = t_{\\alpha/2, 2n-2}*SD*sqrt(2/n)\n  ## SE  = MSD*n/(t*sqrt(2))\n  if (\"MSD\" %in% data$statname) {\n    msdi <- which(data$statname == \"MSD\")\n    data$stat[msdi] <- data$stat[msdi] * data$n[msdi] / (qt(0.975,2*data$n[lsdi]-2)*sqrt(2))\n    data$statname[msdi] <- \"SE\"\n  }\n  if (FALSE %in% c('SE','none') %in% data$statname) {\n    print(paste(trait, ': ERROR!!! data contains untransformed statistics'))\n  }\n  return(data)\n}\n</code></pre></li>\n</ol>\n\n<p><strong>References</strong></p>\n\n<p><a href=\"http://eskes.psychiatry.dal.ca/Files/2003_-_Saville_-_Basic_statistics_and_the_inconsistency_of_m.pdf\" rel=\"noreferrer\">Saville 2003Can J. Exptl Psych. (pdf)</a></p>\n\n<p><a href=\"http://apsjournals.apsnet.org/doi/abs/10.1094/PHYTO.2004.94.9.1013\" rel=\"noreferrer\">Rosenberg et al 2004 (link)</a></p>\n\n<p><a href=\"http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/etc.5620190113/full\" rel=\"noreferrer\">Wang et al. 2000 Env. Tox. and Chem 19(1):113-117 (link)</a></p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-20T23:14:27.380000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2771", "provsql": "4c1086eb-e6ee-4df7-a7f3-2def74e509c7"}, "posts_2829": {"id": 2981, "owneruserid": 1007, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2986, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Interpreting output of igraph's fastgreedy.community clustering method", "tags": "<clustering><networks><partitioning><igraph><modularity>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>With the help of several people in this community I have been wetting my feet in clustering some social network data using <a href=\"http://igraph.sourceforge.net/doc/R/fastgreedy.community.html\" rel=\"noreferrer\">igraph's implementation of modularity-based clustering</a>.</p>\n<p>I am having some trouble interpreting the output of this routine and how to use it to generate lists of members of each community detected.</p>\n<p>This routine outputs a two-column matrix and a list of modularity values. From <a href=\"http://igraph.sourceforge.net/doc/R/fastgreedy.community.html\" rel=\"noreferrer\">the docs</a>:</p>\n<blockquote>\n<p>merges: A matrix with two column, this\nrepresents a dendogram and contains\nall the merges the algorithm\nperformed. Each line is one merge and\nit is given by the ids of the two\ncommunities merged. The community ids\nare integer numbers starting from zero\nand the communities between zero and\nthe number of vertices (N) minus one\nbelong to individual vertices. The\nfirst line of the matrix gives the\nfirst merge, this merge creates\ncommunity N, the number of vertices,\nthe second merge creates community\nN+1, etc.</p>\n<p>modularity:  A numeric vector\ncontaining the modularity value of the\ncommunity structure after performing\nevery merge.</p>\n</blockquote>\n<p>Working with this explanation and looking at the example at the bottom of the man page, I think the communities in this graph are</p>\n<pre><code>1st community: 0 1 2 3 4\n2nd community: 10 11 12 13 14\n3rd community: 5 6 7 8 9\n</code></pre>\n<p>Can someone who has used this method before confirm whether the right approach produces this result? I have basically (i) ignored the last two merges and (ii) gone over each row in the 'merges' matrix, combining each pair of vertices into a set while watching out for vertex values that are larger than the number of vertices (and therefore refer to another row in the 'merges' matrix).</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-22T18:49:28.433000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2829", "provsql": "828e67fd-8aba-4ce4-ae0f-f755f76898e7"}, "posts_3020": {"id": 3194, "owneruserid": 1456, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3198, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How can I test the fairness of a d20?", "tags": "<hypothesis-testing><chi-squared-test><goodness-of-fit><uniform-distribution><dice>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>How can I test the fairness of a twenty sided die (d20)?  Obviously I would be comparing the distribution of values against a uniform distribution.  I vaguely remember using a Chi-square test in college.  How can I apply this to see if a die is fair?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-30T13:04:31.537000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3020", "provsql": "a5a5d0f6-5312-4ed5-95e0-b25f5f821313"}, "posts_3061": {"id": 3238, "owneruserid": 1216, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3257, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Time series 'clustering' in R", "tags": "<r><time-series><clustering><cointegration>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I have a set of time series data. Each series covers the same period, although the actual dates in each time series may not all 'line up' exactly.</p>\n\n<p>That is to say, if the Time series were to be read into a 2D matrix, it would look something like this:</p>\n\n<pre><code>date     T1   T2   T3 .... TN\n1/1/01   100  59   42      N/A\n2/1/01   120  29   N/A     42.5\n3/1/01   110  N/A  12      36.82\n4/1/01   N/A  59   40      61.82\n5/1/01    05  99   42      23.68\n...\n31/12/01  100  59   42     N/A\n\netc \n</code></pre>\n\n<p>I want to write an R script that will segregate the time series {T1, T2, ... TN} into 'families' where a family is defined as a set of series which \"tend to move in sympathy\" with each other. </p>\n\n<p>For the 'clustering' part, I will need to select/define a kind of distance measure. I am not quite sure how to go about this, since I am dealing with time series, and a pair of series that may move in sympathy over one interval, may not do so in a subsequent interval.</p>\n\n<p>I am sure there are far more experienced/clever people than me on here, so I would be grateful for any suggestions, ideas on what algorithm/heuristic to use for the distance measure and how to use that in clustering the time series. </p>\n\n<p>My guess is that there is NOT an established robust statistic method for doing this, so I would be very interested to see how people approach/solve this problem - thinking like a statistician.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-01T14:58:01.400000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3061", "provsql": "a65bb297-9d5a-4d30-8197-1db5058cfb8b"}, "posts_3211": {"id": 3400, "owneruserid": 1499, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3411, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "From a statistical perspective, can one infer causality using propensity scores with an observational study?", "tags": "<causality><propensity-scores>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p><strong>Question:</strong> From the standpoint of statistician (or a practitioner), can one infer causality using <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propensity_score\">propensity scores</a> with an observational study (<strong>not an experiment</strong>)?</p>\n\n<p>Please, do not want to start a flame war or a fanatical debate.</p>\n\n<p><strong>Background:</strong> Within our stat PhD program, we've only touched on causal inference through working groups and a few topic sessions.  However, there are some very prominent researchers in other departments (e.g. HDFS, Sociology) who are actively using them.</p>\n\n<p>I've already witnessed some pretty heated debate on this issue. It is not my intention to start one here.  That said, what references have you encountered?  What viewpoints do you have?  For example, one argument I've heard against propensity scores as a causal inference technique is that one can never infer causality due omitted variable bias -- if you leave out something important, you break the causal chain. Is this an unresolvable problem?</p>\n\n<p><strong>Disclaimer:</strong> This question may not have a correct answer -- completely cool with clicking cw, but I'm personally very interested in the responses and would be happy with a few good references which include real-world examples.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-07T23:27:47.727000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3211", "provsql": "eb03c3d1-4284-4f07-b238-3f1bcf6ccde2"}, "posts_7021": {"id": 7515, "owneruserid": 2260, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 7516, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What are some techniques for sampling two correlated random variables?", "tags": "<correlation><sampling><monte-carlo><stochastic-processes><copula>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>What are some techniques for sampling two correlated random variables:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><p>if their probability\ndistributions are parameterized\n(e.g., log-normal)</p></li>\n<li><p>if they have non-parametric\ndistributions.</p></li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>The data are two time series for which we can compute non-zero correlation coefficients.  We wish to simulate these data in the future, assuming the historical correlation and time series CDF is constant.</p>\n\n<p>For case (2), the 1-D analogue would be to construct the CDF and sample from it.  So I guess, I could construct a 2-D CDF and do the same thing.  However, I wonder if there is a way to come close by using the individual 1-D CDFs and somehow linking the picks.</p>\n\n<p>Thanks!</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-02-22T20:43:25.633000", "posts_rownum": "posts_7021", "provsql": "e8d046df-d5e2-40ab-9771-218158def42c"}, "posts_3221": {"id": 3412, "owneruserid": 601, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3415, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Comparing mixed effect models with the same number of degrees of freedom", "tags": "<r><mixed-model><model-selection>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I have an experiment that I'll try to abstract here.  Imagine I toss three white stones in front of you and ask you to make a judgment about their position.  I record a variety of properties of the stones and your response.   I do this over a number of subjects.  I generate two models.  One is that the nearest stone to you predicts your response, and the other is that the geometric center of the stones predicts your response.  So, using lmer in R I could write.</p>\n\n<pre><code>mNear   <- lmer(resp ~ nearest + (1|subject), REML = FALSE)\nmCenter <- lmer(resp ~ center  + (1|subject), REML = FALSE)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p><strong>UPDATE AND CHANGE - more direct version that incorporates several helpful comments</strong></p>\n\n<p>I could try</p>\n\n<pre><code>anova(mNear, mCenter)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Which is incorrect, of course, because they're not nested and I can't really compare them that way.  I was expecting anova.mer to throw an error but it didn't.  But the possible nesting that I could try here isn't natural and still leaves me with somewhat less analytical statements.  When models are nested naturally (e.g. quadratic on linear) the test is only one way.  But in this case what would it mean to have asymmetric findings?</p>\n\n<p>For example, I could make a model three:</p>\n\n<pre><code>mBoth <- lmer(resp ~ center + nearest + (1|subject), REML = FALSE)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Then I can anova.</p>\n\n<pre><code>anova(mCenter, mBoth)\nanova(mNearest, mBoth)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>This is fair to do and now I find that the center adds to the nearest effect (the second command) but BIC actually goes up when nearest is added to center (correction for the lower parsimony).  This confirms what was suspected.</p>\n\n<p>But is finding this sufficient?  And is this fair when center and nearest are so highly correlated?</p>\n\n<p>Is there a better way to analytically compare the models when it's not about adding and subtracting explanatory variables (degrees of freedom)?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-08T12:34:11.673000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3221", "provsql": "0741cd53-c968-41ae-b36e-5951f4dbbc24"}, "posts_3271": {"id": 3458, "owneruserid": 253, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3459, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Alternatives to classification trees, with better predictive (e.g: CV) performance?", "tags": "<r><machine-learning><classification><cart>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I am looking for an alternative to Classification Trees which might yield better predictive power.</p>\n\n<p>The data I am dealing with has factors for both the explanatory and the explained variables.</p>\n\n<p>I remember coming across random forests and neural networks in this context, although never tried them before, are there another good candidate for such a modeling task (in R, obviously)?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-10T09:27:49.817000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3271", "provsql": "391be5c0-25c8-4ac5-b6b7-c1d1da931212"}, "posts_3341": {"id": 3532, "owneruserid": 8, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3535, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Random numbers and the multicore package", "tags": "<r><random-generation><parallel-computing><multicore>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>When programming in R, I've used the <a href=\"http://www.rforge.net/doc/packages/multicore/multicore.html\" rel=\"noreferrer\">multicore</a> package a few times. However, I've never seen a statement about how it handles it's random numbers. When I use openMP with C, I'm careful to use a proper parallel RNG, but with R I've assume that something sensible happens. Can anyone confirm that something sensible does happen?</p>\n\n<p><strong>Example</strong></p>\n\n<p>From the documentation, we have </p>\n\n<pre><code>x <- foreach(icount(1000), .combine = \"+\") %do% rnorm(4)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>How are the <code>rnorm</code>`s generated?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-12T20:14:49.203000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3341", "provsql": "9771ea2e-a573-4f95-a868-6b1569b8ac7b"}, "posts_3348": {"id": 3539, "owneruserid": 1564, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3546, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Inter-rater reliability for ordinal or interval data", "tags": "<reliability><psychometrics><agreement-statistics><cohens-kappa>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Which inter-rater reliability methods are most appropriate for ordinal or interval data?</p>\n\n<p>I believe that \"Joint probability of agreement\" or \"Kappa\" are designed for nominal data. Whilst \"Pearson\" and \"Spearman\" can be used, they are mainly used for two raters (although they can be used for more than two raters).</p>\n\n<p>What other measures are suitable for ordinal or interval data, i.e. more than two raters?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-12T22:48:56.690000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3348", "provsql": "8a6f0731-ecfb-4def-a787-62b71085bd14"}, "posts_3367": {"id": 3559, "owneruserid": 442, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3562, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Which pseudo-$R^2$ measure is the one to report for logistic regression (Cox & Snell or Nagelkerke)?", "tags": "<logistic><goodness-of-fit><r-squared><pseudo-r-squared>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I have <code>SPSS</code> output for a logistic regression model. The output reports two measures for the model fit, <code>Cox & Snell</code> and <code>Nagelkerke</code>.</p>\n\n<p>So as a rule of thumb, which of these $R^²$ measures would you report as the model fit?</p>\n\n<p>Or, which of these fit indices is the one that is usually reported in journals?</p>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p>Some Background: The regression tries to predict the presence or absence of a bird (capercaillie) from some environmental variables (e.g., steepness, vegetation cover, ...). Unfortunately, the bird did not appear very often (35 hits to 468 misses) so the regression performs rather poorly. Cox & Snell is .09, Nagelkerke, .23.  </p>\n\n<p>The subject is environmental sciences or ecology.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-13T16:12:57.630000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3367", "provsql": "700dc725-1c0d-4a56-b781-8511e9797a77"}, "posts_3467": {"id": 3661, "owneruserid": 1603, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Repeatability and measurement error from and between observers", "tags": "<anova><error><measurement><reliability><agreement-statistics>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I have 3 observers that each take 2 measurements (length and weight) on 100 individuals; these procedures are repeated once (i.e., the same measurements are taken on the same 100 individuals by the same 3 observers), so that the data set is duplicated (i.e., early reading and late reading). </p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>What is the best way to figure out how each individual observer's measurements vary between the late and early trial measurements?</li>\n<li>How can I best compare how close or different the measurements of length (or weight) differ among the 3 observers? Let's call these new variables <code>z</code>.
