Can I make any other deductions from this result?</p>\n\n<p>Also, I was suggested that I look into adding additional variates like $A^2$ etc. but if $A$ is the area, what does saying \"time\" depends on $A^2$ actually mean? </p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-03-16T03:51:14.743000", "posts_rownum": "posts_7782", "provsql": "a4ed81e8-9f4a-4780-9a4a-94871829038a"}, "posts_4281": {"id": 4551, "owneruserid": 364, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What are common statistical sins?", "tags": "<fallacy>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm a grad student in psychology, and as I pursue more and more independent studies in statistics, I am increasingly amazed by the inadequacy of my formal training. Both personal and second hand experience suggests that the paucity of statistical rigor in undergraduate and graduate training is rather ubiquitous within psychology. As such, I thought it would be useful for independent learners like myself to create a list of \"Statistical Sins\", tabulating statistical practices taught to grad students as standard practice that are in fact either superseded by superior (more powerful, or flexible, or robust, etc.) modern methods or shown to be frankly invalid. Anticipating that other fields might also experience a similar state of affairs, I propose a community wiki where we can collect a list of statistical sins across disciplines. Please, submit one \"sin\" per answer.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-11-15T18:46:37.113000", "posts_rownum": "posts_4281", "provsql": "c91a7d46-9b87-487e-9175-1dcc75dca66a"}, "posts_4832": {"id": 5135, "owneruserid": 2091, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 5138, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Interpretation of R's lm() output", "tags": "<r><regression><interpretation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>The help pages in R assume I know what those numbers mean, but I don't.\nI'm trying to really intuitively understand every number here. I will just post the output and comment on what I found out. There might (will) be mistakes, as I'll just write what I assume. Mainly I'd like to know what the t-value in the coefficients mean, and why they print the residual standard error. </p>\n\n<pre><code>Call:\nlm(formula = iris$Sepal.Width ~ iris$Petal.Width)\n\nResiduals:\n     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max \n-1.09907 -0.23626 -0.01064  0.23345  1.17532 \n</code></pre>\n\n<p>This is a 5-point-summary of the residuals (their mean is always 0, right?). The numbers can be used (I'm guessing here) to quickly see if there are any big outliers. Also you can already see it here if the residuals are far from normally distributed (they should be normally distributed).</p>\n\n<pre><code>Coefficients:\n                 Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    \n(Intercept)       3.30843    0.06210  53.278  < 2e-16 ***\niris$Petal.Width -0.20936    0.04374  -4.786 4.07e-06 ***\n---\nSignif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1 \n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Estimates $\\hat{\\beta_i}$, computed by least squares regression. Also, the standard error is $\\sigma_{\\beta_i}$. I'd like to know how this is calculated.  I have no idea where the t-value and the corresponding p-value come from. I know $\\hat{\\beta}$ should be normal distributed, but how is the t-value calculated?</p>\n\n<pre><code>Residual standard error: 0.407 on 148 degrees of freedom\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>$\\sqrt{ \\frac{1}{n-p} \\epsilon^T\\epsilon }$, I guess. But why do we calculate that, and what does it tell us?</p>\n\n<pre><code>Multiple R-squared: 0.134,  Adjusted R-squared: 0.1282 \n</code></pre>\n\n<p>$ R^2 = \\frac{s_\\hat{y}^2}{s_y^2} $, which is $ \\frac{\\sum_{i=1}^n (\\hat{y_i}-\\bar{y})^2}{\\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\\bar{y})^2} $. The ratio is close to 1 if the points lie on a straight line, and 0 if they are random.  What is the adjusted R-squared?</p>\n\n<pre><code>F-statistic: 22.91 on 1 and 148 DF,  p-value: 4.073e-06 \n</code></pre>\n\n<p>F and p for the <strong>whole</strong> model, not only for single $\\beta_i$s as previous. The F value is $ \\frac{s^2_{\\hat{y}}}{\\sum\\epsilon_i} $. The bigger it grows, the more unlikely it is that the $\\beta$'s do not have any effect at all.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-12-04T11:28:14.300000", "posts_rownum": "posts_4832", "provsql": "1f3eee4a-e9f9-400f-99d5-297c55816ffd"}, "posts_4944": {"id": 5249, "owneruserid": 183, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Simple, reliable, open, and interoperable plain text format for storing data", "tags": "<project-management>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>In a previous question I asked about tools for editing <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/5238/strategy-for-editing-comma-separated-value-csv-files\">CSV files</a>.</p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/5238/strategy-for-editing-comma-separated-value-csv-files/5239#5239\">Gavin</a>\nlinked to a comment on R Help by <a href=\"http://thread.gmane.org/gmane.comp.lang.r.general/213174/focus=213179\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Duncan Murdoch</a>\nsuggesting that Data Interchange Format is a more reliable way to store data than CSV.</p>\n\n<p>For some applications a dedicated database management system is what is needed.\nHowever, for small scale data analysis projects something more light weight seems more suitable.</p>\n\n<p>Consider the following criteria for evaluating a file format:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><strong>reliabile</strong>: the data entered should stay true to what has been entered; \ndata should open consistently in different software; </li>\n<li><strong>simple</strong>: it would be nice if the file format is easy to understand and ideally be\nreadable with a simple text editor; it should be easy to write a simple program to read and write the format.</li>\n<li><strong>open</strong>: the format should be open</li>\n<li><strong>interoperable</strong>: the file format should be supported by many systems</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>I find tab and comma separated value formats fail on the reliability criterion.\nAlthough I suppose I could blame the importing and exporting programs rather than the file format.\nI often find myself having to make little adjustments to the options in \n<code>read.table</code> in order to prevent some strange character from breaking the loading of the data frame.</p>\n\n<p>Questions</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>Which file format best meets these needs?</li>\n<li>Is Data Interchange Format a better alternative? or does it have its own problems?</li>\n<li>Is there some other format that is preferable?</li>\n<li>Am I unfairly evaluating TSV and CSV? Is there a simple set of tips for working with such files that make the file format more reliable?</li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2010-12-08T10:43:56.587000", "posts_rownum": "posts_4944", "provsql": "d63c30bc-806f-4d68-9551-9068fcb362df"}, "posts_6200": {"id": 6575, "owneruserid": 2820, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 6589, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to do primary component analysis on multi-mode data with non-orthogonal primary components?", "tags": "<pca><multivariate-analysis><mode>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Consider the following picture representing the experimental data sequence obtained by two 1D-sensors (each point of the sequence is plotted on XY plane according to the respective sensor reading):<br>\n<img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/U6fWb.png\" alt=\"experimental raw data\"></p>\n\n<p>It's visually obvious that two modes have been registered. Let's assume that generally those two modes interfere, so there's no easy possibility to separate them by isolating certain sequence segments. I try the classic principal component analysis by finding the covariance matrix, then finding the set of eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors:<br>\n<img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/osv6x.png\" alt=\"experimental data pca\"></p>\n\n<p>White box dimensions represents the magnitude if the eigenvalues, box orientation represents the direction of eigenvectors.  </p>\n\n<p>It's clear that PCA first component deviates slightly from the high-magnitude mode direction, while the second component deviates greatly due to skewness of the lower-magnitude mode original direction.</p>\n\n<p>It is known that PCA, being based on eigenvectors, results in orthogonal basis of primary components. </p>\n\n<p>Is there other elegant methods (or PCA-derived methods) to obtain the non-orthogonal basis of primary skewed components?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-01-26T15:51:26.317000", "posts_rownum": "posts_6200", "provsql": "f17ead26-dc29-46cf-9f0c-7cbcad80b976"}, "posts_5038": {"id": 5347, "owneruserid": 634, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 5358, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How can I efficiently model the sum of Bernoulli random variables?", "tags": "<r><distributions><binomial-distribution><random-variable><poisson-binomial-distribution>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I am modeling a random variable (<span class=\"math-container\">$Y$</span>) which is the sum of some ~15-40k independent Bernoulli random variables (<span class=\"math-container\">$X_i$</span>), each with a different success probability (<span class=\"math-container\">$p_i$</span>). Formally, <span class=\"math-container\">$Y=\\sum X_i$</span> where <span class=\"math-container\">$\\Pr(X_i=1)=p_i$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$\\Pr(X_i=0)=1-p_i$</span>.</p>\n<p>I am interested in quickly answering queries such as <span class=\"math-container\">$\\Pr(Y\\leq k)$</span> (where <span class=\"math-container\">$k$</span> is given).</p>\n<p>Currently, I use random simulations to answer such queries. I randomly draw each <span class=\"math-container\">$X_i$</span> according to its <span class=\"math-container\">$p_i$</span>, then sum all <span class=\"math-container\">$X_i$</span> values to get <span class=\"math-container\">$Y'$</span>. I repeat this process a few thousand times and return the fraction of times <span class=\"math-container\">$\\Pr(Y'\\leq k)$</span>.</p>\n<p>Obviously, this is not totally accurate (although accuracy greatly increases as the number of simulations increases). Also, it seems I have enough data about the distribution to avoid the use simulations. Can you think of a reasonable way to get the exact probability <span class=\"math-container\">$\\Pr(Y\\leq k)$</span>?</p>\n<p>p.s.</p>\n<p>I use Perl & R.</p>\n<p><strong>EDIT</strong></p>\n<p>Following the responses I thought some clarifications might be needed. I will shortly describe the setting of my problem. Given is a circular genome with  circumference <code>c</code> and a set of <code>n</code> ranges mapped to it. For example, <code>c=3*10^9</code> and <code>ranges={[100,200],[50,1000],[3*10^9-1,1000],...}</code>. Note all ranges are closed (both ends are inclusive). Also note that we only deal with integers (whole units).</p>\n<p>I am looking for regions on the circle that are undercovered by the given <code>n</code> mapped ranges. So to test whether a given a range of length <code>x</code> on the circle is undercovered, I test the hypothesis that the <code>n</code> ranges are mapped randomly. The probability a mapped range of length <code>q>x</code> will fully cover the given range of length <code>x</code> is <code>(q-x)/c</code>. This probability becomes quite small when <code>c</code> is large and/or <code>q</code> is small. What I'm interested is the number of ranges (out of <code>n</code>) which cover <code>x</code>. This is how <code>Y</code> is formed.</p>\n<p>I test my null hypothesis vs. one sided alternative (undercoverage). Also note I am testing multiple hypothesis (different <code>x</code> lengths), and sure to correct for this.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-12-10T11:06:05.337000", "posts_rownum": "posts_5038", "provsql": "06b9b725-e942-424c-8dbd-e6feca6d0345"}, "posts_5051": {"id": 5360, "owneruserid": 569, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 5361, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Stepwise logistic regression and sampling", "tags": "<logistic><spss><stepwise-regression>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I am fitting a stepwise logistic regression on a set of data in SPSS.  In the procedure, I am fitting my model to a random subset that is approx. 60% of the total sample, which is about 330 cases.</p>\n\n<p>What I find interesting is that every time I re-sample my data, I am getting different variables popping in and out in the final model.  A few predictors are always present in the final model, but others pop in and out depending on the sample.</p>\n\n<p>My question is this.  What is the best way to handle this?  I was hoping to see the convergence of predictor variables, but that isn't the case.  Some models make much more intuitive sense from an operational view (and would be easier to explain to the decision makers), and others fit the data slightly better.  </p>\n\n<p>In short, since variables are shuffling around, how would you recommend dealing with my situation?</p>\n\n<p>Many thanks in advance.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-12-10T18:42:31.760000", "posts_rownum": "posts_5051", "provsql": "be57cea6-b30a-4a75-b56f-4d0cdad69552"}, "posts_5130": {"id": 5443, "owneruserid": 253, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 5547, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Estimate the \"meaningful\" predictors for a value in a CART model (rpart)", "tags": "<r><cart><rpart>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>When building a CART model (specifically classification tree) using rpart (in R), it is sometimes obvious that there are variables (X's) that are meaningful for predicting some of the outcome (y) variables - while other predictors are relevant for other y's only.</p>\n\n<p><strong>How can it be estimated, which explanatory variable is \"used\" for which of the predicted value in the outcome variable?</strong></p>\n\n<p>Here is an example code in which x2 is the only important variable for predicting \"b\" (one of the y outcomes).  There is no predicting variable for \"c\", and x1 is a predictor for \"a\", assuming that x2 permits it.</p>\n\n<p>How can this situation be extracted from the fitted model? </p>\n\n<pre><code>N <- 200\nset.seed(5123)\nx1 <- runif(N)\nx2 <- runif(N)\nx3 <- runif(N)\ny <- sample(letters[1:3], N, T)\ny[x1 <.5] <- \"a\"\ny[x2 <.1] <- \"b\"\n\nfit <- rpart(y ~ x1+x2)\nfit2 <- prune(fit, cp= 0.07)\nplot(fit2)\ntext(fit2, use.n=TRUE)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Thanks.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-12-13T19:24:57.693000", "posts_rownum": "posts_5130", "provsql": "20736d17-17b9-470c-bbef-9d901424c52f"}, "posts_5275": {"id": 10981, "owneruserid": 4670, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 17139, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Computing mathematical expectation of the correlation coefficient or $R^2$ in linear regression", "tags": "<regression><correlation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm re-posting a question from <a href=\"https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/32569/a-question-about-linear-regression\">math.stackexchange.com</a>, I think the current answer in math.se is not right.</p>\n\n<p>Select $n$ numbers from a set $\\{1,2,...,U\\}$, $y_i$ is the $i$th number selected, and $x_i$ is the rank of $y_i$ in the $n$ numbers. The selection is without replacement. $n$ is always smaller than $U$. The rank is the order of the a number after the $n$ numbers are sorted in ascending order.</p>\n\n<p>We can get $n$ data points $(x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2), ..., (x_n, y_n)$, And a best fit line for these data points can be found by linear regression.  $r_{xy}$ (correlation coefficient) is the goodness of the fit line, I want to calculate $\\mathbb{E}(r_{xy})$ or $\\mathbb{E}(r_{xy}^2)$ (correlation of determination).</p>\n\n<p>If the $\\mathbb{E}[r_{xy}]$ cannot be calculated, an estimation or lower bound is still OK.</p>\n\n<p>Updated:\nBy calculating the sample correlation coefficient using randomly generated data, we can see that $r_{xy}$ is quite closed to 1, so I want to proof it from the theoretical view, or theoretically say the data generated by the above method is very linear.</p>\n\n<p>Updated:\nIs it possible to get the distribution of sample correlation coefficient?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-05-19T15:21:04.487000", "posts_rownum": "posts_5275", "provsql": "8ef7f1e3-b39c-4fb6-ba05-398ce3f1f854"}, "posts_5997": {"id": 6364, "owneruserid": 2833, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Making square-root of covariance matrix positive-definite (Matlab)", "tags": "<matlab><covariance-matrix><numerics>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p><strong>Motivation</strong>: I'm writing a state estimator in MATLAB (the unscented Kalman filter), which calls for the update of the (upper-triangular) square-root of a covariance matrix $S$ at every iteration (that is, for a covariance matrix $P$, it is true that $P=SS^{T}$). In order for me to perform the requisite calculations, I need to do a Rank-1 Cholesky Update and Downdate using MATLAB's <code>cholupdate</code> function. </p>\n\n<p><strong>Problem</strong>: Unfortunately, during the course of the iterations, this matrix $S$ can sometimes lose positive definiteness. "posts_8274": {"id": 13314, "owneruserid": 1106, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 13317, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Is $R^2$ useful or dangerous?", "tags": "<regression><r-squared>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I was skimming through <a href=\"http://www.stat.cmu.edu/~cshalizi/402/\">some lecture notes</a> by Cosma Shalizi (in particular, section 2.1.1 of the <a href=\"http://www.stat.cmu.edu/~cshalizi/402/lectures/02-truth-about-linear-regression/lecture-02.pdf\">second lecture</a>), and was reminded that you can get very low $R^2$ even when you have a completely linear model.</p>\n\n<p>To paraphrase Shalizi's example: suppose you have a model $Y = aX + \\epsilon$, where $a$ is known. Then $\\newcommand{\\Var}{\\mathrm{Var}}\\Var[Y] = a^2 \\Var[x] + \\Var[\\epsilon]$ and the amount of explained variance is $a^2 \\Var[X]$, so $R^2 = \\frac{a^2 \\Var[x]}{a^2 \\Var[X] + \\Var[\\epsilon]}$. This goes to 0 as $\\Var[X] \\rightarrow 0$ and to 1 as $\\Var[X] \\rightarrow \\infty$.</p>\n\n<p>Conversely, you can get high $R^2$ even when your model is noticeably non-linear. (Anyone have a good example offhand?)</p>\n\n<p>So when is $R^2$ a useful statistic, and when should it be ignored?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-07-20T20:32:55.510000", "posts_rownum": "posts_8274", "provsql": "27bfe520-5c9a-4bfc-8c77-576b50ab5d28"}, "posts_8336": {"id": 8955, "owneruserid": 3136, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 8964, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Advice on explaining heterogeneity / heteroscedasticty", "tags": "<regression><mixed-model><references><residuals><heteroscedasticity>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am looking for any help, advice or tips in how to explain heterogeneity / heteroscedasticity to biologists in my department. Currently, I focus largely on the nlme package in R and the use of variance covariates, this is pretty simple and most people here use R so providing scripts is useful. I am also using the MCMCglmm package as well, but other suggestions are welcome, particularly for non-normal data.  </li>\n<li>Any other suggestions are welcome.  </li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2011-03-30T09:12:59.377000", "posts_rownum": "posts_8336", "provsql": "b44ba644-f14e-4d97-bbaf-73ecaca8b2eb"}, "posts_8439": {"id": 9071, "owneruserid": 2958, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 9073, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Intuitive explanation of contribution to sum of two normally distributed random variables", "tags": "<normal-distribution><conditional-probability>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>If I have two normally distributed independent random variables $X$ and $Y$ with means $\\mu_X$ and $\\mu_Y$ and standard deviations $\\sigma_X$ and $\\sigma_Y$ and I discover that $X+Y=c$, then (assuming I have not made any errors) the conditional distribution of $X$ and $Y$ given $c$ are also normally distributed with means \n$$\\mu_{X|c} = \\mu_X + (c - \\mu_X - \\mu_Y)\\frac{ \\sigma_X^2}{\\sigma_X^2+\\sigma_Y^2}$$ $$\\mu_{Y|c} = \\mu_Y + (c - \\mu_X - \\mu_Y)\\frac{ \\sigma_Y^2}{\\sigma_X^2+\\sigma_Y^2}$$\nand standard deviation \n$$\\sigma_{X|c} = \\sigma_{Y|c} = \\sqrt{ \\frac{\\sigma_X^2 \\sigma_Y^2}{\\sigma_X^2 + \\sigma_Y^2}}.$$</p>\n\n<p>It is no surprise that the conditional standard deviations are the same as, given $c$, if one goes up the other must come down by the same amount.  It is interesting that the conditional standard deviation does not depend on $c$.</p>\n\n<p>What I cannot get my head round are the conditional means, where they take a share of the excess $(c - \\mu_X - \\mu_Y)$ proportional to the original variances, not to the original  standard deviations.   </p>\n\n<p>For example, if they have zero means, $\\mu_X=\\mu_Y=0$, and standard deviations $\\sigma_X =3$ and $\\sigma_Y=1$ then conditioned on $c=4$ we would have $E[X|c=4]=3.6$ and $E[Y|c=4]=0.4$, i.e. in the ratio $9:1$ even though I would have intuitively thought that the ratio $3:1$ would be more natural.  <strong>Can anyone give an intuitive explanation for this?</strong></p>\n\n<p>This was provoked by <a href=\"https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/30365/posterior-distribution-after-having-partial-information-on-some-linear-combinatio\">a Math.SE question</a> </p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-04-02T01:28:12.757000", "posts_rownum": "posts_8439", "provsql": "67ee8b2a-f217-44c0-98e7-0d11c88a485a"}, "posts_8573": {"id": 9220, "owneruserid": 1913, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 10731, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What is the distribution of the Euclidean distance between two normally distributed random variables?", "tags": "<normal-distribution><distance-functions>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Assume you are given two objects whose exact locations are unknown, but are distributed according to normal distributions with known parameters (e.g. $a \\sim N(m, s)$ and $b \\sim N(v, t))$. "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I've read that the chi square test is useful to see if a sample is significantly different from a set of expected values.</p>\n<p>For example, here is a table of results of a survey regarding people's favourite colours (n=15+13+10+17=55 total respondents):</p>\n<pre><code>red, blue, green, yellow\n\n15, 13, 10, 17\n</code></pre>\n<p>A chi square test can tell me if this sample is significantly different from the null hypothesis of equal probability of people liking each colour.</p>\n<p>Question: Can the test be run on the proportions of total respondents who like a certain colour? Like below:</p>\n<pre><code>red, blue, green, yellow\n\n0.273, 0.236, 0.182, 0.309\n</code></pre>\n<p>Where, of course, <span class=\"math-container\">$0.273 + 0.236 + 0.182 + 0.309=1$</span>.</p>\n<p>If the chi square test is not suitable in this case, what test would be?</p>\n<p><strong>Edit</strong>: I tried @Roman Luštrik answer below, and got the following output, why am I not getting a p-value and why does R say "Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect"?</p>\n<pre class=\"lang-r prettyprint-override\"><code>chisq.test(c(0, 0, 0, 8, 6, 2, 0, 0), p = c(0.406197174, 0.088746395, \n             0.025193306, 0.42041479, 0.03192905, 0.018328576, \n             0.009190708, 0))\n    \n        Chi-squared test for given probabilities\n    \n    data:  c(0, 0, 0, 8, 6, 2, 0, 0) \n    X-squared = NaN, df = 7, p-value = NA\n    \n    Warning message:\n    In chisq.test(c(0, 0, 0, 8, 6, 2, 0, 0), p = c(0.406197174, \n           0.088746395,  :\n      Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect  \n</code></pre>\n", "creationdate": "2011-04-16T21:08:05.087000", "posts_rownum": "posts_8943", "provsql": "e780abc3-3006-4b72-a38e-3f503686a3a1"}, "posts_9099": {"id": 9807, "owneruserid": 4262, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Working with Likert scales in SPSS", "tags": "<spss><likert>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I performed a survey using a Likert 1 to 5 scale (totally agree/agree/neutral/ disagree/totally disagree) on 12 questions which are split into 3 statements which the respondent places a value of between 1 to 5 dependent on how much they agree or disagree - there are 36 statements in total.</p>\n\n<p>Respondents:</p>\n\n<pre><code>Group 1                          Group 2\narchitects UK   140 replied      Architects US   100 replied\nengineers UK    140 replied      Engineers US    100 replied\nContractors Uk  140 replied      Contractors US  100 replied\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>The data is in Excel.</p>\n\n<h3>Questions:</h3>\n\n<ol>\n<li>How do I input them in SPSS?</li>\n<li>How do I work out the frequency of replies for each recipient?</li>\n<li>How do I work out frequency of replies i.e agrees/disagrees etc for each group?</li>\n<li>How can I rank each individual question (12 of them)? Remember, there are 3 individual statements to each question.</li>\n<li>How do I compare UK architects to US architects to show congruence or not?</li>\n<li>How would show correlation between the two groups UK and US?</li>\n<li>Will SPSS develop graphs etc for me showing frequency or correlation?</li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2011-04-20T22:57:58.130000", "posts_rownum": "posts_9099", "provsql": "d7b43025-ca74-447f-9f47-17cdb5c4ee05"}, "posts_9147": {"id": 9859, "owneruserid": 3019, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 14654, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What are the disadvantages of the profile likelihood?", "tags": "<maximum-likelihood><likelihood><profile-likelihood>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Consider a vector of parameters $(\\theta_1, \\theta_2)$, with $\\theta_1$ the parameter of interest, and $\\theta_2$ a nuisance parameter.</p>\n\n<p>If $L(\\theta_1, \\theta_2 ; x)$ is the likelihood constructed from the data $x$, the profile likelihood for $\\theta_1$ is defined as $L_P(\\theta_1 ; x) = L(\\theta_1, \\hat{\\theta}_2(\\theta_1) ; x)$ where $ \\hat{\\theta}_2(\\theta_1)$ is the MLE of $\\theta_2$ for a fixed value of $\\theta_1$.</p>\n\n<p>$\\bullet$ Maximising the profile likelihood with respect to $\\theta_1$ leads to same estimate $\\hat{\\theta}_1$ as the one obtained by maximising the likelihood simultaneously with respect to $\\theta_1$ and $\\theta_2$.</p>\n\n<p>$\\bullet$ I think the standard deviation of $\\hat{\\theta}_1$ may also be estimated from the second derivative of the profile likelihood.</p>\n\n<p>$\\bullet$ The likelihood statistic for $H_0: \\theta_1 = \\theta_0$ can be written in terms of the profile likelihood: $LR = 2 \\log( \\tfrac{L_P(\\hat{\\theta}_1 ; x)}{L_P(\\theta_0 ; x)})$.</p>\n\n<p>So, it seems that the profile likelihood can be used exactly as if it was a genuine likelihood. Is it really the case ? What are the main drawbacks of that approach ? And what about the 'rumor' that the estimator obtained from the profile likelihood is biased (edit: even asymptotically) ? </p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-04-22T07:01:16.563000", "posts_rownum": "posts_9147", "provsql": "028f7ebd-fe0e-4034-a5ac-1acbe8928b25"}, "posts_9173": {"id": 9885, "owneruserid": 2148, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 9915, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Application of machine learning methods in StackExchange websites", "tags": "<machine-learning>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I have a <strong>Machine Learning</strong> course this semester and the professor asked us to find a <strong>real-world problem</strong> and solve it by one of machine learning methods introduced in the class, as:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_tree_learning\">Decision Trees</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_neural_network\">Artificial Neural Networks</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Support_vector_machine\">Support Vector Machines</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instance-based_learning\">Instance-based Learning</a> (<a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-nearest_neighbor_algorithm\">kNN</a>, <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_weighted_regression\">LWL</a>)</li>\n<li><a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_network\">Bayesian Networks</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning\">Reinforcement learning</a></li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>I am one of fans of <strong>stackoverflow</strong> and <strong>stackexchange</strong> and know <a href=\"http://blog.stackoverflow.com/category/cc-wiki-dump/\">database dumps</a> of these websites are provided to the public because they are awesome! I hope I could find a good machine learning challenge about these databases and solve it. </p>\n\n<p><strong>My idea</strong></p>\n\n<p>One idea came to my mind is predicting tags for questions based on the entered words in question body. I think the Bayesian network is the right tool for learning tags for a question but need more research.\nAnyway, after learning phase when user finishes entering the question some tags should be suggested to him. </p>\n\n<p><strong>Please tell me</strong>:</p>\n\n<p>I want to ask the stats community as experienced people about ML two questions:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li><p>Do you think tag suggestion is at least a problem which has any chance to solve? Do you have any advice about it? I am a little worried because stackexchange does not implement such feature yet. </p></li>\n<li><p>Do you have any other/better idea for the ML project that is based on stackexchange database? I find it really hard to find something to <strong>learn</strong> from stackexchange databases. </p></li>\n</ol>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p><strong>Consideration about database errors:</strong>\nI would like to point that although the databases are huge and have many instances, they are not perfect and are prune to error. The obvious one is the age of users that is unreliable. Even selected tags for the question are not 100% correct. Anyway, we should consider the percent of correctness of data in selecting a problem. </p>\n\n<p><strong>Consideration about the problem itself:</strong> My project should not be about <code>data-mining</code> or something like this. It just should be an application of ML methods in real-world.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-04-22T22:27:24.467000", "posts_rownum": "posts_9173", "provsql": "064a40a0-f8d2-41a4-ab56-a0d2ec1e1fdf"}, "posts_9277": {"id": 10005, "owneruserid": 4340, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to convert a table into a graph in R", "tags": "<r><data-visualization>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I have a table I want to convert into a graph (bar-graph or line-graph)</p>\n<p>The first column has fixed values. Twenty different values are simulated for these fixed values and kept in the next columns. I want to plot a graph of the fixed column against all the different twenty simulated columns.</p>\n<p>How do I go about it?</p>\n<h2>Edit</h2>\n<blockquote>\n<p>table name:bygrace</p>\n</blockquote>\n<pre><code>V1    V2   V3   V4   V5                 \n100    16   11   -6    1                               \n120   -17  -12    7   -2                               \n140    18   13   -8    3                              \n150   -19  -14    9   -4                              \n210    20   15  -10   -5\n</code></pre>\n<p>Actually, my table looks like the one above.\nThe first column V1 represents Premiums charged by an insurance company,say last year (for 5 policyholders/policies)\nAfter critical analysis of the portfolio, the company decides to increase or decrease the premium amount for some of the customers.\nHowever, the company does not know exactly by how much it should increase of decrease the premiums for fear that it would lose customers.\nFor this reason, four different scenarios/simulations are considered which are represented by the next four columns(V2 through V5) respectively.</p>\n<p>Now the task is to plot the premium amounts in V1 against these four different scenarios(bar-graph or line-graph; I think bar will be better).</p>\n<p>And my question is can this be done on one graph/at once? If yes, how shoul I go about it?\nOr do I have to plot the premium against each column separately?</p>\n<p>In fact, I have spent the whole of yesterday and today on this but I have not been able to get the desired result.</p>\n<p>Someone gave me an answer to try.And I am going to do that because it has given me an idea and I am very thankful to the one!</p>\n<p>Many thanks to everyone for their help</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-04-26T20:15:47.633000", "posts_rownum": "posts_9277", "provsql": "6b13d104-5ecf-4fc8-ae84-450883ff870e"}, "posts_9508": {"id": 10251, "owneruserid": 74, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 10256, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What is the objective function of PCA?", "tags": "<pca>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Principal component analysis <em>can use</em> matrix decomposition, but that is just a tool to get there.</p>\n\n<p>How would you find the principal components without the use of matrix algebra?</p>\n\n<p>What is the objective function (goal), and what are the constraints?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-05-02T23:10:16.580000", "posts_rownum": "posts_9508", "provsql": "e1d8dd8d-e900-41b6-9539-d80578d847d2"}, "posts_9612": {"id": 10363, "owneruserid": 914, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Data mining: How should I go about finding the functional form?", "tags": "<regression><machine-learning><algorithms><model-selection><data-mining>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm curious about repeatable procedures that can be used to discover the functional form of the function <code>y = f(A, B, C) + error_term</code> where my only input is a set of observations (<code>y</code>, <code>A</code>, <code>B</code> and <code>C</code>). Please note that the functional form of <code>f</code>is unknown.</p>\n\n<p>Consider the following dataset:</p>\n\n<pre>\nAA  BB  CC  DD  EE  FF\n==  ==  ==  ==  ==  ==\n98  11  66  84  67  10500\n71  44  48  12  47  7250\n54  28  90  73  95  5463\n34  95  15  45  75  2581\n56  37  0   79  43  3221\n68  79  1   65  9   4721\n53  2   90  10  18  3095\n38  75  41  97  40  4558\n29  99  46  28  96  5336\n22  63  27  43  4   2196\n4   5   89  78  39  492\n10  28  39  59  64  1178\n11  59  56  25  5   3418\n10  4   79  98  24  431\n86  36  84  14  67  10526\n80  46  29  96  7   7793\n67  71  12  43  3   5411\n14  63  2   9   52  368\n99  62  56  81  26  13334\n56  4   72  65  33  3495\n51  40  62  11  52  5178\n29  77  80  2   54  7001\n42  32  4   17  72  1926\n44  45  30  25  5   3360\n6   3   65  16  87  288\n</pre>\n\n<p>In this example, assume that we know that <code>FF = f(AA, BB, CC, DD, EE) + error term</code>, but we're not sure about the functional form of <code>f(...)</code>.</p>\n\n<p>What procedure/what methods would you use to arrive at finding the functional form of <code>f(...)</code>?</p>\n\n<p>(Bonus point: What is your best guess at the definiton of <code>f</code> given the data above? :-) And yes, there is a \"correct\" answer that will yield an <code>R^2</code> in excess of 0.99.)</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-05-05T16:26:00.037000", "posts_rownum": "posts_9612", "provsql": "98e822cc-d319-4caa-b759-29a6bc524854"}, "posts_9620": {"id": 10382, "owneruserid": 4487, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "General advice on forming an index of attitude to the environment from a set of Likert items", "tags": "<factor-analysis><scales><reliability>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am going to make an environmental index to be used as an explanatory variable in a regression model. For making this index, I asked  respondents a set of questions about their environmental attitudes. Each question has 5 response options from 1=“completely agree” to 5=“completely disagree”.\nI'm going to summarize each these categories as one index.</p>\n\n<p><strong>What general advice can be offered for creating such an index?</strong></p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-05-06T01:11:14.787000", "posts_rownum": "posts_9620", "provsql": "c78d1644-f302-4549-842b-be80f68ad444"}, "posts_9741": {"id": 10510, "owneruserid": 364, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "References containing arguments against null hypothesis significance testing?", "tags": "<hypothesis-testing><statistical-significance><references><p-value>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>In the last few years I've read a number of papers arguing against the use of null hypothesis significance testing in science, but didn't think to keep a persistent list. A colleague recently asked me for such a list, so I thought I'd ask everyone here to help build it. To start things off, here's what I have so far:</p>\n<ul>\n<li><a href=\"https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21077903/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Johansson (2011) "Hail the impossible: p-values, evidence, and likelihood."</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"https://web.archive.org/web/20201025053416/https://www.dgps.de/fachgruppen/methoden/mpr-online/issue16/art1/article.html\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Haller & Kraus (2002) "Misinterpretation of significance: A problem students share with their teachers."</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18087943/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Wagenmakers (2007) "A practical solution to the pervasive problem of p-values."</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2009-24989-001\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Rodgers (2010) "The epistemology of mathematical and statistical modeling: A quiet methodological revolution."</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"https://doi.org/10.3758%2FBF03208815?from=SL\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Dixon (1998) "Why scientists value p-values."</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15732688/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Glover & Dixon (2004) "Likelihood ratios: a simple and flexible statistic for empirical psychologists."</a></li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2011-05-08T16:09:04.040000", "posts_rownum": "posts_9741", "provsql": "4da5187e-a035-462e-a997-186bc3defc1d"}, "posts_10000": {"id": 10789, "owneruserid": 4608, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 10791, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Why are random variables defined as functions?", "tags": "<probability><random-variable><measure-theory>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm having problems understanding the concept of a random variable as a function.  I understand the mechanics (I think) but I do not understand the motivation...</p>\n\n<p>Say $(\\Omega, B, P) $ is a probability triple, where $\\Omega = [0,1]$, $B$ is the Borel-$\\sigma$-algebra on that interval and $P$ is the regular Lebesgue measure.  Let $X$ be a random variable from $B$ to $\\{1,2,3,4,5,6\\}$ such that $X([0,1/6)) = 1$, $X([1/6,2/6)) = 2$, ..., $X([5/6,1]) = 6$, so $X$ has a discrete uniform distribution on the values 1 through 6.  </p>\n\n<p>That's all good, but I do not understand the necessity of the original probability triple... we could have directly constructed something equivalent as $(\\{1,2,3,4,5,6\\}, S, P_x)$ where $S$ is all the appropriate $\\sigma$-algebra of the space, and $P_x$ is a measure that assigns to each subset the measure (# of elements)/6.  Also, the choice of $\\Omega=[0,1]$ was arbitrary-- it could've been $[0,2]$, or any other set.</p>\n\n<p>So my question is, why bother constructing an arbitrary $\\Omega$ with a $\\sigma$-algebra and a measure, and define a random variable as a map from the $\\sigma$-algebra to the real line?  </p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-05-13T22:24:15.883000", "posts_rownum": "posts_10000", "provsql": "34d76778-f547-4ab2-9b5d-2e6bdede5044"}, "posts_10147": {"id": 10964, "owneruserid": 3248, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 10972, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "In convergence in probability or a.s. convergence w.r.t which measure is the probability?", "tags": "<random-variable><probability>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I was presenting proofs of WLLN and a version of SLLN (assuming bounded 4th central moment) when somebody asked which measure is the probability with respect too and I realised that, on reflection, I wasn't quite sure.</p>\n\n<p>It seems that it is straightforward, since in both laws we have a sequence of $X_{i}$'s, independent RVs with identical mean and finite variance. There is only one random variable in sight, namely the $X_{i}$, so the probability must be w.r.t the distribution of the $X_{i}$, right? But then that doesn't seem quite right for the strong law since the typical proof technique is then to define a new RV $S_{n} := \\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{i}$ and work with that, and the limit is <em>inside</em> the probability:</p>\n\n<p>$\nPr \\left[\\lim_{n \\rightarrow \\infty}\\frac{1}{n}\\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{i} = E[X_{i}]\\right]=1\n$</p>\n\n<p>So now it looks as if the RV is the sums over $n$ terms, so the probability is over the distribution of the sums $S_{n}$, where $n$ is no longer fixed. Is that correct? If it is, how would we go about constructing a suitable probability measure on the sequences of partial sums?</p>\n\n<p>Happy to receive intuitive responses as to what is going on as well as formal ones using e.g. real or complex analysis, undergrad probability/statistics, basic measure theory. I've read <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/2230\">Convergence in probability vs. almost sure convergence</a> and associated links, but find no help there.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-05-19T10:43:13.270000", "posts_rownum": "posts_10147", "provsql": "637519e1-f1cf-4209-8c0e-3151a63bb3ba"}, "posts_10255": {"id": 11102, "owneruserid": 1977, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 11103, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Factor analysis problem -- singular covariance matrix?", "tags": "<spss><factor-analysis><python>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm having trouble performing factor analysis on my dataset.</p>\n\n<p>When I perform the factor analysis in SPSS (default settings), it works fine.  \n\n<ul>\n<li>If so, why would one not just always use MANOVA? </li>\n</ul></li>\n<li>I am trying to conduct a repeated measures ANOVA with multiple DVs, what is the appropriate approach?   </li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2011-07-18T15:20:42.077000", "posts_rownum": "posts_12157", "provsql": "73a8a3dd-9a6a-450a-8d0b-76af7837207c"}, "posts_12217": {"id": 13259, "owneruserid": 5471, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 13286, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What is the distribution of maximum of a pair of iid draws, where the minimum is an order statistic of other minima?", "tags": "<distributions><probability><extreme-value><order-statistics>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Consider $n\\cdot m$ independent draws from cdf $F(x)$, which is defined over 0-1, where $n$ and $m$ are integers.  Arbitrarily group the draws into $n$ groups with m values in each group.  Look at the minimum value in each group.  Take the group that has the greatest of these minima.  Now, what is the distribution that defines the maximum value in that group?\nMore generally, what is the distribution for the $j$-th order statistic of $m$ draws of $F(x)$, where the kth order of those m draws is also the pth order of the n draws of that kth order statistic?</p>\n\n<p>All of that is at the most abstract, so here is a more concrete example.\nConsider 8 draws of $F(x)$.  Group them into 4 pairs of 2.  Compare the minimum value in each pair.  Select the pair with the highest  of these 4 minima.  Label that draw \"a\".  Label the other value in that same pair as \"b\".  What is the distribution $F_b(b)$?  We know $b>a$.  We know a is the maximum of 4 minimums of $F(x)$, of $F_a(a) = (1-(1-F(x))^2)^4$.  What is $F_b(b)$? </p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-07-19T18:05:43.903000", "posts_rownum": "posts_12217", "provsql": "1d0f39c4-bf0c-4735-bc44-b44d56807e70"}, "posts_12439": {"id": 13518, "owneruserid": 5558, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 13525, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How do I develop a metric for comparisons that involves a combination of variables at different scales?", "tags": "<correlation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am trying to select the best answer from a set of samples, using two variables at different scales. </p>\n\n<p>In the data below, each row indicates the accuracy of a given measurement, the number of times it occurs in the sample set, and the answer that it indicates.  </p>\n\n<p>Accuracy:0.00886982324861, Frequency:5.0, Answer:1.0<br>\nAccuracy:0.0104663914334,  Frequency:1.0, Answer:2.0<br>\nAccuracy:0.0112727390014,  Frequency:1.0, Answer:2.0<br>\nAccuracy:0.0143046058573,  Frequency:3.0, Answer:1.0<br>\nAccuracy:0.0251741710747,  Frequency:1.0, Answer:1.0<br>\nAccuracy:0.0322055218681,  Frequency:1.0, Answer:2.0<br></p>\n\n<p>Until now, I have been ignoring the accuracy and simply selecting the answer that occurs more frequently i.e., Answer 1 occurs 9 times, Answer 2 occurs 3 times, so select answer 1.  </p>\n\n<p>A product of frequency and accuracy produces a metric that takes both into account, but the different scales weights frequency disproportionately more than accuracy.</p>\n\n<p>How can I calculate a metric that allows me to use both accuracy and frequency, but accounts for their different scales? </p>\n\n<p>Your help is greatly appreciated,\nJohn</p>\n\n<p>*EDIT\nThanks for your response. What if I had a sample that occurs once but its accuracy is .9. That would have a product of .9 which is  larger than the first sample. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-07-26T20:55:39.590000", "posts_rownum": "posts_12439", "provsql": "72278e6d-dab9-4c97-8f8a-a7e14010be73"}, "posts_12692": {"id": 13805, "owneruserid": 5647, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Is there a difference between an index score and a composite score?", "tags": "<correlation><latent-variable><composite>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Following on from <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/13757/how-do-i-weigh-several-variables-at-two-levels-to-create-an-overall-composite-var/13790\">my previous question</a> on forming scale scores, my sample has 100 people who have answered 10 likert scale questions each on two academic subjects: Maths and English. </p>\n\n<p>The likert scale is a 5 point scale, going from not important to absolute importance.</p>\n\n<p>I have aggregated the scores: </p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><p>The maximum score a person can get is 40 (which is 10 responses x 4 which is the maximum score on the likert scale e.g. 4 = absolute importance). </p></li>\n<li><p>The minimum is 0 (which is 10 responses x 0 which is the minimum score on the likert scale e.g. 0 = not important) </p></li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>If a person gets 20 points (total of 10 likert scale responses for Maths) and 30 points (total of 10 likert scale responses for English), my questions are:</p>\n\n<p><strong>1. Is 20 or 30 a composite score or an index score?</strong> (given that they are both based on subjective weighting aligned with the likert scale response)</p>\n\n<p><strong>2. Can I do a correlation analysis on the two scores?</strong> (given they are composite/index scores, hence represent a latent variable)</p>\n\n<p>Many thanks</p>\n", "creationdate": if the samples span the $d$ dimensions and not in any sub-space of $d$.</p>\n\n<p>In short, for $n \\le d + 1$, where $n$ is the number of samples, there exists a separating hyperplane.</p>\n\n<p>How can it be proved?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-08-28T18:34:04", "posts_rownum": "posts_13679", "provsql": "869aa79f-a7bf-4608-b263-71480519997b"}, "posts_13821": {"id": 15076, "owneruserid": 740, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 15267, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Determining the variables when training a/classifying with a random forest", "tags": "<classification><random-forest>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Based on a <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/124/statistical-classification-of-text/143#143\">response</a> to the question \"<a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/124/statistical-classification-of-text\">Statistical classification of text</a>\", I've decided that I want to use a <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_forest\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">random forest</a> to perform various classifications of text.</p>\n\n<p>Specifically, I am getting YouTube video data from their XML feeds.  Here is <a href=\"http://gdata.youtube.com/feeds/api/videos/ltkMAcv2cas\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">an example</a>:</p>\n\n<pre><code><entry gd:etag=\"W/\"DUQBR347eCp7I2A9WhdXFEQ.\"\">\n    <id>tag:youtube.com,2008:video:ltkMAcv2cas</id>\n    <published>2010-12-23T18:11:28.000Z</published>\n    <updated>2011-08-28T02:09:16.000Z</updated>\n    <category scheme=\"http://schemas.google.com/g/2005#kind\"\n        term=\"http://gdata.youtube.com/schemas/2007#video\"/>\n    <category scheme=\"http://gdata.youtube.com/schemas/2007/keywords.cat\" \n        term=\"SSF4AE\"/>\n    <!-- More categories/keywords here -->\n    <title>SSF4AE Mago 2D God VS Kazunoko aka Inoue</title>\n    <!-- More video information here, description, etc -->\n</entry>\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>With that, I have very specific data that I believe I can use as the basis for variables in a random forest:</p>\n\n<pre><code>Variable    Value\n--------    -----\nTitle       SSF4AE Mago 2D God VS Kazunoko aka Inoue\nCategory    SSF4AE\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Looking at the video and based on the title/categories, I know that this is a video of the game <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Street_Fighter_IV#Arcade_Edition\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Super Street Fighter 4: Arcade Edition</a> (SSF4AE).</p>\n\n<p>Looking at the <a href=\"http://www.alglib.net/dataanalysis/decisionforest.php\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">alglib Decision Forest</a>, I also read the <a href=\"http://www.alglib.net/dataanalysis/generalprinciples.php\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">general principals of data analysis methods</a>, which speaks about encoding specifically for the algorithms on alglib; while I won't use it specifically, I believe it expanded my understanding of how data should be represented for a random forest.</p>\n\n<p>Basically, using the above data, I'd need to transform each data point into a number of some sort.</p>\n\n<p>For example, I could transform this into the following variables:</p>\n\n<pre><code>Variable                 Value\n--------                 -----\nHas \"SSF4AE\" in Title        1\nEquals \"SSF4AE\"              1\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Now, assuming I know that this video is for SSF4AE, and that I know that SSF4AE is a common acronym used to identify the game, would using the above as variables work for a random forest for training and classification?</p>\n\n<p>Of course, that's a small set, and it's a very rough set of variables; my understanding is that a random forest basically will create nodes where there is a threshold for the variable, values over this fall on one side of the tree, values under on the other side.</p>\n\n<p>In the above example, there are only two options, true or false.</p>\n\n<p>However, I imagine I can do something like get the <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tf%E2%80%93idf\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">term-frequency/inverse document frequency</a> and use that (using <a href=\"http://incubator.apache.org/lucene.net/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Lucene.NET</a> or <a href=\"http://www.elasticsearch.org/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">elasticsearch</a>), like so (numbers are not accurate)</p>\n\n<pre><code>Variable                               Value\n--------                               -----\nTerm Query for \"SSF4AE\" in Title        0.36\nTerm Query for \"SSF4AE\" in Category     1.00\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>And then train the random forest on that.</p>\n\n<p>I assume that if the variables were done as above, then I could also place things such as boosts on the variables (in the tf/idf calculation) where I see that they are more prominent or I feel I want them to have more weight.</p>\n\n<p>And finally, I can add more variables, but they have to be very specific.  For example, I <em>know</em> that if there is a character <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Street_Fighter_characters#Yun_and_Yang\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Yun</a> that only appears in SSF4AE, (not previous versions of Street Fighter 4), as well as in <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_Fighter_III\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Street Fighter III</a>.  To that end, I can add two more variables:</p>\n\n<pre><code>Variable                               Value\n--------                               -----\nTerm Query for \"SSF4AE\" in Title        0.36\nTerm Query for \"SSF4AE\" in Category     1.00\nOne character is Yun                       1\nTerm Query for \"3S\" in Title            0.00\nTerm Query for \"3SO\" in Title           0.00\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>(\"3SO\" and \"3S\" being common acronyms for Street Fighter III: Third Strike)</p>\n\n<p>However, for another video, which I know is for 3S, I the variables might look like this:</p>\n\n<pre><code>Variable                               Value\n--------                               -----\nTerm Query for \"SSF4AE\" in Title        0.00\nTerm Query for \"SSF4AE\" in Category     0.00\nOne character is Yun                       1\nTerm Query for \"3S\" in Title            0.54\nTerm Query for \"3SO\" in Title           0.00\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Where the training set would indicate that video is for 3S.</p>\n\n<p>That said, are these feasible ways of going about determining the variables of a random forest?</p>\n\n<p>Also, if I understand correctly, the random forest will also indicate which variables contributed the most to the classification, so I can discard them during classification later (if I want) or add different ones to get better classifications from my training data.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-09-01T18:59:02.627000", "posts_rownum": "posts_13821", "provsql": "5e45c86b-b67e-4641-8cb9-02cbcbe6738f"}, "posts_13945": {"id": 15211, {"id": 15913, "owneruserid": 6432, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 15915, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Add a column to a dataframe based on a probability distribution", "tags": "<r><data-imputation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Suppose I have two dependent categorical attributes A, B. I have a dataframe X that lists probabilities (or expected counts) for all combinations of all categories of A and B. Let's assume two categories in each attribute, the dataframe could then look like this:</p>\n\n<pre><code>X <- data.frame(A = c(1,1,2,2), B = 1:2, PROB = c(0.1,0.3,0.2,0.4))\nX\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Output:</p>\n\n<pre><code>  A B PROB\n1 1 1   .1\n2 1 2   .3\n3 2 1   .2\n4 2 2   .4\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Now I would like to add a B column to another dataframe Y that has only an A column. Y exists and has many more rows than X, and also additional columns. A synthetic Y could look like this:</p>\n\n<pre><code>Y <- data.frame(A=sample(2, size=10000, replace=TRUE),\n                B=NA,\n                C=sample(5, size=10000, replace=TRUE),\n                D=sample(3, size=10000, replace=TRUE))\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>The contents of the new B column should be sampled at random using the conditional probabilities for B given the value of the A column.</p>\n\n<p>I am new to R, and I was wondering whether this operation can be handled more elegantly than writing a loop that iterates over all A categories. Perhaps a dedicated model class for which <code>predict</code> could be applied? Also, I lack the knowledge of statistical terminology -- I would appreciate any hint on how this kind of imputation (?) is referred to in the literature.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-09-22T10:49:23.863000", "posts_rownum": "posts_14581", "provsql": "12aa7c9c-f364-4082-849c-e8818c720490"}, "posts_14612": {"id": 15958, "owneruserid": 6178, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to interpret and report  eta squared / partial eta squared in statistically significant and non-significant analyses?", "tags": "<anova><statistical-significance><effect-size>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I have data that has eta squared values and partial eta squared values calculated as a measure of effect size for group mean differences.</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><p>What is the difference between eta squared and partial eta squared? Can they both be interpreted using the same Cohen's guidelines (1988 I think: 0.01 = small, 0.06 = medium, 0.13 = large)?</p></li>\n<li><p>Also, is there use in reporting effect size if the comparison test (ie t-test or one-way ANOVA) is non-significant? In my head, this is like saying \"the mean difference did not reach statistical significance but is still of particular note because the effect size indicated from the eta squared is medium\". Or, is effect size a replacement value for significance testing, rather than complementary? </p></li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2011-09-23T07:22:39.713000", "posts_rownum": "posts_14612", "provsql": "9c051962-1c95-45ba-bf35-b0586a4ae7b2"}, "posts_2189": {"id": 2272, "owneruserid": 71, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2287, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What's the difference between a confidence interval and a credible interval?", "tags": "<bayesian><confidence-interval><frequentist><credible-interval><fiducial>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Joris and Srikant's exchange <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/2182/can-you-explaining-why-statistical-tie-is-not-naively-when-p-1-p-2-2-moe/2242#2242\">here</a> got me wondering (again) if my internal explanations for the difference between confidence intervals and credible intervals were the correct ones.  How you would explain the difference?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-01T13:53:07.183000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2189", "provsql": "11b37a97-b8e5-4566-8369-e0b3a72cab07"}, "posts_3369": {"id": 3561, "owneruserid": 1077, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3569, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Dealing with correlated regressors", "tags": "<regression><multicollinearity>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>In a multiple linear regression with  highly correlated regressors, what is the best strategy to use? Is it a legitimate approach to add the product of all the correlated regressors?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-13T17:34:00.057000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3369", "provsql": "291e9f87-e967-462f-b380-a16134581c3d"}, "posts_135": {"id": 146, "owneruserid": 144, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 149, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Can one use multiple regression to predict one principal component (PC) from several other PCs?", "tags": "<regression><pca>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>A while ago a user on R-help mailing list asked about the soundness of using PCA scores in a regression. The user is trying to use some PC scores to explain variation in another PC (see full discussion <a href=\"http://r.789695.n4.nabble.com/PCA-and-Regression-td2280038.html\" rel=\"nofollow\">here</a>). The answer was that no, this is not sound because PCs are orthogonal to each other.</p>\n\n<p>Can someone explain in a bit more detail why this is so?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-19T21:52:51.707000", "posts_rownum": "posts_135", "provsql": "469eab65-ca36-4f8c-b3ae-8cb5b9c9461f"}, "posts_396": {"id": 414, "owneruserid": 89, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 439, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Introduction to statistics for mathematicians", "tags": "<references>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>What is a good introduction to statistics for a mathematician who is already well-versed in probability?  I have two distinct motivations for asking, which may well lead to different suggestions:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li><p>I'd like to better understand the statistics motivation behind many problems considered by probabilists.</p></li>\n<li><p>I'd like to know how to better interpret the results of Monte Carlo simulations which I sometimes do to form mathematical conjectures.</p></li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>I'm open to the possibility that the best way to go is not to look for something like \"Statistics for Probabilists\" and just go to a more introductory source.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-21T13:50:08.847000", "posts_rownum": "posts_396", "provsql": "742933c9-437e-43a4-aca7-95fbc5592ab9"}, "posts_7": {"id": 7, "owneruserid": 38, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 18, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Locating freely available data samples", "tags": "<dataset><sample><population><teaching>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I've been working on a new method for analyzing and parsing datasets to identify and isolate subgroups of a population without foreknowledge of any subgroup's characteristics.  While the method works well enough with artificial data samples (i.e. datasets created specifically for the purpose of identifying and segregating subsets of the population), I'd like to try testing it with live data.</p>\n\n<p>What I'm looking for is a freely available (i.e. non-confidential, non-proprietary) data source.  Preferably one containing bimodal or multimodal distributions or being obviously comprised of multiple subsets that cannot be easily pulled apart via traditional means.  Where would I go to find such information?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-19T19:15:59.303000", "posts_rownum": "posts_7", "provsql": "6b22cecb-4ee6-4832-941b-3b78ea4b51f0"}, "posts_28": {"id": 30, "owneruserid": 69, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 55, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Testing random variate generation algorithms", "tags": "<algorithms><hypothesis-testing><random-variable><random-generation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Which methods are used for testing random variate generation algorithms?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-19T19:28:34.220000", "posts_rownum": "posts_28", "provsql": "5b9923a0-4ead-41cc-995d-66cf81e690c4"}, "posts_76": {"id": 118, "owneruserid": 83, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 151, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Why square the difference instead of taking the absolute value in standard deviation?", "tags": "<standard-deviation><definition><absolute-value><faq>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>In the definition of standard deviation, why do we have to <strong>square</strong> the difference from the mean to get the mean (E) and take the <strong>square root back</strong> at the end? Can't we just simply take <strong>the absolute value</strong> of the difference instead and get the expected value (mean) of those, and wouldn't that also show the variation of the data? The number is going to be different from square method (the absolute-value method will be smaller), but it should still show the spread of data. Anybody know why we take this square approach as a standard?</p>\n\n<p>The definition of standard deviation:</p>\n\n<p>$\\sigma = \\sqrt{E\\left[\\left(X - \\mu\\right)^2\\right]}.$\r</p>\n\n<p>Can't we just take the absolute value instead and still be a good measurement?</p>\n\n<p>$\\sigma = E\\left[|X - \\mu|\\right]$\r</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-19T21:04:39.057000", "posts_rownum": "posts_76", "provsql": "dd249142-48a3-4540-adfb-dd4c476f4376"}, "posts_171": {"id": 183, "owneruserid": 166, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 518, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What tools could be used for applying clustering algorithms on MovieLens?", "tags": "<clustering>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I need to analyze the 100k MovieLens dataset for clustering with two algorithms of my choice, between the likes of k-means, agnes, diana, dbscan, and several others. What tools (like Rattle, or Weka) would be best suited to help me make some simple clustering analysis over this dataset?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-20T00:20:51.767000", "posts_rownum": "posts_171", "provsql": "fe502fcd-9c19-4f1f-92c6-cbd3c3afa037"}, "posts_192": {"id": 203, "owneruserid": 183, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Group differences on a five point Likert item", "tags": "<t-test><ordinal-data><likert><scales>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Following on from <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/10/under-what-conditions-should-likert-scales-be-used-as-ordinal-or-interval-data\">this question</a>:\nImagine that you want to test for differences in central tendency between two groups (e.g., males and females)\non a 5-point Likert item (e.g., satisfaction with life: Dissatisfied to Satisfied).\nI think a t-test would be sufficiently accurate for most purposes,\n but that a bootstrap test of differences between group means would often provide more accurate estimate of confidence intervals.\nWhat statistical test would you use?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-20T03:31:45.820000", "posts_rownum": "posts_192", "provsql": "b93c90d7-3606-4136-a4e1-24252b857d55"}, "posts_293": {"id": 305, "owneruserid": 196, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 796, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "When conducting a t-test why would one prefer to assume (or test for) equal variances rather than always use a Welch approximation of the df?", "tags": "<variance><t-test><heteroscedasticity>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>It seems like when the assumption of homogeneity of variance is met that the results from a Welch adjusted t-test and a standard t-test are approximately the same.  Why not simply always use the Welch adjusted t?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-20T14:19:41.383000", "posts_rownum": "posts_293", "provsql": "9f8a5fb6-f06b-46f2-9f1d-c1cfa87a0850"}, "posts_567": {"id": 577, "owneruserid": 196, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 767, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Is there any reason to prefer the AIC or BIC over the other?", "tags": "<modeling><aic><cross-validation><bic><model-selection>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>The AIC and BIC are both methods of assessing model fit penalized for the number of estimated parameters.  As I understand it, BIC penalizes models more for free parameters than does AIC.  Beyond a preference based on the stringency of the criteria, are there any other reasons to prefer AIC over BIC or vice versa?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-23T20:49:12.340000", "posts_rownum": "posts_567", "provsql": "bca852bd-9196-40e1-80bf-820d2744b111"}, "posts_353": {"id": 372, "owneruserid": 252, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 381, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What are the key statistical concepts that relate to data mining?", "tags": "<probability><data-mining><cart>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>What topics in statistics are most useful/relevant to data mining?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-21T04:26:07.550000", "posts_rownum": "posts_353", "provsql": "5ebf8c3c-e01f-44b1-afab-9b8cfe9594d6"}, "posts_393": {"id": 411, "owneruserid": 89, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Motivation for Kolmogorov distance between distributions", "tags": "<distributions><probability><hypothesis-testing><mathematical-statistics>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>There are many ways to measure how similar two probability distributions are.  Among methods which are popular (in different circles) are:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li><p>the Kolmogorov distance: the sup-distance between the distribution functions;</p></li>\n<li><p>the Kantorovich-Rubinstein distance: the maximum difference between the expectations w.r.t. the two distributions of functions with Lipschitz constant $1$, which also turns out to be the $L^1$ distance between the distribution functions;</p></li>\n<li><p>the bounded-Lipschitz distance: like the K-R distance but the functions are also required to have absolute value at most $1$.</p></li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>These have different advantages and disadvantages.  Only convergence in the sense of 3. actually corresponds precisely to convergence in distribution; convergence in the sense of 1. or 2. is slightly stronger in general.  (In particular, if $X_n=\\frac{1}{n}$ with probability $1$, then $X_n$ converges to $0$ in distribution, but not in the Kolmogorov distance. However, if the limit distribution is continuous then this pathology doesn't occur.) </p>\n\n<p>From the perspective of elementary probability or measure theory, 1. is very natural because it compares the probabilities of being in some set. A more sophisticated probabilistic perspective, on the other hand, tends to focus more on expectations than probabilities. Also, from the perspective of functional analysis, distances like 2. or 3. based on duality with some function space are very appealing, because there is a large set of mathematical tools for working with such things.</p>\n\n<p>However, my impression (correct me if I'm wrong!) is that in statistics, the Kolmogorov distance is the usually preferred way of measuring similarity of distributions.  I can guess one reason: if one of the distributions is discrete with finite support -- in particular, if it is the distribution of some real-world data -- then the Kolmogorov distance to a model distribution is easy to compute.  (The K-R distance would be slightly harder to compute, and the B-L distance would probably be impossible in practical terms.)</p>\n\n<p>So my question (finally) is, are there other reasons, either practical or theoretical, to favor the Kolmogorov distance (or some other distance) for statistical purposes?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-21T13:39:06.783000", "posts_rownum": "posts_393", "provsql": "fcd6efec-cee1-4c8d-8ceb-24f1b285224e"}, "posts_477": {"id": 490, "owneruserid": 223, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 606, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Variable selection procedure for binary classification", "tags": "<machine-learning><classification><multiple-comparisons><multivariate-analysis><feature-selection>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>What are the <strong>variable/feature  selection that you prefer</strong> for binary classification when there are many more variables/feature than observations in the learning set? The aim here is to discuss what is the feature selection procedure that reduces the best the classification error. </p>\n\n<p>We can <strong>fix notations</strong> for consistency: for $i \\in \\{0, 1\\}$, let $\\{x_1^i,\\dots, x_{n_i}^i\\}$ be the learning set of observations from group $i$.   So $n_0 + n_1 = n$ is the size of the learning set. We set $p$ to be the number of features (i.e. the dimension of the feature space). Let $x[i]$ denote the $i$-th coordinate of $x \\in \\mathbb{R}^p$. </p>\n\n<p>Please give full references if you cannot give the details. </p>\n\n<p>EDIT (updated continuously):  Procedures proposed in the answers below </p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Greedy forward selection</strong> <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/490/variable-selection-procedure-for-binary-classification/497#497\">Variable selection procedure for binary classification</a></li>\n<li><strong>Backward elimination</strong> <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/490/variable-selection-procedure-for-binary-classification/501#501\">Variable selection procedure for binary classification</a></li>\n<li><strong>Metropolis scanning / MCMC</strong> <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/490/variable-selection-procedure-for-binary-classification/505#505\">Variable selection procedure for binary classification</a></li>\n<li><strong>penalized logistic regression</strong> <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/490/variable-selection-procedure-for-binary-classification/606#606\">Variable selection procedure for binary classification</a></li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>As this is community wiki there can be more discussion and update</p>\n\n<p>I have one remark: in a certain sense, you all give a procedure that permit ordering of variables but not variable selection (you are quite evasive on how to select the number of features, I guess you all use cross validation?) Can you improve the answers in this direction? (as this is community wiki you don't need to be the answer writter to add an information about how to select the number of variables? I have openned a question in this direction here <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/880/cross-validation-to-select-the-number-of-used-variables-in-very-high-dimensional\">Cross validation in very high dimension (to select the number of used variables in very high dimensional classification)</a>)</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-22T11:10:29.417000", "posts_rownum": "posts_477", "provsql": "0883ce4d-5d24-4956-934d-ffe0520216ec"}, "posts_565": {"id": 575, "owneruserid": 196, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 762, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Post-hocs for within subjects tests?", "tags": "<r><repeated-measures><multiple-comparisons><post-hoc><sphericity>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>What is the preferred method for for conducting post-hocs for within subjects tests?  I've seen published work where Tukey's HSD is employed but a review of Keppel and Maxwell & Delaney suggests that the likely violation of sphericity in these designs makes the error term incorrect and this approach problematic.  Maxwell & Delaney provide an approach to the problem in their book, but I've never seen it done that way in any stats package.  Is the approach they offer appropriate?  Would a Bonferroni or Sidak correction on multiple paired sample t-tests be reasonable?  An acceptable answer will provide general R code which can conduct post-hocs on simple, multiple-way, and mixed designs as produced by the <code>ezANOVA</code> function in the <code>ez</code> package, and appropriate citations that are likely to pass muster with reviewers.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-23T20:14:05.327000", "posts_rownum": "posts_565", "provsql": "38bc16f9-4d7e-4480-9e62-b7fcb23a8e20"}, "posts_882": {"id": 899, "owneruserid": 219, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Separating two populations from the sample", "tags": "<dataset><outliers><expectation-maximization>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm trying to separate two groups of values from a single data set. The simulation returns a variable, $p$, that can be either 1 or 0. I then weight the simulations based on predefined criteria and calculate the probability of $p$. I also calculate a risk ratio using $p$:</p>\n\n<p>$$\\text{Risk ratio} = P(p|\\text{test case}) / P(p|\\text{control case})$$</p>\n\n<p>I had eight Monte Carlo runs, which consist of one control case and seven test cases. </p>\n\n<p>I need to know if the probabilities of $p$ are statistically different compared to the other cases. I know I can use a multiple comparison test or nonparametric ANOVA to test individual variables, but how do I do this for probabilities? </p>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p>For example are these two probabilities statistically different?:</p>\n\n<p><em>Probabilities</em>:</p>\n\n<p>$P(p|\\text{test #3}) = 4.08 \\times 10^{-5}$</p>\n\n<p>$P(p|\\text{test #4}) = 6.10 \\times 10^{-5}$</p>\n\n<p><em>Risk Ratios</em>:</p>\n\n<p>$\\text{Risk Ratio}(\\text{test #3}) = 0.089$</p>\n\n<p>$\\text{Risk Ratio}(\\text{test #4}) = 0.119$ </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-28T17:15:09.090000", "posts_rownum": "posts_901", "provsql": "1b84cfc9-86f2-4d2a-9783-972e51835113"}, "posts_954": {"id": 973, "owneruserid": 223, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1020, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Free data set for very high dimensional classification", "tags": "<machine-learning><classification><dataset><large-data>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>What are the <strong>freely available data set for classification with more than 1000 features</strong> (or sample points if it contains curves)? </p>\n\n<p>There is already a community wiki about free data sets:\n<a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/7/locating-freely-available-data-samples/\">Locating freely available data samples</a></p>\n\n<p>But here, it would be nice to have a <strong>more focused list that can be used more conveniently</strong>, also I propose the following rules:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>One post <strong>per dataset</strong> </li>\n<li><strong>No</strong> link to set of dataset </li>\n<li><p>each data set <strong>must</strong> be associated with</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><p>a <strong>name</strong> (to figure out what it is about)  and a link to the dataset (R datasets can be named with package name)</p></li>\n<li><p>the number of features (let say it is <strong>p</strong>) the size of the dataset (let say it is <strong>n</strong>) and the number of labels/class (let say it is <strong>k</strong>)    </p></li>\n<li><p>a typical <strong>error rate</strong> from your experience (state the used algorithm in to words) or from the litterature (in this last case link the paper) </p></li>\n</ul></li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-29T12:02:28.347000", "posts_rownum": "posts_954", "provsql": "984388d0-2cd3-47d2-bfc4-a7b3e69faf68"}, "posts_5423": {"id": 5750, "owneruserid": 888, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 5754, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Look and you shall find (a correlation)", "tags": "<correlation><multiple-comparisons><permutation-test>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I have several hundred measurements.
