In my experience, careful study design with special thought with regards to the statistical analysis is often neglected (working in biology/ecology, this seems to be a prevailing occurrence). Statisticians often find themselves in a gridlock with insufficient (or outright wrong) collected data. To paraphrase Ronald Fisher, they are forced to do a post-mortem on the data, which often leads to weaker conclusions, if at all.</p>\n\n<p>I would like to know which references you use to construct a successful study design, preferably for a wide range of methods (e.g. <em>t</em>-test, GLM, GAM, ordination techniques...) that helps you avoid pitfalls mentioned above.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-06T08:06:13.193000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1293", "provsql": "1c925137-22a9-40e3-9b23-9d7cd57118b7"}, "posts_1240": {"id": 1292, "owneruserid": 217, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1297, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What is the weak side of decision trees?", "tags": "<machine-learning><nonparametric><cart>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p><a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_tree\">Decision trees</a> seems to be a very understandable machine learning method.\nOnce created it can be easily inspected by a human which is a great advantage in some applications. </p>\n\n<p>What are the practical weak sides of Decision Trees?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-05T10:42:44.327000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1240", "provsql": "74c07014-31af-40a1-97a0-275fe3d395c0"}, "posts_1329": {"id": 1386, "owneruserid": 795, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1390, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Robust t-test for mean ", "tags": "<hypothesis-testing><t-test><finance><robust>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am trying to test the null $E[X] = 0$, against the local alternative $E[X] > 0$, for a random variable $X$, subject to mild to medium skew and kurtosis of the random variable. Following suggestions by Wilcox in 'Introduction to Robust Estimation and Hypothesis Testing', I have looked at tests based on the trimmed mean, the median, as well as the M-estimator of location (Wilcox' \"one-step\" procedure). These robust tests do outperform the standard t-test, in terms of power, when testing with a distribution that is non-skewed, but leptokurtotic.</p>\n\n<p>However, when testing with a distribution that is skewed, these one-sided tests are either far too liberal or far too conservative under the null hypothesis, depending on whether the distribution is left- or right-skewed, respectively. For example, with 1000 observations, the test based on the median will actually reject ~40% of the time, at the nominal 5% level. The reason for this is obvious: for skewed distributions, the median and the mean are rather different. However, in my application, I really need to test the mean, not the median, not the trimmed mean.</p>\n\n<p><strong>Is there a more robust version of the t-test that actually tests for the mean, but is impervious to skew and kurtosis?</strong></p>\n\n<p>Ideally the procedure would work well in the no-skew, high-kurtosis case as well. The 'one-step' test is almost good enough, with the 'bend' parameter set relatively high, but it is less powerful than the trimmed mean tests when there is no skew, and has some troubles maintaining the nominal level of rejects under skew.</p>\n\n<p><strong>background:</strong> the reason I really care about the mean, and not the median, is that the test would be used in a financial application. For example, if you wanted to test whether a portfolio had positive expected log returns, the mean is actually appropriate because if you invest in the portfolio, you will experience all the returns (which is the mean times the number of samples), instead of $n$ duplicates of the median.  That is, I really care about the sum of $n$ draws from the R.V. $X$. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-07T05:18:58.967000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1329", "provsql": "fdfce3a9-21fe-4db1-9bd4-f78024914e68"}, "posts_1423": {"id": 1475, "owneruserid": null, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1491, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": "anonymous", "title": "Visualization software for clustering", "tags": "<data-visualization><clustering><software>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I want to cluster ~22000 points. Is this valid?</p></li>\n<li><p>Is it preferable to use FET when expected cell counts in a contingency table are < 5?</p></li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-17T23:42:12.133000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1725", "provsql": "af59b505-9c1f-4247-868e-ad7cddb35b98"}, "posts_1730": {"id": 1812, "owneruserid": 339, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2043, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "FA: Choosing Rotation matrix, based on \"Simple Structure Criteria\"", "tags": "<r><algorithms><factor-analysis><psychometrics><matlab>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>One of the most important issues in using factor analysis is its interpretation. Factor analysis often uses factor rotation to enhance its interpretation. After a satisfactory rotation, the rotated factor loading matrix <strong>L'</strong> will have the same ability to represent the correlation matrix and it can be used as the factor loading matrix, instead of the unrotated matrix <strong>L</strong>.</p>\n\n<p>The purpose of rotation is to make the rotated factor loading matrix have some desirable properties. One of the methods used is to rotate the factor loading matrix such that the rotated matrix will have a <strong>simple structure</strong>.</p>\n\n<p>L. L. Thurstone introduced the Principle of Simple Structure, as a general guide for factor rotation:</p>\n\n<h2>Simple Structure Criteria:</h2>\n\n<ol>\n<li>Each row of the factor matrix should contain at least one zero</li>\n<li>If there are m common factors, each column of the factor matrix should have at least m zeros</li>\n<li>For every pair of columns in the factor matrix, there should be several variables for which entries approach zero in the one column but not in the other</li>\n<li>For every pair of columns in the factor matrix, a large proportion of the variables should have entries approaching zero in both columns when there are four or more factors</li>\n<li>For every pair of columns in the factor matrix, there should be only a small number of variables with nonzero entries in both columns</li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>The ideal simple structure is such that:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>each item has a high, or meaningful, loading on one factor only and</li>\n<li>each factor have high, or meaningful, loadings for only some of the items.</li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>The problem is that, trying several combinations of rotation methods along with the parameters that each one accepts (especially for oblique ones), the number of candidate matrices increases and it is very difficult to see which one better meets the above criteria.</p>\n\n<p>When I first faced that problem I realized that I was unable to select the best match by merely 'looking' at them, and that I needed an algorithm to help me decide. Under the stress of project's deadlines, the most I could do was to write the following code in MATLAB, which accepts one rotation matrix at a time and returns (under some assumptions) whether each criterion is met or not.\nA new version (If I would ever tried to upgrade it) would accept a 3d matrix (a set of 2d matrices) as an argument, and the algorithm should return the one that better fits the above criteria.</p>\n\n<p>How would you extract an algorithm out of those criteria? I am just asking for your opinions (I also think that there's been criticism over the usefulness of the method by itself) and perhaps better approaches to the rotation matrix selection problem. </p>\n\n<p>Also, I would like to know what software do you prefer to perform FA. If it's R, what package do you use? (I must admit that if I had to do FA, I would turn to SPSS again). If someone wants to provide some code, I would prefer R or MATLAB. </p>\n\n<p>P.S. The above <a href=\"http://books.google.gr/books?id=5Jyaa2LQWbQC&pg=PA132&lpg=PA132&dq=%22The+criteria+of+simple+structure+was+originally+proposed%22&source=bl&ots=OXsCeU0Nzi&sig=qfiLMUyXsgwPunWBgNdSEeBNm34&hl=el&ei=huZeS5nkApTE4gaC67HsCw&sa=X&oi=book_result&ct=result&resnum=1&ved=0CAcQ6AEwAA#v=onepage&q=%22The%20criteria%20of%20simple%20structure%20was%20originally%20proposed%22&f=false\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Simple Structure Criteria formulation</a> can be found in the book <em>\"Making Sense of Factor Analysis\"</em> by PETT, M., LACKEY, N., SULLIVAN, J.</p>\n\n<p>P.S.2 (from the same book): <em>\"A test of successful factor analysis is the extent to which it can reproduce the original corr matrix. If you also used oblique solutions, among all select the one that generated the greatest number of highest and lowest factor loadings.\"</em> \nThis sounds like another constraint that the algorithm could use.</p>\n\n<p>P.S.3 This question has also been asked <a href=\"https://stackoverflow.com/questions/2139703/fa-choosing-rotation-matrix-based-on-simple-structure-criteria\">here</a>. However, I think it fits better on this site.</p>\n\n<pre><code>function [] = simple_structure_criteria (my_pattern_table)\n%Simple Structure Criteria\n%Making Sense of Factor Analysis, page 132\n\ndisp(' ');\ndisp('Simple Structure Criteria (Thurstone):');\ndisp('1. Each row of the factor matrix should contain at least one zero');\ndisp( '2. If there are m common factors, each column of the factor matrix should have at least m zeros');\ndisp( '3. For every pair of columns in the factor matrix, there should be several variables for which entries approach zero in the one column but not in the other');\ndisp( '4. For every pair of columns in the factor matrix, a large proportion of the variables should have entries approaching zero in both columns when there are four or more factors');\ndisp( '5. For every pair of columns in the factor matrix, there should be only a small number of variables with nonzero entries in both columns');\ndisp(' ');\ndisp( '(additional by Pedhazur and Schmelkin) The ideal simple structure is such that:');\ndisp( '6. Each item has a high, or meaningful, loading on one factor only and');\ndisp( '7. Each factor have high, or meaningful, loadings for only some of the items.');\n\ndisp('')\ndisp('Start checking...')\n\n%test matrix\n%ct=[76,78,16,7;19,29,10,13;2,6,7,8];\n%test it by giving: simple_structure_criteria (ct)\n\nct=abs(my_pattern_table);\n\nitems=size(ct,1);\nfactors=size(ct,2);\nmy_zero = 0.1;\napproach_zero = 0.2;\nseveral = floor(items / 3);\nsmall_number = ceil(items / 4);\nlarge_proportion = 0.30;\nmeaningful = 0.4;\nsome_bottom = 2;\nsome_top = floor(items / 2);\n\n% CRITERION 1\ndisp(' ');\ndisp('CRITERION 1');\nfor i = 1 : 1 : items\n    count = 0;\n    for j = 1 : 1 : factors\n        if (ct(i,j) < my_zero)\n            count = count + 1;\n            break\n        end\n    end\n    if (count == 0)\n        disp(['Criterion 1 is NOT MET for item ' num2str(i)])\n    end\nend\n\n\n% CRITERION 2\ndisp(' ');\ndisp('CRITERION 2');\nfor j = 1 : 1 : factors \n    m=0;\n    for i = 1 : 1 : items\n        if (ct(i,j) < my_zero)\n            m = m + 1;\n        end\n    end\n    if (m < factors)\n        disp(['Criterion 2 is NOT MET for factor ' num2str(j) '. m = ' num2str(m)]);\n    end\nend\n\n% CRITERION 3\ndisp(' ');\ndisp('CRITERION 3');\nfor c1 = 1 : 1 : factors - 1\n    for c2 = c1 + 1 : 1 : factors\n        test_several = 0;\n        for i = 1 : 1 : items\n            if ( (ct(i,c1)>my_zero && ct(i,c2)<my_zero) || (ct(i,c1)<my_zero && ct(i,c2)>my_zero) ) % approach zero in one but not in the other\n                test_several = test_several + 1;\n            end\n        end\n        disp(['several = ' num2str(test_several) ' for factors ' num2str(c1) ' and ' num2str(c2)]);\n        if (test_several < several)\n            disp(['Criterion 3 is NOT MET for factors ' num2str(c1) ' and ' num2str(c2)]);\n        end\n    end\nend\n\n% CRITERION 4\ndisp(' ');\ndisp('CRITERION 4');\nif (factors > 3)\n    for c1 = 1 : 1 : factors - 1\n        for c2 = c1 + 1 : 1 : factors\n            test_several = 0;\n            for i = 1 : 1 : items\n                if (ct(i,c1)<approach_zero && ct(i,c2)<approach_zero) % approach zero in both\n                    test_several = test_several + 1;\n                end\n            end\n            disp(['large proportion = ' num2str((test_several / items)*100) '% for factors ' num2str(c1) ' and ' num2str(c2)]);\n            if ((test_several / items) < large_proportion)\n                pr = sprintf('%4.2g',  (test_several / items) * 100 );\n                disp(['Criterion 4 is NOT MET for factors ' num2str(c1) ' and ' num2str(c2) '. Proportion is ' pr '%']);\n            end\n        end\n    end\nend\n\n% CRITERION 5\ndisp(' ');\ndisp('CRITERION 5');\nfor c1 = 1 : 1 : factors - 1\n    for c2 = c1 + 1 : 1 : factors\n        test_number = 0;\n        for i = 1 : 1 : items\n            if (ct(i,c1)>approach_zero && ct(i,c2)>approach_zero) % approach zero in both\n                test_number = test_number + 1;\n            end\n        end\n        disp(['small number = ' num2str(test_number) ' for factors ' num2str(c1) ' and ' num2str(c2)]);\n        if (test_number > small_number)\n            disp(['Criterion 5 is NOT MET for factors ' num2str(c1) ' and ' num2str(c2)]);\n        end\n    end\nend\n\n% CRITERION 6\ndisp(' ');\ndisp('CRITERION 6');\nfor i = 1 : 1 : items\n    count = 0;\n    for j = 1 : 1 : factors\n        if (ct(i,j) > meaningful)\n            count = count + 1;\n        end\n    end\n    if (count == 0 || count > 1)\n        disp(['Criterion 6 is NOT MET for item ' num2str(i)])\n    end\nend\n\n% CRITERION 7\ndisp(' ');\ndisp('CRITERION 7');\nfor j = 1 : 1 : factors \n    m=0;\n    for i = 1 : 1 : items\n        if (ct(i,j) > meaningful)\n            m = m + 1;\n        end\n    end\n    disp(['some items = ' num2str(m) ' for factor ' num2str(j)]);\n    if (m < some_bottom || m > some_top)\n        disp(['Criterion 7 is NOT MET for factor ' num2str(j)]);\n    end\nend\ndisp('')\ndisp('Checking completed.')\nreturn\n</code></pre>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-18T07:36:59.733000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1730", "provsql": "c57e7280-1373-4d9b-8aa9-e5e43683b721"}, "posts_1766": {"id": 1848, "owneruserid": 991, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1849, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Bayesian rating system with multiple categories for each rating", "tags": "<bayesian>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I'm implementing a rating system to be used on my website, and I think the Bayesian average is the best way to go about it. Every item will be rated in six different categories by the users. I don't want items with only one high rating to shoot to the top though, which is why I want to implement a Bayesian system.</p>\n\n<p>Here is the formula:</p>\n\n<pre><code>Bayesian Rating = ( (avg_num_votes * avg_rating) + (this_num_votes * this_rating) ) / (avg_num_votes + this_num_votes)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Because the items will be rated in 6 different categories, should I use the average of the sums of those categories as \"this_rating\" for the Bayesian system? For instance, take one item with two ratings (scale of 0-5):</p>\n\n<pre><code>Rating 1:\n  Category A: 3\n  Category B: 1\n  Category C: 2\n  Category D: 4\n  Category E: 5\n  Category F: 3\n  Sum: 18\n\nRating 2:\n  Category A: 2\n  Category B: 3\n  Category C: 3\n  Category D: 5\n  Category E: 0\n  Category F: 1\n  Sum: 14\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Should \"this_rating\" be simply the average of the sums listed above? Is my thinking correct, or should a Bayesian system be implemented for each category as well (or is that overthinking it)?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-18T16:43:11.870000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1766", "provsql": "1fb74925-9822-48d5-b63e-49580f2054ad"}, "posts_1882": {"id": 1961, "owneruserid": 253, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1981, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Can you use normal correlation for vectors with only 2 (or 3), ordered, levels?", "tags": "<r><correlation><association-measure><ordinal-data>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>When one wants to compute the correlation of two vectors of a continues variables, one uses pearson (or spearman) correlation.</p>\n\n<p><strong>But what should (can) one use for the case of two vectors with 2 (or 3) ordered levels only?  Is spearman enough, or does it require another method?</strong></p>\n\n<p>I remember coming across someone who once claimed to me that OR (odds ratio) is more fitting for such situations (for 2 by 2 tables, where order has no meaning), is this true?</p>\n\n<p>Here is an example R code, for allowing of answers relating to the same example:</p>\n\n<pre><code>set.seed(10)\n\nx2 <- sample(c(-1,1),50, T)\nx3 <- sample(c(-1:1),50, T)\ny3 <- sample(c(-1:1),50, T)\ny2 <- sample(c(-1,1),50, T)\n\ncor(x3,y3, method = c(\"spearman\"))\ncor(x2,y2, method = c(\"spearman\"))\ncor(x3,y2, method = c(\"spearman\"))\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>p.s: for the 2 by 2 case, I followed from the comments that categorical \"measures of association\" is the term to look for.  However, Part of the time I am comparing 2 on 3 tables, where on the factor with 3 levels there is order - so I would like to take use of that information.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-20T17:15:43.887000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1882", "provsql": "19c21947-8cd0-44e1-b410-49fb2c6e9bcc"}, "posts_1884": {"id": 1963, "owneruserid": 919, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1976, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Looking for good introductory treatment of meta-analysis", "tags": "<modeling><meta-analysis>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>A (non-statistician) colleague has been encountering meta-analyses in papers he reviews for medical journals and is looking for a good introductory level treatment so he can educate himself.  Any recommendations?  Favorites?  Books, monographs, nontechnical survey articles would all be fine.</p>\n\n<p>(Yes, he's familiar with the Wikipedia entry and other stuff readily accessible by a Google search, such as <a href=\"http://www.jerrydallal.com/LHSP/meta.htm\">Jerry Dallal's nice little article</a>.)</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-20T18:06:04.580000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1884", "provsql": "9f3cb6c2-7700-4669-a079-12336711478a"}, "posts_3093": {"id": 3270, "owneruserid": 776, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3278, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Interpreting 2D correspondence analysis plots", "tags": "<interpretation><correspondence-analysis><biplot>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I've been searching the internet far and wide... I have yet to find a really good overview of how to interpret 2D correspondence analysis plots. Could someone offer some advice on interpreting the distances between points? </p>\n\n<p>Perhaps an example would help, here is a plot that's found on many of the websites I've seen that discuss correspondence analysis. The red triangles represent eye colour and the black dots represent hair colour.</p>\n\n<p><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/nVOUx.jpg\" alt=\"alt text\"></p>\n\n<p>Looking at the graph above, could you make a few statements about what you see in these data. Points of interest about the different dimensions and relationships between triangles and dots? </p>\n\n<p>An explanation of row-points verses column points, and the use of the word \"profile\" with particular focus on the example would be instrumental. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-02T22:12:51.957000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3093", "provsql": "e5b83207-1c07-4466-83f8-4f8e508eddaa"}, "posts_1901": {"id": 1980, "owneruserid": 183, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Complete substantive examples of reproducible research using R", "tags": "<r><references><reproducible-research>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p><strong>The Question:</strong> Are there any good examples of <a href=\"https://reproducibleresearch.net/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">reproducible research</a> using R that are freely available online?</p>\n<p><strong>Ideal Example:</strong>\nSpecifically, ideal examples would provide:</p>\n<ul>\n<li>The raw data (and ideally meta data explaining the data),</li>\n<li>All R code including data import, processing, analyses, and output generation,</li>\n<li>Sweave or some other approach for linking the final output to the final document,</li>\n<li>All in a format that is easily downloadable and compilable on a reader's computer.</li>\n</ul>\n<p>Ideally, the example would be a journal article or a thesis where the emphasis is on an actual applied topic as opposed to a statistical teaching example.</p>\n<p><strong>Reasons for interest:</strong>\nI'm particularly interested in applied topics in journal articles and theses, because in these situations, several additional issues arise:</p>\n<ul>\n<li>Issues arise related to data cleaning and processing,</li>\n<li>Issues arise related to managing metadata,</li>\n<li>Journals and theses often have style guide expectations regarding the appearance and formatting of tables and figures,</li>\n<li>Many journals and theses often have a wide range of analyses which raise issues regarding workflow (i.e., how to sequence analyses) and processing time (e.g., issues of caching analyses, etc.).</li>\n</ul>\n<p>Seeing complete working examples could provide good instructional material for researchers starting out with reproducible research.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-21T04:58:11.600000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1901", "provsql": "c6082c68-75be-4a2c-bbb9-1a8f2efbd3cd"}, "posts_2149": {"id": 2230, "owneruserid": 1106, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2232, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Convergence in probability vs. almost sure convergence", "tags": "<probability><random-variable>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I've never really grokked the difference between these two measures of convergence. (Or, in fact, any of the different types of convergence, but I mention these two in particular because of the Weak and Strong Laws of Large Numbers.)</p>\n\n<p>Sure, I can quote the definition of each and give an example where they differ, but I still don't quite get it.</p>\n\n<p>What's a good way to understand the difference? Why is the difference important? Is there a particularly memorable example where they differ?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-31T03:57:21.193000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2149", "provsql": "309a2389-7ab6-4366-8e4a-a8e2245ffafa"}, "posts_2153": {"id": 2234, "owneruserid": 253, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2235, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Alternatives to logistic regression in R", "tags": "<r><regression><logistic><classification><predictive-models>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I would like as many algorithms that perform the same task as logistic regression.  That is  algorithms/models that can give a prediction to a binary response (Y) with some explanatory variable (X).</p>\n\n<p>I would be glad if after you name the algorithm, if you would also show how to implement it in R.  Here is a code that can be updated with other models:</p>\n\n<pre><code>set.seed(55)\nn <- 100\nx <- c(rnorm(n), 1+rnorm(n))\ny <- c(rep(0,n), rep(1,n))\nr <- glm(y~x, family=binomial)\nplot(y~x)\nabline(lm(y~x), col='red', lty=2)\nxx <- seq(min(x), max(x), length=100)\nyy <- predict(r, data.frame(x=xx), type='response')\nlines(xx, yy, col='blue', lwd=5, lty=2)\ntitle(main='Logistic regression with the \"glm\" function')\n</code></pre>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-31T10:02:07.947000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2153", "provsql": "526c4b36-f5ea-4840-b5db-0c83d0f7a9d6"}, "posts_2221": {"id": 2306, "owneruserid": 1150, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2307, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Feature selection for \"final\" model when performing cross-validation in machine learning", "tags": "<machine-learning><classification><cross-validation><feature-selection><genetics>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I am getting a bit confused about feature selection and machine learning\nand I was wondering if you could help me out.  I have a microarray dataset that is\nclassified into two groups and has 1000s of features.  My aim is to get a small number of genes (my features) (10-20) in a signature that I will in theory be able to apply to\nother datasets to optimally classify those samples.  As I do not have that many samples (<100), I am not using a test and training set but using Leave-one-out cross-validation to help\ndetermine the robustness.  I have read that one should perform feature selection for each split of the samples i.e.</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>Select one sample as the test set</li>\n<li>On the remaining samples perform feature selection</li>\n<li>Apply machine learning algorithm to remaining samples using the features selected</li>\n<li>Test whether the test set is correctly classified</li>\n<li>Go to 1.</li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>If you do this, you might get different genes each time, so how do you\nget your \"final\" optimal gene classifier? i.e. what is step 6.</p>\n\n<p>What I mean by optimal is the collection of genes that any further studies\nshould use.  For example, say I have a cancer/normal dataset and I want\nto find the top 10 genes that will classify the tumour type according to\nan SVM.  I would like to know the set of genes plus SVM parameters that\ncould be used in further experiments to see if it could be used as a\ndiagnostic test.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-02T10:25:42.330000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2221", "provsql": "8ea2a2b0-12ae-46b6-af0c-ececa452e8dc"}, "posts_2286": {"id": 2374, "owneruserid": 1154, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2375, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Factor analysis of questionnaires composed of Likert items", "tags": "<factor-analysis><scales><psychometrics><likert><psychology>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I used to analyse items from a psychometric point of view. But now I am trying to analyse other types of questions on motivation and other topics. These questions are all on Likert scales. My initial thought was to use factor analysis, because the questions are hypothesised to reflect some underlying dimensions.</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>But is factor analysis appropriate?</li>\n<li>Is it necessary to validate each question regarding its dimensionality ? </li>\n<li>Is there a problem with performing factor analysis on likert items?</li>\n<li>Are there any good papers and methods on how to conduct factor analysis on Likert and other categorical items?</li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-04T11:15:48.317000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2286", "provsql": "1ac9f93d-9de8-4c4d-bd17-ac2435f77e5e"}, "posts_2392": {"id": 2493, "owneruserid": 1227, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2497, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Managing error with GPS routes (theoretical framework?)", "tags": "<error><sampling>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I'm looking for the appropriate theoretical framework or speciality to help me deal with understanding how to deal with the errors that the GPS system has - especially when dealing with routes.</p>\n<p>Fundamentally, I'm looking for the requirements on the data and any algorithms to use to be able to establish the length of a trail. The answer needs to be trustworthy.</p>\n<p>A friend of mine was the race director of a race which was billed as 160km but the Garmin watches everybody has makes it more like 190km+. It caused quite some grief at the finish line, let me tell you!</p>\n<p>So my friend went back to the course with various GPS devices in order to remap it and the results are interesting.</p>\n<p>Using a handheld Garmin Oregon 300 she got 33.7km for one leg. For the same leg on a wrist watch Garmin Forerunner 310xt it came out to 38.3km.</p>\n<p>When I got the data from the Oregon it was obvious that it was only recording data every 90 seconds or so. The Forerunner does it every couple of seconds.</p>\n<p>When I plotted the data from the Oregon I could see that it got confused by some switchbacks and put a line straight through them and a curve was made a little less.</p>\n<p>However, I muse that the difference in the recording frequency is much of the explanation. i.e. by recording every couple of seconds the Forerunner is closer to the real route. However, there will be an amount of error because of the way GPS works. If the points recorded are spread around the real route randomly (because of the error) then the total distance will be larger than the real route. (A wiggle line going either side of a straight line is longer than the straight line).</p>\n<p>So, my questions: 1. Are there any techniques I can use on a single dataset to reduce the error in a valid way? 2. Does my theory about the difference in recording frequency hold water? 3. If I have multiple recordings of the same routes are there any valid techniques to combine them to get closer to the real route?</p>\n<p>As I say, I don't really know what to search for to find any useful science about this. I'm looking for ways to establish just how long a given piece of trail is and it is very important to people. An extra 30km in a race is an extra 5+ hours we weren't expecting.</p>\n<p>As requested here is some sample data:\n<img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/GZGCh.jpg\" alt=\"Summary image\" /></p>\n<p><a href=\"https://web.archive.org/web/20151008094933/https://s3.amazonaws.com/trailhunger-stackexchange/trapper-lake-detailed.csv\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Detailed high-frequency sample data</a></p>\n<p><a href=\"https://web.archive.org/web/20151011123503/https://s3.amazonaws.com/trailhunger-stackexchange/trapper-lake-low-sample.csv\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Low-frequency sample data</a></p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-08T19:48:42.110000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2392", "provsql": "bc83cec6-73d0-46b9-a4e9-68098531d7e1"}, "posts_3119": {"id": 3294, "owneruserid": 1495, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Resources for learning Markov chain and hidden Markov models", "tags": "<references><markov-process><hidden-markov-model><bioinformatics>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am looking for resources (tutorials, textbooks, webcast, etc) to learn about Markov Chain and HMMs. My background is as a biologist, and I'm currently involved in a bioinformatics-related project. </p>\n\n<p>Also, what are the necessary mathematical background I need to have a sufficient understanding of Markov models & HMMs?</p>\n\n<p>I've been looking around using Google but, so far I have yet to find a good introductory tutorial. But what if I don't care about unbiasedness and linearity?", "tags": "<regression><unbiased-estimator>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>The Gauss-Markov theorem tells us that the OLS estimator is the best linear unbiased estimator for the linear regression model. </p>\n\n<p>But suppose I don't care about linearity and unbiasedness. Then is there some other (possible nonlinear/biased) estimator for the linear regression model which is the most efficient under the Gauss-Markov assumptions or some other general set of assumptions?</p>\n\n<p>There is of course one standard result: OLS itself is the best unbiased estimator if in addition to the Gauss-Markov assumptions we also assume that the errors are normally distributed. For some other particular distribution of errors I could compute the corresponding maximum-likelihood estimator.</p>\n\n<p>But I was wondering if there is some estimator which is better-than-OLS in some relatively general set of circumstances?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-22T01:15:49.873000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2806", "provsql": "10400973-f692-49f9-9743-4106ce6aa2c5"}, "posts_2876": {"id": 3038, "owneruserid": 183, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to test hypothesis of no group differences?", "tags": "<hypothesis-testing><t-test><equivalence><tost>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Imagine you have a study with two groups (e.g., males and females) looking at a numeric dependent variable (e.g., intelligence test scores) and you have the hypothesis that there are no group differences.</p>\n\n<p><strong>Question:</strong></p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>What is a good way to test whether there are no group differences?</li>\n<li>How would you determine the sample size needed to adequately test for no group differences?</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p><strong>Initial Thoughts:</strong> </p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>It would not be enough to do a standard t-test because a failure to reject the null hypothesis does not mean that the parameter of interest is equal or close to zero; this is particularly the case with small samples.</li>\n<li>I could look at the 95% confidence interval and check that all values are within a sufficiently small range; perhaps plus or minus 0.3 standard deviations.</li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-24T05:24:00.240000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2876", "provsql": "b2d8ee15-574c-4da8-b5dd-25180b656ed1"}, "posts_2899": {"id": 3062, "owneruserid": 1417, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How do we find concordance between two sets of non-linear, non-monotonic data", "tags": "<correlation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Is there a statistical procedure that can measure the concordance between two sets of data that have, say, a sinusoidal tendency?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-24T19:09:28.577000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2899", "provsql": "1d0a5732-187a-4b64-aa84-f0977d90ce85"}, "posts_3143": {"id": 3331, "owneruserid": 179, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3363, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Is it possible to do time-series clustering based on curve shape?", "tags": "<r><time-series><clustering>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I have sales data for a series of outlets, and want to categorise them based on the shape of their curves over time. But, typing:</p>\n\n<pre><code>install.packages(\"~/Documents/R.classes_0.62.tar.gz\", CRAN=NULL)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Gives </p>\n\n<pre><code>Error in do_install(pkg) : \n  this seems to be a bundle -- and they are defunct\nWarning message:\nIn install.packages(\"~/Documents/R.classes_0.62.tar.gz\",  :\n  installation of package '~/Documents/R.classes_0.62.tar.gz' had non-zero exit status\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>How to get thru ? </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-22T14:08:01.243000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3684", "provsql": "e93fec51-5132-43b9-882c-e881410c9a45"}, "posts_4476": {"id": 4756, "owneruserid": null, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": "Oleg", "title": "Confidence interval for Bernoulli sampling", "tags": "<confidence-interval><binomial-distribution><bernoulli-distribution><faq>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I have a random sample of Bernoulli random variables $X_1 ... X_N$, where $X_i$ are i.i.d. r.v. and $P(X_i = 1) = p$, and $p$ is an unknown parameter.</p>\n\n<p>Obviously, one can find an estimate for $p$: $\\hat{p}:=(X_1+\\dots+X_N)/N$.</p>\n\n<p>My question is how can I build a confidence interval for $p$?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-11-20T12:05:26.533000", "posts_rownum": "posts_4476", "provsql": "4e06b4d4-caf2-4ffd-acb8-c1325d043068"}, "posts_3704": {"id": 3911, "owneruserid": 1393, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "When are confidence intervals useful?", "tags": "<confidence-interval><interpretation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>If I understand correctly a confidence interval of a parameter is an interval constructed by a <em>method</em> which yields intervals containing the true value for a specified proportion of samples. So the 'confidence' is about the method rather than the interval I compute from a particular sample. </p>\n\n<p>As a user of statistics I have always felt cheated by this since the space of all samples is hypothetical. All I have is one sample and I want to know what that sample tells me about a parameter.</p>\n\n<p>Is this judgement wrong? Are there ways of looking at confidence intervals, at least in some circumstances, which would be meaningful to users of statistics?</p>\n\n<p>[This question arises from second thoughts after dissing confidence intervals in a math.se answer <a href=\"https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/7564/calculating-a-sample-size-based-on-a-confidence-level/7572#7572\">https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/7564/calculating-a-sample-size-based-on-a-confidence-level/7572#7572</a> ]</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-23T07:48:41.417000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3704", "provsql": "af182210-daf0-44d0-b302-a10d5b231f0c"}, "posts_3739": {"id": 3947, "owneruserid": 1224, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3954, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Help me understand Support Vector Machines", "tags": "<machine-learning><classification><svm>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I understand the basics of what a Support Vector Machines' aim is in terms of classifying an input set into several different classes, but what I don't understand is some of the nitty-gritty details. For starters, I'm a bit confused by the use of Slack Variables. What is their purpose?</p>\n\n<p>I'm doing a classification problem where I've captured pressure readings from sensors I've placed on the insole of a shoe. A subject will sit, stand, and walk for a couple of minutes while pressure data is recorded. I want to train a classifier to be able to determine whether a person is sitting, standing or walking and be able to do that for any future test data. What classifier type do I need to try? What is the best way for me to train a classifier from the data I've captured? I have 1000 entries for sitting, standing and walking (3x1000=3000 total), and they all have the following feature vector form. (pressurefromsensor1, pressurefromsensor2, pressurefromsensor3, pressurefromsensor4)</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-24T15:11:52.427000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3739", "provsql": "a4a6f4a4-fe79-4a61-8e95-9440132025d5"}, "posts_3802": {"id": 4023, "owneruserid": 1727, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Chi-square test for equality of distributions: how many zeroes does it tolerate?", "tags": "<distributions><chi-squared-test><contingency-tables>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I am comparing two groups of mutants each of which can have only one out of 21 different phenotypes. I would like to see whether distribution of these outcomes is similar between two groups. I found an <a href=\"http://www.fon.hum.uva.nl/Service/Statistics/EqualDistribX2.html\">online test</a> \n that calculates the \"Chi-square test for equality of distributions\" and gives me some plausible results. However, I have quite a few zeroes in this Table, so can I use chi-square in this case at all? </p>\n\n<p>Here is the table with two groups and counts of particular phenotypes:</p>\n\n<pre><code>2 1\n2 3\n1 6\n1 4\n13 77\n7 27\n0 1\n0 4\n0 2\n2 7\n2 3\n1 5\n1 9\n2 6\n0 3\n3 0\n1 3\n0 3\n1 0\n1 2\n0 1\n</code></pre>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-27T14:39:11.707000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3802", "provsql": "7d9549a1-40a1-48df-95da-326c4d5e0fc0"}, "posts_3938": {"id": 4175, "owneruserid": 1614, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 4324, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Resampling, binomial, z- and t-test: help with real data", "tags": "<r><hypothesis-testing>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I am trying to understand how I can use resampling techniques to compliment my pre-planned analyses. This is not homework. I have a 5 sided die. 30 subjects call a number (1-5) and then roll the die. If it matches it's a hit, if not it's a miss. Each subject does this 25 times. </p>\n\n<p>N is the the number of trials (=25) and p is the probability of getting it correct (=.2) then the population value (mu) of the mean number correct is n*p=5. The population standard deviation, sigma, is square-root(n*p*[1-p]), which is 2.</p>\n\n<p>The experimental hypothesis (H1) is that subjects in this study will score above chance (above mu). The null hypothesis (H0) assumes a binomial distribution for each subject (they will score at mu).</p>\n\n<p>[<em>Please don't get too worried about why I am doing this. If it helps you to understand the problem then you can think of it as an ESP test (and therefore I am testing the ability of subjects to score above mu). Also if it helps, imagine that the task is a virtual reality die throwing task, where the virtual 5-sided die performs according to chance. There can be no bias from an imperfect die because the die is virtual.</em>]</p>\n\n<p>Okay. So before I conducted the \"experiment\" I had planned to compare the 30 subjects score with a one-sample t-test (comparing it to the null that mu=5). Then I discovered that the one-sample z-test was a more powerful test given what we know about the null hypothesis. Okay.</p>\n\n<p>Here is a simulation of my data in R:</p>\n\n<pre><code>binom.samp1 <- as.data.frame(matrix(rbinom(30*1, size=25, prob=0.2), ncol=1))\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Now R has a binom.test function, which gives the p-value regarding the number of successes over the number of trials. For my collected data (not the simulated data given):</p>\n\n<pre><code>>binom.test(174, 750, 1/5, alternative=\"g\")\nnumber of successes = 174, number of trials = 750, p-value = 0.01722\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Now the one-sample t-test that I had originally planned to use (mainly because I'd never heard of the alternatives - should've paid more attention in higher statistics):</p>\n\n<pre><code>>t.test(binom.samp1-5, alternative=\"g\")\nt = 1.7647, df = 29, p-value = 0.04407\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>and for completedness sake: the one-sample z-test (<a href=\"http://rgm2.lab.nig.ac.jp/RGM2/R_man-2.9.0/library/BSDA/man/z.test.html\" rel=\"nofollow\">BSDA package</a>):</p>\n\n<pre><code>>z.test(binom.samp1, mu=5, sigma.x=2, alternative=\"g\")\nz = 2.1909, p-value = 0.01423\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>So. My first question is, <strong>am I right in concluding that the <a href=\"http://sekhon.berkeley.edu/stats/html/binom.test.html\" rel=\"nofollow\">binom.test</a> is the correct test given the data and hypothesis?</strong> In other words, does <em>t</em> approximate to <em>z</em> which approximates to the exact binom.test (<a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernoulli_trial\" rel=\"nofollow\">Bernoulli trial</a>)?</p>\n\n<p>Now my second question relates to the resampling methods. I have several books by Philip Good and I've read plenty on permutation and bootstrapping. I was just going to use the one-sample permutation test given in the <a href=\"http://pbil.univ-lyon1.fr/library/DAAG/html/onet.permutation.html\" rel=\"nofollow\">DAAG</a> package:</p>\n\n<pre><code>>onet.permutation(binom.samp1-5)\n0.114\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>And the perm.test function in the <a href=\"http://www.stat.ucl.ac.be/ISdidactique/Rhelp/library/exactRankTests/html/perm.test.html\" rel=\"nofollow\">exactRankTests</a> package gives this:</p>\n\n<pre><code>>perm.test(binom.samp1, mu=5, alternative=\"g\", exact=TRUE)\nT = 42, p-value = 0.05113\n</code></pre>\n\n<p><strong>I have the feeling that what I want to do is conduct a one-sample permutation binom.test.</strong> The only way I can see it working is if I take a subset of the 30 subjects and calculate the binom.test and then repeat it for a large number of N. <strong>Does this sound like a reasonable idea?</strong></p>\n\n<p>Finally, I did repeat this experiment with the same equipment (the 5 sided die) but a larger sample size (50 people) and I got exactly what I expected. My understanding is that the two studies are like a <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bean_machine\" rel=\"nofollow\">Galton box</a> that hasn't filled up yet. The 30 n experiment has a bit of a skew, but had it been run for longer it would have filled up to the binomial. <strong>Is this all gibberish?</strong></p>\n\n<pre><code>>binom.test(231, 1250, 1/5, alternative=\"g\")\nnumber of successes = 231, number of trials = 1250, p-value = 0.917\n\n>t.test(binom.samp2-5)\nt = -1.2249, df = 49, p-value = 0.2265\n\n>z.test(binom.samp2, mu=5, sigma.x=2)\nz = -1.3435, p-value = 0.1791\n\n>onet.permutation(binom.samp2-5)\n0.237\n\n>perm.test(binom.samp2, mu=5, alternative=\"g\", exact=TRUE)\nT = 35, p-value = 0.8991\n</code></pre>\n", "creationdate": "2010-11-03T15:07:30.070000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3938", "provsql": "ccb276e0-fe20-44c5-b944-3623b73814e2"}, "posts_3975": {"id": 4220, "owneruserid": 226, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 4223, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Can a probability distribution value exceeding 1 be OK?", "tags": "<probability><distributions><normal-distribution><density-function><faq>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>On the <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naive_Bayes_classifier#Testing\">Wikipedia page about naive Bayes classifiers</a>, there is this line: </p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>$p(\\mathrm{height}|\\mathrm{male}) = 1.5789$ (A probability distribution over 1 is OK. the gain in explained variance thanks to the correlation of Y and X?", "tags": "<r><data-visualization><regression><correlation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm searching how to to the mean)</p>\n\n<p>Here is an example of such a visualization:\n<img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/Pe2ul.png\" alt=\"alt text\"></p>\n\n<p>And the R code to produce =mean(y), col = 2, lwd = 2)\n\nplot(c(residuals(lm(y~x)) + mean(y))~rep(1, length(y)), axes = F, xlab = \"\", ylab = \"\", ylim = range(y))\npoints(1,mean(y), col = 2, pch = 19, cex = 2)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Which leads me to my question: I would appreciate any <strong>suggestions on how this graph can be enhanced</strong> (either with text, marks, or any other type of relevant visualizations). Adding relevant R code will also be nice.</p>\n\n<p>One direction is to add some information of the R^2 (either by text, or by somehow adding lines presenting the magnitude of the variance before and after the introduction of x)\nAnother option is to highlight one point and showing how it is \"better explained\" thanks to the regression line.  Any input will be appreciated.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-01-15T06:36:34.710000", "posts_rownum": "posts_5900", "provsql": "43b43daf-20cc-4057-8ab0-daa8c014a5e2"}, "posts_5935": {"id": 6304, "owneruserid": 795, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 6307, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What is the sum of squared t variates?", "tags": "<central-limit-theorem><t-distribution><chi-squared-distribution><sums-of-squares>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Let $t_i$ be drawn i.i.d from a Student t distribution with $n$ degrees of freedom, for moderately sized $n$ (say less than 100). The forecast package for R contains a lot of useful functions, but one thing it doesn't do is any kind of data transformation before running auto.arima().  In some cases forecast pro decides to log transform data before doing forecasts, but I haven't yet figured out why.</p>\n\n<p>So my question is: when should I log-transform my time series before trying ARIMA methods on it?</p>\n\n<p>/edit: after reading your answers, I'm going to use something like this, where x is my time series:</p>\n\n<pre><code>library(lmtest)\nif ((gqtest(x~1)$p.value < 0.10) {\n    x<-log(x)\n}\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Does this make sense?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-01-18T02:50:01.373000", "posts_rownum": "posts_5961", "provsql": "245875f2-a0e4-4906-ac53-2e44048276c6"}, "posts_6111": {"id": 6481, "owneruserid": 588, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 6510, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Consequence of ignoring the order of a categorical variable with different levels in logistic regression", "tags": "<logistic><ordinal-data>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>As the title suggests, I am hesitating on whether to use ordinal logistic regression or not. Thanks.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-01-31T08:43:05.747000", "posts_rownum": "posts_6354", "provsql": "8c71d080-3ab1-4993-8f25-15d41e9fda75"}, "posts_6700": {"id": 7155, "owneruserid": 1347, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 7158, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Rigorous definition of an outlier?", "tags": "<outliers><definition>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>People often talk about dealing with outliers in statistics.  The thing that bothers me about this is that, as far as I can tell, the definition of an outlier is completely subjective.  For example, if the true distribution of some random variable is very heavy-tailed or bimodal, any standard visualization or summary statistic for detecting outliers will incorrectly remove parts of the distribution you want to sample from.  What is a rigorous definition of an outlier, if one exists, and how can outliers be dealt with without introducing unreasonable amounts of subjectivity into an analysis?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-02-13T15:07:40.937000", "posts_rownum": "posts_6700", "provsql": "257e6596-1a05-4dca-a3bd-6e6fcfb20fbf"}, "posts_6747": {"id": 7208, "owneruserid": 1205, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 7338, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Can one use Cohen's Kappa for two judgements only?", "tags": "<reliability><information-retrieval>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I am using <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen%27s_kappa\" rel=\"nofollow\">Cohen's Kappa</a> to calculate the inter-agreement between two judges.</p>\n\n<p>It is calculated as:</p>\n\n<p>$ \\frac{P(A) - P(E)}{1 - P(E)}  $</p>\n\n<p>where $P(A)$ is the proportion of agreement and $P(E)$ the probability of agreement by chance.</p>\n\n<p>Now for the following dataset, I get the expected results:</p>\n\n<pre><code>User A judgements: \n  - 1, true\n  - 2, false\nUser B judgements: \n  - 1, false\n  - 2, false\nProportion agreed: 0.5\nAgreement by chance: 0.625\nKappa for User A and B: -0.3333333333333333\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>We can see that both judges have not agreed very well. However in the following case where both judges evaluate one criteria, kappa evaluates to zero:</p>\n\n<pre><code>User A judgements: \n  - 1, false\nUser B judgements: \n  - 1, false\nProportion agreed: 1.0\nAgreement by chance: 1.0\nKappa for User A and B: 0\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Now I can see that the agreement by chance is obviously 1, which leads to kappa being zero, but does this count as a reliable result? The problem is that I normally don't have more than two judgements per criteria, so these will all never evaluate to any kappa greater than 0, which I think is not very representative.</p>\n\n<p>Am I right with my calculations? Can I use a different method to calculate inter-agreement?</p>\n\n<p>Here we can see that kappa works fine for multiple judgements:</p>\n\n<pre><code>User A judgements: \n  - 1, false\n  - 2, true\n  - 3, false\n  - 4, false\n  - 5, true\nUser A judgements: \n  - 1, true\n  - 2, true\n  - 3, false\n  - 4, true\n  - 5, false\nProportion agreed: 0.4\nAgreement by chance: 0.5\nKappa for User A and B: -0.19999999999999996\n</code></pre>\n", "creationdate": "2011-02-14T17:16:52.580000", "posts_rownum": "posts_6747", "provsql": "c83e9066-d13e-44a5-94f6-91a0b1a4e48a"}, "posts_6931": {"id": 7402, "owneruserid": null, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 7404, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": "user3062", "title": "How do I find the probability of a type II error?", "tags": "<probability><statistical-power><type-i-and-ii-errors>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I know that a Type II error is where H1 is true, but H0 is not rejected. </p>\n\n<h3>Question</h3>\n\n<p>How do I calculate the probability of a Type II error involving a normal distribution, where the standard deviation is known?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-02-19T20:56:08.153000", "posts_rownum": "posts_6931", "provsql": "15392415-6d1f-487a-b6c7-3b24ba74febd"}, "posts_7050": {"id": 7542, "owneruserid": 3342, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to perform goodness of fit test and how  to assign probability with uniform distribution?", "tags": "<distributions><chi-squared-test><goodness-of-fit><uniform-distribution>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I have to demonstrate that a generator of VoIP calls generates calls uniformly distributed between callers.\nIn particular the distribution is the uniform (min, max) one where the volume per caller distribution is uniformly distributed between a minimum and maximum. So by running a test with 10000 users and a min value equal to 30 calls per week and a max value equal to 90 calls/week i obtain that not all the users respect this limits.</p>\n\n<p>The situation is depicted in figure:</p>\n\n<p>The few users that generate <30 or >90 calls spoil the chi-square goodness of fit test and I don't know how can i proceed with a goodness of fit test. Most of the values is within the interval (and from these we obtain low chi-square value), but the few out-of-range values spoil the final chi-square calculation.</p>\n\n<p>In your opinion what is the best way to operate? What should I do with the \"out-of-range\"values? Thank you.</p>\n\n<p>PS: the chi-square goodness-of-fit test performed is reported in the following figure:\n<img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/ulmcI.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></p>\n\n<p>where still I don't know what to do with the out-of-range values. </p>\n\n<p><strong>UPDATE</strong></p>\n\n<p>after talking with people linked with the project we concluded that the generator does not satisfy the uniform distribution. We have to do a theoretic analysis of what we expect really to be the distribution at the end of the generation based on the inputs.</p>\n\n<p>This means that I have to do it!\nMore details: \nThe generator assigns a \"probability\" between 0 and 1 to the callers (with a particular method, that probably is the problem). Then it generates a random value from 0 to 1 and it finds the associated user and assigns the call to him.</p>\n\n<p>The generator generates calls for a week with the constant rate equal to 1 call per second, this means that it generates ca. 604800 total calls.</p>\n\n<p>My goal is to distribute the callers between the min and max number of calls in a week. For example if I have 10000 users and the min limit is equal to 30 calls per week and max = 90 calls per week I should obtain something about:</p>\n\n<p>30 calls : 163 users.</p>\n\n<p>31 calls : 163 users.</p>\n\n<p>....</p>\n\n<p>90 calls : 163 users.</p>\n\n<p>So 163 users generate 30 calls in a week..etc, etc and finally 163 users generate 90 calls in a week. How should I assign the probability to callers in order that the generator distributes the callers uniformly between the range 30-90?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-02-23T16:03:54.663000", "posts_rownum": "posts_7050", "provsql": "0d2b5fb0-11cb-4228-becf-b23df2ab8b2e"}, "posts_7218": {"id": 7727, "owneruserid": 3479, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to correlate two time series with gaps and different time bases?", "tags": "<time-series><correlation><unevenly-spaced-time-series>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I asked <a href=\"https://stackoverflow.com/questions/5130808/how-to-correlate-two-time-series-with-gaps-and-different-time-bases\"><strong>this question</strong></a> over on StackOverflow, and was recommended to ask it here. </p>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p>I have two time series of 3D accelerometer data that have different time bases (clocks started at different times, with some very slight creep during the sampling time), as well as containing many gaps of different size (due to delays associated with writing to separate flash devices).</p>\n\n<p>The accelerometers I'm using are the inexpensive <a href=\"http://www.gcdataconcepts.com/x250-2.html\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">GCDC X250-2</a>.  I'm running the accelerometers at their highest gain, so the data has a significant noise floor.</p>\n\n<p>The time series each have about 2 million data points (over an hour at 512 samples/sec), and contain about 500 events of interest, where a typical event spans 100-150 samples (200-300 ms each).  Many of these events are affected by data outages during flash writes.</p>\n\n<p>So, the data isn't pristine, and isn't even very pretty.  But my eyeball inspection shows it clearly contains the information I'm interested in.  (I can post plots, if needed.)</p>\n\n<p>The accelerometers are in similar environments but are only moderately coupled, meaning that I can tell by eye which events match from each accelerometer, but I have been unsuccessful so far doing so in software.  Due to physical limitations, the devices are also mounted in different orientations, where the axes don't match, but they are as close to orthogonal as I could make them.  So, for example, for 3-axis accelerometers A & B, +Ax maps to -By (up-down), +Az maps to -Bx (left-right), and +Ay maps to -Bz (front-back).</p>\n\n<p>My initial goal is to correlate shock events on the vertical axis, though I would eventually like to a) automatically discover the axis mapping, b) correlate activity on the mapped aces, and c) extract behavior differences between the two accelerometers (such as twisting or flexing).</p>\n\n<p>The nature of the time series data makes Python's numpy.correlate() unusable.  I've also looked at R's Zoo package, but have made no headway with it.  I've looked to different fields of signal analysis for help, but I've made no progress.</p>\n\n<p>Anyone have any clues for what I can do, or approaches I should research?</p>\n\n<p>Update 28 Feb 2011: Added some plots <a href=\"https://picasaweb.google.com/FlyMyPG/VibData?authkey=Gv1sRgCLPo0u-7jafQjwE#\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><strong>here</strong></a> showing examples of the data.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-03-01T01:13:29.410000", "posts_rownum": "posts_7218", "provsql": "c9752676-ecd3-4c92-be07-4f4a700ab30e"}, "posts_7254": {"id": 7772, "owneruserid": 3499, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 7819, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Is it possible to fit a multivariate regression model where the independent variable is latent?", "tags": "<regression><multivariate-analysis><latent-variable>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I'm trying to fit a multivariate multiple regression model where the independent variable X is latent but I don't know where to start (I have prior information about the coefficient matrix so I can use some iterative method).</p>\n\n<p>The dependent variable Y is a NxM matrix denoting N observations each from M variables. The latent variable X is a NxP matrix about which we know nothing except the dimensions. In addition to these, we have an initial estimate of the coefficient matrix beta based on prior knowledge. My goal is to find the estimates of latent X and coefficient matrix beta by both using the data matrix Y and the initial coefficient matrix. I thought of constructing an EM algorithm but because of the complexity of multivariate data and latent variable concept, I am totally confused.</p>\n\n<p>Thank you.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-03-02T03:05:21.403000", "posts_rownum": "posts_7254", "provsql": "d6dd4138-23f8-4228-ad0e-eb21339e7863"}, "posts_7650": {"id": 8196, "owneruserid": 3725, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Why is the null hypothesis always a point value rather than a range in hypothesis testing?", "tags": "<hypothesis-testing>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>This is somewhat related to <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/8192/hypothesis-test-for-whether-correlation-coefficient-is-greater-than-specified-val\">another question</a> that I asked. The question I have is, when doing hypothesis testing, when the alternative hypothesis is a range, the null hypothesis is still a point value.<br/> As an example, when  testing whether a correlation coefficient is greater than 0.5, the null hypothesis is \"correlation = 0.5\" instead of \"correlation <= 0.5\". Why is this the case? (or have I got it wrong?)</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-03-12T09:27:27.410000", "posts_rownum": "posts_7650", "provsql": "1a0f194e-c768-47e3-b80f-144a084d3e4a"}, "posts_7682": {"id": 8232, "owneruserid": 3725, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What is an example of a chi-squared distribution?", "tags": "<chi-squared-distribution>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p><br>\nI'm trying to figure out the usage of the $\\chi^2$ distribution. In other words, in what kind of situations it occurs and how is it useful in that situations.<br>\nI read the wikipedia definition of $\\chi^2$. Can someone give an example of a $\\chi^2$ distribution so that I can better understand it?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-03-13T13:17:04.273000", "posts_rownum": "posts_7682", "provsql": "7d6cb94f-6acc-4fb6-9683-4c04656e6097"}, "posts_7744": {"id": 8300, "owneruserid": null, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": "user3720", "title": "Correlation analysis and correcting $p$-values for multiple testing", "tags": "<correlation><multiple-comparisons><permutation-test>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am investigating the effect of a drug on EEG and cognition in epilepsy patients.\nWe have done EEG and neuropsychological (NP) tests twice, before and after medical treatment.\nSome of parameters in EEG and NP tests were significantly altered after drug treatment (done by Wilcoxon rank sum test, as the distribution was not normal).</p>\n\n<p>Now, I would like to calculate correlation between change in EEG parameters and change in NP tests.\nThere are 7 parameters in EEG parameters and 27 in NP tests. I would like to run correlation analysis on every pair and see if any pair is significantly correlated.</p>\n\n<p>My questions are:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li><p>Should I use nonparametric correlation, say Spearman, to calculate $\\rho$? (as values of EEG and NP paramaters are not normal)</p></li>\n<li><p>Since there are 7 parameters in EEG and 27 parameters in NP tests, there should be 7*27 number of testing, which requires correction of p value for multiple comparisons. Which method should I use? </p></li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>I am looking for not-so-conservative method. I have seen from another posting that I can use permutation test for multiple comparisons. Could someone explain how I can do this?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-03-15T06:59:28.983000", "posts_rownum": "posts_7744", "provsql": "1b3e3de7-1f16-4d1a-bf76-d7cd36ccf036"}, "posts_7852": {"id": 8419, "owneruserid": 3681, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 8434, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Bayesian classifier with multivariate normal densities", "tags": "<machine-learning><naive-bayes>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Supposing a Bayesian classifier with multivariate normal densities, how do I find the error rate of the classifier when we have two classes?</p>\n\n<p>I am using this:</p>\n\n<p>When dimension $d = 1$:</p>\n\n<p>$$P(x | \\mu , \\sigma^2) = N(x, \\mu, \\sigma^2) = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi \\sigma^2}} e^{-\\frac{(x-\\mu)^2}{2\\sigma^2}} $$</p>\n\n<p>In $d$ dimensions:</p>\n\n<p>$$P(x | \\mu, \\Sigma) = \\frac{1}{(2\\pi)^{d/2} |\\Sigma|^{1/2}} \\cdot e^{-\\frac{1}{2}{(x-μ)^T\\Sigma^{-1}(x-μ)}}$$</p>\n\n<p>where $\\mu$ is in $\\mathbb{R}^d$ and $\\Sigma$ is a $d \\times d$ variance-covariance matrix.</p>\n\n<p>What would be the algebra to get the error rate, or could you give an example? I would like to do this in <code>Matlab</code>.</p>\n\n<p>Lets say I have 2 classes and 2 atributes with 20 examples:</p>\n\n<pre><code>features:\n    1.8756    1.4236\n    2.0677    1.3759\n    0.8540    0.7782\n    0.5651   -0.3511\n    0.6103   -0.6901\n   -0.1945    1.6438\n   -0.2620    0.8022\n    1.5326    0.0188\n    0.3334    1.0578\n    0.8535   -1.8545\n    0.3066    1.9716\n   -1.4424    0.4216\n    0.3275   -0.2844\n   -0.0079    2.8506\n    0.0114    1.4001\n   -0.4049   -0.3981\n   -0.0913    2.2094\n    0.3376   -1.0467\n    0.3455    2.4960\n    0.3232   -0.5614\n\n\nand targets\n\n     2\n     2\n     1\n     1\n     1\n     2\n     1\n     1\n     2\n     1\n     2\n     1\n     1\n     2\n     2\n     1\n     2\n     1\n     2\n     1\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>What is the process to classify them and get the error rate of this examples, so we divide the set in 15 examples for training and the other 5 for testing?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-03-17T17:18:25.883000", "posts_rownum": "posts_7852", "provsql": "4192ef0f-4952-44b0-9a22-ef5bf5d2e39f"}, "posts_7931": {"id": 8502, "owneruserid": 3491, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 8684, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Combining 2 sets of coefficients, weighting one of the sets", "tags": "<time-series><multivariate-analysis><predictive-models>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I have two sets of coefficients from similar data taken at different times.  What I want to do is combine the two sets of coefficients giving greater weight to the more most recent set.</p>\n\n<p>The goal is building a predictive model.  So say I have dataset A from 2009, and dataset B from 2010.</p>\n\n<p>My coefficients for A are:</p>\n\n<pre><code>param1: 0.33\nparam2: 1.224\nparam3: -0.119\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>My coefficients for B are:</p>\n\n<pre><code>param1: 0.42\nparam2: 1.309\nparam3: -0.011\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>If I wanted B to be considered twice as important, would it be sound to use a formula like this:</p>\n\n<pre><code>(2*B + A) / 3 = New Coeeficient\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>And do that for each parameter?  Or am I suggesting something that is fundamentally flawed?</p>\n\n<p>In general could one combine coefficients effectively using the basic forumula:</p>\n\n<pre><code>(Weight * DatasetACoeffcient + DatasetBCoeffient) / (Weight + 1)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p><strong>Edit</strong>\nThis is a multivariate linear regression problem where the datasets may not be available when someone decides something like this needs to be done.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-03-19T16:32:07.477000", "posts_rownum": "posts_7931", "provsql": "0c9a8411-943e-41da-abf6-16962cc4a242"}, "posts_8121": {"id": 8718, "owneruserid": 3883, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Comparing logistic regression coefficients across models?", "tags": "<regression><logistic><spss><regression-coefficients>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I've developed a logit model to be applied to six different sets of cross-sectional data. What I'm trying to uncover is whether there are changes in the substantive effect of a given independent variable (IV) on the dependent variable (DV) controlling for other explanations at different times and across time.</p>\n<p>My questions are:</p>\n<ul>\n<li><p>How do I assess increased / decreased size in the association between the IV and DV?</p>\n</li>\n<li><p>Can I simply look at the different magnitudes (sizes) of the coefficients across the models or do I need to go through some other process?</p>\n</li>\n<li><p>If I need to do something else, what is it and can it be done/how do I do it in SPSS?</p>\n<p>Also, within a single model,</p>\n</li>\n<li><p>Can I compare the relative size of independent variables based on unstandardised scores if all are coded 0-1 or do I need to convert them to standardised scores?</p>\n</li>\n<li><p>Are there problems involved with standardised scores?</p>\n</li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2011-03-24T09:06:46.867000", "posts_rownum": "posts_8121", "provsql": "85d08907-a9ee-42c1-86da-3402e97804c0"}, "posts_8785": {"id": 9464, "owneruserid": 4127, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 9466, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Can someone give me details about a particular confidence interval formula?", "tags": "<confidence-interval><binomial-distribution>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm trying to fully understand the confidence interval formal given on <a href=\"http://www.iro.umontreal.ca/~lisa/twiki/bin/view.cgi/Public/DeepVsShallowComparisonICML2007#Results\" rel=\"nofollow\">this site</a>:</p>\n\n<p>$$\\hat{\\mu}\\pm z_{1-\\alpha/2}\\sqrt{\\frac{\\hat{\\mu}(1-\\hat{\\mu})}{n}}$$</p>\n\n<p>so I can reproduce the same type of intervals for my own data.  But I don't quite understand what the parameters such as $\\alpha$ and $Z$ mean.  I'm guessing they're related to defining a 95% confidence interval if your data were distributed normally.</p>\n\n<p>Can explain to me how that formula works or a reference I can find a description of the formula used?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-04-12T06:54:42.497000", "posts_rownum": "posts_8785", "provsql": "3b9f9c1b-5829-4157-9838-86af7572a0f7"}, "posts_8236": {"id": 8844, "owneruserid": 3919, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 8860, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Discrete functions: Confidence interval coverage?", "tags": "<confidence-interval><discrete-data>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>How to calculate discrete interval coverage?</p>\n\n<p>What I know how to do: </p>\n\n<p>If I had a continuous model, I could define a 95% confidence interval for each of my predicted values, and then see how often the actual values were within the confidence interval.
